passages.original: quod si hoc Lucilius, qui primus condidit stili nasum, dicendum sibi putavit, Cicero mutuandum, praesertim cum de re publica scriberet, quanto nos causatius ab aliquo iudice defendimur? sed haec ego mihi nunc patrocinia ademi nuncupatione, quoniam plurimum refert, sortiatur aliquis iudicem an eligat, multumque apparatus interest 'apud invitatum hospitem et oblatum. cum apud Catonem, ilium ambitus hostem et repulsis tamquam honoribus inemptis gaudentem, flagrantibus comitiis pecunias deponerent candidati, hoc se facere, quod tum pro innocentia ex rebus humanis summum esset, profitebantur.
passages.english: But if Lucilius, who first established the satirical nose of the pen, thought he had to say this, and Cicero to borrow it, especially when he was writing on the state, how much more reason do we have to be defended against some judge? But I have now taken these protections away from myself by the dedication, since it makes a great difference whether someone gets a judge by lot or chooses him, and there is a great difference in preparation between a host who has been invited and one who has offered himself. When the candidates, at the height of a heated election, deposited sums of money with Cato, that enemy of electoral bribery who rejoiced in his defeats as though they were honours not bought, they declared that they were doing this as the highest thing then possible in human affairs on behalf of integrity.
passages.notes: 'stili nasum' (the 'nose' of the pen, i.e. satirical sneer) is idiomatic. 'causatius' is an uncertain reading; rendered as 'with more reason'. 'ilium' read as 'illum'. The sense of 'apud invitatum hospitem et oblatum' is somewhat obscure.

passages.original: at cum intraveris, di deaeque, quam nihil in medio invenies! nostri graviores Antiquitatium, Exemplorum Artiumque , facetissimi Lucubrationum, puto quia Bibaculus erat et vocabatur paulo minus asserit Varro in satiris suis Sesculixe et Flextabula apud Graecos desiit nugari Diodorus et βιβλιοθήκης historiam suam inscripsit. Apion quidem grammaticus -hic quem Tiberius Caesar cymbalum mundi vocabat, cum propriae famae tympanum potius videri posset—immortalitate donari a se scripsit ad quos aliqua componebat.
passages.english: But once you have gone inside, gods and goddesses, how little you will find in the middle! Our more serious writers [use titles like] Antiquities, Examples and Arts; the wittiest, Lucubrations, I suppose because [the author] was Bibaculus and was called so. Varro makes a little less of a claim in his satires Sesculixes and Flextabula. Among the Greeks, Diodorus stopped trifling and titled his history Library. Apion the grammarian indeed (the man whom Tiberius Caesar used to call the cymbal of the world, though he might rather have seemed the drum of his own fame) wrote that those to whom he addressed any of his compositions were presented by him with immortality.
passages.notes: The sentence about the Roman titles is elliptical and the text around 'puto quia Bibaculus erat et vocabatur' is likely corrupt; the joke turns on 'Bibaculus' (little drinker) and lamp-lit 'lucubrations' (night work, with drinking). 'Sesculixe' (One-and-a-half Ulysses) and 'Flextabula' are titles of Varro's Menippean satires; the sense of 'paulo minus asserit' is uncertain.

passages.original: ceu vero nesciam adversus Theophrastum, hominem in eloquentia tantum, ut nomen divinum inde invenerit, scripsisse etiam feminam, et proverbium inde natum suspendio arborem eligendi. non queo mihi temperare quo minus ad hoc pertinentia ipsa censorii Catonis verba ponam, ut appareat etiam Catoni de militari disciplina commentanti, qui sub Africano, immo vero et sub Hannibale didicisset militare et ne Africanum quidem ferre potuisset, qui imperator triumphum reportasset, paratos fuisse istos, qui obtrectatione alienae scientiae famam sibi aucupantur: Quid enim?
passages.english: As if indeed I did not know that even a woman wrote against Theophrastus, a man so great in eloquence that he got his divine name from it, and that from this arose the proverb about choosing a tree to hang oneself on. I cannot restrain myself from setting down the very words of Cato the Censor that bear on this, so that it may be clear that even against Cato, when he wrote on military discipline, a man who had learned soldiering under Africanus, and indeed under Hannibal too, and who could not bear even Africanus, who as commander had won a triumph, those people stood ready who hunt for reputation for themselves by disparaging the knowledge of others: "What then?
passages.notes: Theophrastus' name was taken to mean 'divine speaker'. The woman is not named here.

passages.original: quisquis est deus, si modo est alius, et quacumque in parte, totus est sensus, totus visus , totus auditus, totus animae, totus animi, totus sui. innumeros quidem credere atque etiam ex vitiis hominum, ut Pudicitiam , Concordiam, Mentem, Spem, Honorem, Clementiam, Fidem, aut, ut Democrito placuit, duos omnino, Poenam et Beneficium, maiorem ad socordiam accedit. fragilis et laboriosa mortalitas in partes ita digessit infirmitatis suae 15 memor, ut portionibus coleret quisque quo maxime indigeret.
passages.english: Whoever god is, if indeed there is any other, and in whatever part [he is], he is wholly sense, wholly sight, wholly hearing, wholly soul, wholly mind, wholly himself. To believe in countless [gods], and even ones drawn from human vices [and virtues], such as Chastity, Concord, Mind, Hope, Honour, Clemency, Faith, or, as Democritus held, in just two, Punishment and Benefit, comes to an even greater folly. Frail and toiling mortality, mindful of its own weakness, has divided [the deity] into parts in such a way that each person might worship in portions what he most needed.
passages.notes: 'ex vitiis' is odd since the list gives virtues; some read 'ex virtutibus' or similar. Stray numeral '15' omitted. 'si modo est alius' (if there is any other [than the sun]) refers to preceding discussion.

passages.original: Sed Pythagoras interdum et musica ratione appellat tonum quantum absit a terra luna, ab ea ad Mercurium dimidium spatii et ab eo ad Veneris, a quo ad solem sescuplum, a sole ad Martem tonum [id est quantum ad lunam a terra], ab eo ad Iovem dimidium et ab eo ad Saturni, et inde sescuplum ad signiferum;
passages.english: But Pythagoras sometimes also, on a musical principle, calls the distance of the moon from the earth a tone; from it to Mercury half that interval, and from him to Venus [the same]; from her to the sun one and a half [tones]; from the sun to Mars a tone [that is, as much as from the earth to the moon]; from him to Jupiter a half, and from him to Saturn [the same]; and from there one and a half to the zodiac;
passages.notes: 'Sescuplum' (one and a half times) is here taken as a tone and a half. The bracketed gloss 'id est quantum ad lunam a terra' is bracketed in the edition, probably as an interpolation.

passages.original: Moventur autem aliae errantium modo, aliae inmobiles haerent, omnes ferme sub ipso septentrione aliqua eius parte non certa, sed maxime in candida, quae lactei circuli nomen accepit. Aristoteles tradit et simul plures cerni, nemini conpertum alteri, quod equidem sciam, ventos autem ab iis graves aestusve significari. fiunt et hibernis mensibus et in austrino polo, sed ibi citra ullum iubar.
passages.english: Some of them move in the manner of the planets, others stay fixed and motionless. Almost all are under the north itself, in no fixed part of it, but especially in the white [region] which has received the name of the Milky Circle. Aristotle records that several are also seen at once, something no one else has found, so far as I know; and that they signify heavy winds or heats. They also occur in the winter months and at the southern pole, but there without any radiance.
passages.notes: The subject (comets) is implied from the wider context.

passages.original: praeterea Nepos Cornelius auctor est Eudoxum quendam sua aetate, cum Lathyrum regem fugeret, Arabico sinu egressum Gades usque pervectum, multoque ante eum Caelius Antipater vidisse se qui navigasset ex Hispania in Aethiopiam commercii gratia. idem Nepos de septentrionali circuitu tradit Quinto Metello Celeri, Afrani in consulatu collegae, sed tum Galliae proconsuli, Indos a rege Sueborum dono datos, qui ex India commercii causa navigantes tempestatibus essent in Germaniam abrepti. sic maria circumfusa undique dividuo globo partem orbis auferunt nobis, nec inde huc nec hinc illo pervio tractu.
passages.english: Besides this, Cornelius Nepos records that a certain Eudoxus in his own time, while fleeing King Lathyrus, set out from the Arabian Gulf and was carried all the way to Gades; and long before him Caelius Antipater [records] that he had seen a man who had sailed from Spain to Ethiopia for the sake of trade. The same Nepos reports, concerning the northern circuit, that Quintus Metellus Celer, colleague of Afranius in the consulship but at that time proconsul of Gaul, was given as a gift by the king of the Suebi some Indians, who while sailing from India for trade had been swept away by storms into Germany. So the seas poured round on every side of the globe, which they divide, take away part of the world from us, there being no passable route either from there to here or from here to there.

passages.original: et tota Trogodytice umbras bis quadrag enis quinis diebus in anno Eratosthenes in contrarium cadere prodidit.
passages.english: And Eratosthenes reported that in the whole of Trogodytice shadows fall in the opposite direction on twice forty-five days in the year.
passages.notes: 'quadrag enis' read as 'quadragenis'.

passages.original: similiter in Megalopolitanorum agro. nam si intermisit ille iucundus frondemque densi supra se nemoris non adurens et iuxta gelidum fontem semper ardens Nymphaei crater, dira Apolloniatis suis portendit, ut Theopompus tradidit; augetur imbribus egeritque bitumen temperandum fonte illo ingustabili, et alias omni bitumine dilutius. sed quis haec miretur? in medio mari Hiera et Lipara insulae Aeoliae iuxta Italiam cum ipso mari arsere per aliquot dies sociali bello, donec legatio senatus piavit.
passages.english: Similarly in the territory of the Megalopolitans. For if that pleasant crater of the Nymphaeum ceases [to burn], which does not scorch the foliage of the dense grove above it and burns perpetually beside a cold spring, it portends dire things to its people of Apollonia, as Theopompus reported; it is increased by rains and throws out bitumen, which has to be mixed with that undrinkable spring, and which is in other respects more fluid than any bitumen. But who would wonder at these things? In the middle of the sea, Hiera and Lipara, Aeolian islands near Italy, burned together with the sea itself for several days during the Social War, until a delegation of the senate made expiation.

passages.original: in principio est Ostia colonia ab Romano rege deducta, oppidum Laurentum, lucus Iovis Indigetis, amnis Numicius, Ardea a Danaë Persei matre condita. dein quondam Aphrodisium, Antium colonia, Astura flumen et insula, fluvius Nymphaeus, Clostra Romana, Cercei, quondam insula inmenso quidem mari circumdata, ut creditur Homero , et nunc planitie. mirum est quod hac de re tradere hominum notitiae possumus. Theophrastus, qui primus externorum aliqua de Romanis diligentius scripsit —nam Theopompus, ante quem nemo mentionem habuit, urbem dumtaxat a Gallis captam dixit, Clitarchus, ab eo proximus, legationem tantum ad Alexandrum missam— hic iam plus quam ex fama Cerceiorum insulae et mensuram posuit stadia LXXX in eo volumine, quod scripsit Nicodoro Atheniensium magistratu, qui fuit urbis nostrae CCCCXL anno.
passages.english: At the beginning is Ostia, a colony founded by a Roman king; the town of Laurentum; the grove of Jupiter Indiges; the river Numicius; Ardea, founded by Danaë, the mother of Perseus. Then the former Aphrodisium; the colony of Antium; the river and island Astura; the river Nymphaeus; the Clostra Romana; Circeii, once an island surrounded by the vast sea, as Homer is believed [to say], and now by a plain. It is remarkable what we can hand on to human knowledge on this matter. Theophrastus, who was the first foreigner to write anything about the Romans with some care (for Theopompus, before whom no one made mention [of them], said only that the city had been captured by the Gauls, and Clitarchus, next after him, only that an embassy had been sent to Alexander), this man, going beyond mere report, gave even the measurement of the island of Circeii as 80 stadia, in the volume which he wrote in the archonship of Nicodorus at Athens, which was the 440th year of our city.
passages.notes: 'ut creditur Homero' could also mean 'if we believe Homer'.

passages.original: mox Gallicum ante Narbonensem provinciam; hinc Ligusticum; ab eo ad Siciliam insulam Tuscum, quod ex Graecis alii Notium, alii Tyrrenum, e nostris plurimi Inferum vocant. ultra Siciliam quod est ad sallentinos, Ausonium Polybius appellat, Eratosthenes autem inter ostium oceani et Sardiniam quicquid est Sardoum , inde ad Siciliam Tyrrenum, ab hac Cretam usque Siculum, ab ea Creticum.
passages.english: Next the Gallic [sea] before the province of Narbonensis; after that the Ligurian; from it to the island of Sicily the Tuscan, which some of the Greeks call the Notian, others the Tyrrhenian, and most of our people the Lower Sea. What lies beyond Sicily as far as the Sallentini Polybius calls the Ausonian; but Eratosthenes [calls] whatever is between the mouth of the Ocean and Sardinia the Sardinian, from there to Sicily the Tyrrhenian, from this as far as Crete the Sicilian, and beyond it the Cretan.

passages.original: at ex alia parte Anio, in monte Trebanorum ortus, lacus tris amoenitate nobiles, qui nomen dedere Sublaqueo, defert in Tiberim. in agro Reatino Cutiliae lacum, in quo fluctuetur insula, Italiae umbilicum esse M. Varro tradit. infra Sabinos Latium est, a latere Picenum, a tergo Vmbria, Appennini iugis Sabinos utrimque vallantibus.
passages.english: But on the other side the Anio, rising in the mountain of the Trebani, carries down into the Tiber three lakes famous for their beauty, which gave their name to Sublaqueum. In the territory of Reate, M. Varro records that the lake of Cutiliae, on which an island floats, is the navel of Italy. Below the Sabines is Latium, on their flank Picenum, behind them Umbria, with the ridges of the Apennines walling in the Sabines on both sides.

passages.original: oppida Vibi Forum, Segusio, coloniae ab Alpium radicibus Augusta Taurinorum — inde navigabili Pado — antiqua Ligurum stirpe, dein Salassorum Augusta Praetoria iuxta geminas Alpium fores, Graias atque Poeninas — his Poenos, Grais Herculem transisse memorant —, oppidum Eporedia Sibyllinis a populo Romano conditum iussis. eporedias Galli bonos equorum domitores vocant. Vercellae Libiciorum ex Salluis ortae, Novaria ex Vertamocoris , Vocontiorum hodieque pago, non, ut Cato existimat, Ligurum, ex quibus Laevi et Marici condidere Ticinum non procul a Pado, sicut Boi Transalpibus profecti Laudem Pompeiam, Insubres Mediolanum. Oromobiorum stirpis esse Comum atque Bergomum et Licini Forum aliquotque circa populos auctor est Cato, sed originem gentis ignorare se fatetur, quam docet Cornelius Alexander ortam a graecia interpretatione etiam nomiuis vitam in montibus degentium.
passages.english: The towns are Forum Vibii and Segusio; the colonies at the foot of the Alps are Augusta Taurinorum (from there the Po is navigable), of ancient Ligurian stock, then Augusta Praetoria of the Salassi, beside the twin gateways of the Alps, the Graian and the Poenine (they say the Carthaginians crossed by the latter, Hercules by the Graian); and the town of Eporedia, founded by the Roman people on the orders of the Sibylline Books. The Gauls call good horse-tamers *eporediae*. Vercellae arose from the Libicii, [descended] from the Sallui; Novaria from the Vertamocori, a canton of the Vocontii to this day, not, as Cato thinks, of the Ligurians; from these the Laevi and Marici founded Ticinum not far from the Po, just as the Boii, setting out from beyond the Alps, [founded] Laus Pompeia, and the Insubres Mediolanum. Cato states that Comum, Bergomum, Forum Licinii and some peoples around them are of the stock of the Orumbovii, but he admits that he does not know the origin of the people; Cornelius Alexander teaches that it arose from Greece, also from the interpretation of their name, [meaning] 'those who spend their life in the mountains'.
passages.notes: 'nomiuis' read as 'nominis'. The last clause is compressed and its construction uncertain.

passages.original: Arsiae gens Liburnorum iungitur usque ad flumen Titium. pars eius fuere Mentores, Himani, Encheleae, Bulini et quos Callimachus Peucetios appellat, nunc totum uno nomine Illyricum vocatur generatim. populorum pauca effatu digna aut facilia nomina. conventum Scardonitanum petunt lapudes et Liburnorum civitates XIIII, ex quibus Lacinienses, Stulpinos, Burnistas, Olbonen- ses nominare non pigeat.
passages.english: Adjoining the Arsia is the people of the Liburni, as far as the river Titius. Part of it were the Mentores, Himani, Encheleae, Buli and those whom Callimachus calls Peucetii; now the whole is called by the single general name Illyricum. Few of the peoples' names are worth mentioning or easy to pronounce. The Iapydes and fourteen states of the Liburni resort to the assize-district of Scardona; of these it would not be tiresome to name the Lacinienses, the Stulpini, the Burnistae and the Olbonenses.
passages.notes: 'Bulini' rendered Buli? Kept as Bulini would also be possible; 'lapudes' read as 'Iapudes'.

passages.original: Extra eam in Myrtoo multae, sed maxime inlustres Glauconnesos et Aegilia et a promunturio Geraesto circa Delum in orbem sitae, unde et nomen traxere, Cyclades . prima earum Andrus cum oppido abest a Geraesto X???, a Ceo XXXVIII. ipsam Myrsilus Cauron, deinde Antandron cognominatam tradit, Callimachus Lasiam, alii Nonagriam, Hydrusam, Epagrim; patet circuitu LXXXXIII. ab eadem Andro passus mille et a Delo XV Tenos cum oppido in XV porrecta, quam propter aquarum abundantiam Aristoteles Hydrusam appellatam ait, aliqui Ophiusam . ceterae Myconus cum monte Dimasto a Delo XV, Siphnus, ante Meropia et Acis appellata, circuitu XXVIII, Seriphus XV Prepesinthus, Cythnos ipsaque longe clarissima et Cycladum media ac templo Apollinis et mercatu celebrata Delos, quae diu fluctuata, ut proditur, sola motum terrae non sensit ad M.
passages.english: Outside it, in the Myrtoan Sea, are many [islands], but the most famous are Glauconnesos and Aegilia, and, from the promontory of Geraestus, those set in a circle around Delos, from which they also took their name, the Cyclades. The first of them, Andros, with a town, is [...] miles from Geraestus and 38 from Ceos. Myrsilus records that it was called Cauros, then Antandros; Callimachus [calls it] Lasia, others Nonagria, Hydrusa, Epagris; its circuit is 93 miles. A mile from this same Andros and 15 from Delos is Tenos, with a town, extending 15 miles, which Aristotle says was called Hydrusa because of its abundance of water, some Ophiusa. The others are Myconos with Mount Dimastus, 15 miles from Delos; Siphnos, formerly called Meropia and Acis, 28 miles in circuit; Seriphos, 15; Prepesinthus; Cythnos; and Delos itself, by far the most famous and in the middle of the Cyclades, renowned for its temple of Apollo and its trade, which, after floating for a long time, as is related, alone felt no earthquake up to the time of Marcus
passages.notes: A numeral in the distance of Andros from Geraestus is illegible ('X???'). The sentence continues into the following passage (Marcus Varro's age).

passages.original: Gyara cum oppido, circuitu XV p., abest ab Andro LXII, ab ea Syrnos LXXX, Cynethus, Telos unguento nobilis, a Callimacho Agathusa appellata, Don usa, Patmus circuitu XXX, Corassiae, Lebinthus, Gyrus, Cinara, Sicinus quae antea Oenoe, Heraclia quae Onus, Casos quae Astrabe, Cimolos quae Echinusa, Melos cum oppido, quam Aristides Mimblida appellat, Aristoteles Zephyriam, Callimachus Mimallida, Heraclides Siphin et Acytan; haec insularum rotundissima est. Buporthmos, Machia, Hypere, quondam Patage, ut alii, Platage, nunc Amorgos, Polyaegas, Sapyle, Thera, cum primum emersit, Calliste dicta.
passages.english: Gyara, with a town, 15 miles in circuit, is 62 miles from Andros; from it Syrnos is 80; Cynethus; Telos, famous for its unguent, called Agathusa by Callimachus; Donusa; Patmos, 30 miles in circuit; the Corassiae; Lebinthus; Gyrus; Cinara; Sicinus, formerly Oenoe; Heraclia, formerly Onus; Casos, formerly Astrabe; Cimolos, formerly Echinusa; Melos, with a town, which Aristides calls Mimblis, Aristotle Zephyria, Callimachus Mimallis, Heraclides Siphis and Acytos; this is the roundest of the islands. Buporthmos; Machia; Hypere, once Patage or, according to others, Platage, now Amorgos; Polyaegas; Sapyle; Thera, called Calliste when it first emerged.
passages.notes: 'Don usa' read as Donusa.

passages.original: inde Abdera continentis XXII, Athos LXII.D, tantundem insula Samothrace libera ante Hebrum, ab Imbro XXXII, a Lemno XXII.D p., a Thraciae ora XXXVIII; circuitur XXXV, attollitur monte Saoce X??? p. altitudinis, vel inportuosissima omnium. Callimachus eam antiquo nomine Dardaniam vocat. inter Cherronesum et Samothracen, utrimque fere XV, Halonesos, ultra Gethone, Lamponia, Alopeconnesus haud procula Coelo, Cherronesi portu, et quaedam ignobiles. desertis quoque reddantur in hoc sinu quarum modo inveniri potuere nomina: Avesticos, Sarnos, Cissyros, Charbrusa, Calathusa, Scyllia, Dialeon, Dictaea, Melanthia, Dracanon, Arconesos, Diethusa, Ascapos, Capheris, Mesate, Aeantion, Pateronnesos, Pateria, Calathe, Neriphus, Pelendos.
passages.english: Then Abdera on the mainland is 22 miles away, Athos 62.5, and the same distance the island of Samothrace, free, off the Hebrus, 32 from Imbros, 22.5 from Lemnos, 38 from the coast of Thrace; its circuit is 35 miles; it rises with Mount Saoce, [...] miles high, and is the most harbourless of all. Callimachus calls it by its ancient name Dardania. Between the Chersonese and Samothrace, about 15 miles from each, is Halonesos; beyond it Gethone, Lamponia, Alopeconnesus not far from Coelos, a port of the Chersonese, and some obscure ones. Let the uninhabited islands in this gulf also be listed, of which only the names could be found: Avesticos, Sarnos, Cissyros, Charbrusa, Calathusa, Scyllia, Dialeon, Dictaea, Melanthia, Dracanon, Arconesos, Diethusa, Ascapos, Capheris, Mesate, Aeantion, Pateronnesos, Pateria, Calathe, Neriphus, Pelendos.
passages.notes: The height of Saoce is partly illegible ('X???'). 'circuitur' read as 'circuitu'; 'procula' as 'procul a'.

passages.original: ab Minio, quem supra diximus, CC, ut auctor est Varro, abest Aeminius, quem alibi quidam intellegunt et Limaeam vocant, Oblivionis antiquis dictus multumque fabulosus, ab Durio Tagus CC interveniente Munda. Tagus auriferis harenis celebratur. ab eo CLX promunturium Sacrum e media prope Hispaniae fronte prosilit. |XIIII| inde ad Pyrenaeum medium colligi Varro tradit, ad Anam vero, quo Lusitaniam a Baetica discrevimus , CXXVI, a Gadibus CII additis. gentes Celtici Turduli et circa Tagum Vettones, ab Ana ad Sacrum Lusitani. oppida a Tago memorabilia in ora Olisipo, equarum e favonio vento conceptu nobile, Salacia cognominata Vrbs Imperatoria, Merobrica.
passages.english: From the Minius, which we mentioned above, 200 [miles] away, as Varro states, is the Aeminius, which some locate elsewhere and call the Limaea; it was called by the ancients [the river] of Forgetfulness and is the subject of many fables. From the Durius the Tagus is 200 away, with the Munda between. The Tagus is celebrated for its gold-bearing sands. 160 from it the Sacred Promontory juts out from almost the middle of Spain's front. From there to the middle of the Pyrenees Varro records the total as 1,400, but to the Anas, by which we have separated Lusitania from Baetica, 126, with 102 added from Gades. The peoples are the Celtici, the Turduli and around the Tagus the Vettones; from the Anas to the Sacred [Promontory] the Lusitani. Notable towns on the coast from the Tagus are Olisipo, famous for mares conceiving from the west wind; Salacia, surnamed Urbs Imperatoria; Merobrica.
passages.notes: Distances presumably in Roman miles. '|XIIII|' read as 1,400 (the bars indicating hundreds); numeral uncertain.

passages.original: Ex adverso Celtiberiae conplures sunt insulae, Cassiterides dictae Graecis a fertilitate plumbi, et e regione Arrotrebarum promunturi Deorum VI, quas aliqui Fortunatas appellavere. in ipso vero capite Baeticae ab ostio freti p. XXV Gadis, longa, ut Polybius scribit, XII, lata III. abest a continente proxima parte minus pedes DCC, reliqua plus VII. ipsius spatium XV est. habet oppidum civium Romanorum, qui appellantur Augustani Vrbe Iulia Gaditana. ab eo latere, quo Hispaniam spectat, passibus fere C altera insula est, longa M passus, M lata, in qua prius oppidum Gadium fuit.
passages.english: Opposite Celtiberia are a number of islands, called the Cassiterides by the Greeks from their abundance of tin, and, facing the promontory of the Arrotrebae, the six [islands] of the Gods, which some have called the Fortunate. But at the very head of Baetica, 25 miles from the mouth of the strait, is Gades, 12 miles long, as Polybius writes, and 3 wide. It is less than 700 feet from the mainland at the nearest point, more than 7 miles elsewhere. Its area is 15 [miles]. It has a town of Roman citizens, who are called the Augustani of the City of Julia Gaditana. On the side facing Spain, about 100 paces away, is another island, a mile long and a mile wide, on which the town of Gades formerly was.
passages.notes: 'plumbum' here means tin (plumbum album). The reading 'longa M passus, M lata' is doubtful.

passages.original: Tertius sinus dividitur in geminos, duarum Syrtium vadoso ac reciproco mari diros . ad proximnam, quae minor est, a Carthagine CCC Polybius tradit, ipsam centum milium passuum aditu, trecentorum ambitu.et terra autem siderum observatione ad eam per deserta .... harenis perque serpentes iter est. excipiunt saltus repleti ferarum multitudine et introrsus elephantorum solitudines, mox deserta vasta ultraque Garamantes, ab Augilis dierum XII itinere distantes.
passages.english: The third gulf is divided into two, dreadful for the shallow, ebbing and flowing sea of the two Syrtes. To the nearer, which is the smaller, Polybius records 300 miles from Carthage; it itself has a mouth of 100 miles and a circuit of 300. And by land too the way to it lies through deserts [...] by observation of the stars, through sands and through serpents. Next come forests full of a multitude of wild beasts, and further inland the wildernesses of elephants, then vast deserts, and beyond them the Garamantes, twelve days' journey distant from the Augilae.
passages.notes: There is a lacuna in the text ('....'); the phrase about observing the stars is incomplete. 'proximnam' read as 'proximam'.

passages.original: super eos Aethiopum gentes Nigritae a quo dictum est filumine, Gymnetes Pharusi, iam oceanum attingentes quos in Mauretaniae fine diximus Perorsi. ab his omnibus vastae solitudines orientem versus usque ad Garamantas Augilasque et Trogodytas, verissima opinione eorum, qui desertis Africae duas Aethiopias superponunt, et ante omnes Homeri, qui bipertitos tradit Aethiopas, ad orientem occasumque versos. Nigri fluvio eadem natura quae Nilo. calamum ac papyrum et easdem gignit animantes isdemque temporibus augescit. oritur inter Tarraelios Aethiopas et Oechalicas.
passages.english: Above them are the Ethiopian peoples: the Nigritae, from whom the river is named; the Gymnetes Pharusi; and, now reaching the ocean, the Perorsi, whom we mentioned at the border of Mauretania. From all these, vast wildernesses [stretch] eastward as far as the Garamantes, the Augilae and the Trogodytae, according to the very true opinion of those who place two Ethiopias beyond the deserts of Africa, and above all of Homer, who records that the Ethiopians are divided in two, turned towards the east and the west. The river Nigris has the same nature as the Nile. It produces reed and papyrus and the same animals, and it rises at the same seasons. It rises between the Tarraelian Ethiopians and the Oechalicae.
passages.notes: 'filumine' read as 'flumine'. 'Augescit' and 'oritur' both rendered 'rises' in different senses (swells / has its source).

passages.original: Incipit crescere luna nova, quaecumque post solstitium est, sensim modiceque cancrum sole transeunte, abundantissime autem leonem, et residit in virgine isdem quibus adcrevit modis. in totum autem revocatur intra ripas in libra, ut tradit Herodotus, centesimo die. cum crescit, reges aut praefectos navigare eo nefas iudicatum est. auctus per puteos mensurae notis deprehenduntur. Iustum incrementum est cubitorum XVI. minores aquae non omnia rigant, ampliores detinent tardius recedendo.
passages.english: It begins to rise at the new moon, whichever [new moon] comes after the solstice, gradually and moderately while the sun is passing through the Crab, but most abundantly [while it passes through] the Lion, and it subsides in the Virgin in the same manner in which it rose. It is entirely withdrawn within its banks in the Balance, as Herodotus reports, on the hundredth day. While it is rising, it has been judged unlawful for kings or governors to sail on it. Its increases are detected by marks of measurement in wells. The proper rise is sixteen cubits. Lesser waters do not irrigate everything; greater ones hold [the land] back by receding too slowly.
passages.notes: The subject is the Nile, named earlier in the text.

passages.original: Ex Asia interisse gentes tradit Eratosthenes Solymorum , Lelegum, Bebrycum, Colycantiorum, Tripsedorum, Isidorus Arieneos et Capreatas, ubi sit Apamea condita a Seleuco rege inter Ciliciam, Cappadociam, Cataoniam, Armeniam, et quoniam ferocissimas gentes domuisset, initio Dameam vocatam.
passages.english: Eratosthenes records that from Asia there have perished the peoples of the Solymi, Leleges, Bebryces, Colycantii, Tripsedi; Isidorus [records] the Arienei and Capreatae, where Apamea is situated, founded by King Seleucus between Cilicia, Cappadocia, Cataonia and Armenia, and called at first Damea because he had subdued very fierce peoples.
passages.notes: 'Damea' evidently from Greek damaō, 'tame'. Some of the tribal names cannot be identified.

passages.original: Sed pulcherrima est libera Rhodos, circuitu CXXV aut, si potius Isidoro credimus, CIII, habitata urbibus Lindo, Camiro, Ialyso, nunc Rhodo. distat ab Alexandria Aegypti DLXXXIII, ut Isidorus tradit, ut Eratosthenes, CCCCLXVIIII, ut Mucianus D???, a Cypro CLXXVI. vocitata est antea Ophiusa, Asteria, Aethria, Trinacrie, Corymbia, Poeeessa, Atabyria ab rege, dein Macaria et Oloessa. Rhodiorum insulae Carpathus, quae mari nomen dedit, Casos, Hagne, Eulimna, Nisyros, distans a Cnido XV.D, Porphyris antea dicta, et eodem tractu media inter Rhodum Cnidumque Syme;
passages.english: But the most beautiful is free Rhodes, 125 miles in circuit or, if we prefer to believe Isidorus, 103, inhabited with the cities of Lindus, Camirus and Ialysus, and now Rhodes. It is distant from Alexandria in Egypt 583 [miles], as Isidorus records; as Eratosthenes [records], 469; as Mucianus, 500; from Cyprus 176. It was formerly called Ophiusa, Asteria, Aethria, Trinacrie, Corymbia, Poeeessa, Atabyria from a king, then Macaria and Oloessa. The islands of the Rhodians are Carpathus, which gave its name to the sea, Casos, Hagne, Eulimna, Nisyros, 15½ miles distant from Cnidus, formerly called Porphyris, and in the same stretch, midway between Rhodes and Cnidus, Syme;
passages.notes: The figure for Mucianus is damaged in the text ("D???"); only 500 is legible, and further numerals may be lost. "Poeeessa" is transmitted as given; the form is uncertain.

passages.original: Ioniae ora Aegeas et Corseas habet et Icaron, de qua dictum est, Laden, quae prius Late vocabatur, atque inter ignobiles aliquot duas Camelitas Mileto vicinas, Mycalae Trogilias tres, Philion, Argennon, Sandalion, Samon liberam, circuitu LXXXVII.D aut, ut Isidorus, C???. Partheniam primum appellatam Aristoteles tradit, postea Dryusam, deinde Anthemusam; Aristocritus adicit Melamphyllum, dein Cyparissiam, alii Parthenoarrhusam, Stephanen. amnes in ea Imbrasus, Chesius, Hibiethes, fontes Gigartho, Leucothea, mons Cercetius.
passages.english: The coast of Ionia has Aegeae and Corseae and Icaros, of which [we have] spoken, Lade, which was formerly called Late, and, among several obscure ones, the two Camelitae near Miletus, the three Trogiliae of Mycale, Philion, Argennon, Sandalion, and Samos, a free [state], 87.5 miles in circuit, or, according to Isidorus, 100 [...]. Aristotle reports that it was first called Parthenia, afterwards Dryusa, then Anthemusa; Aristocritus adds Melamphyllus, then Cyparissia; others [call it] Parthenoarrhusa, Stephane. Its rivers are the Imbrasus, Chesius, Hibiethes; its springs Gigartho and Leucothea; its mountain Cercetius.
passages.notes: Isidorus' figure is damaged in the text ("C???"); only "100" is legible.

passages.original: mox oppida Placia, Ariace, Scylace, quorum a tergo mons Olympus, Mysius dictus, civitas Olympena, amnes Horisius et Rhyndacus, ante Lycus vocatus; oritur in stagno Artynia iuxta Miletopolim, recipit Maceston et plerosque alios, Asiam Bithyniamque disterminans . ea appellata est Cronia, dein Thessalis, dein Malianda et Strymonis. hos Homerus Halizonas dixit, quando praecingitur gens mari. urbs fuit inmensa Atussa nomine, nunc sunt XII civitates, inter quas Gordiu Come, quae Iuliopolis vocatur. in ora Dascylos, dein flumen Gelbes et intus Helgas oppidum, quae Germanicopolis, alio nomine Booscoete, sicut Apamea, quae nunc Myrlea Colophoniorum, flumen Echeleos, anticus Troadis finis et Mysiae initium.
passages.english: Next the towns of Placia, Ariace, Scylace, behind which is Mount Olympus, called Mysian, the city of Olympena, the rivers Horisius and Rhyndacus, formerly called the Lycus; it rises in Lake Artynia near Miletopolis, receives the Macestus and very many others, and divides Asia from Bithynia. This [land] was called Cronia, then Thessalis, then Malianda and Strymonis. Homer called these people the Halizones, since the nation is girded by the sea. There was a huge city named Atussa; now there are twelve communities, among them Gordiu Come, which is called Juliopolis. On the coast is Dascylos, then the river Gelbes, and inland the town of Helgas, which is Germanicopolis, by another name Booscoete, as also Apamea, which is now [called] Myrlea of the Colophonians; the river Echeleos, the ancient boundary of the Troad and beginning of Mysia.
passages.notes: The passage appears to conflate or dislocate material (the Bithynia description sits abruptly after the Rhyndacus); text may be disordered here.

passages.original: Nam et inrumpit e Scythico oceano in aversa Asiae; pluribus nominibus accolaram appellatum celeberrimum est duobus, Caspium et Hyrcanium. non minus hoc esse quam Pontum Euxinum Clitarchus putat, Eratosthenes ponit et mensuram ab exortu et meridie per Cadusiae et Albaniae oram V???.CCCC stadia, inde per Anariacos, Amardos, Hyrcanos ad ostium Zoni fluminis IIII. DCCC, ab eo ad ostium Iaxartis MM.CCCC, quae summa efficit XV.
passages.english: For it also bursts in from the Scythian ocean into the far side of Asia; called by many names by those who live around it, it is best known by two, the Caspian and the Hyrcanian. Clitarchus thinks it is no smaller than the Euxine Sea. Eratosthenes also gives its measurement: from the east and south along the coast of Cadusia and Albania, 5,400 stades; thence through the Anariaci, the Amardi and the Hyrcani to the mouth of the river Zonus, 4,800; from there to the mouth of the Iaxartes, 2,400; which sum makes 15,
passages.notes: The first figure is damaged ("V???.CCCC"); 5,400 is read from what survives. The total continues in the following passage ("...LXXV p."), so "15" is incomplete here.

passages.original: Sed unde plane constent gentes, Hemodi montes adsurgunt Indorumque gens incipit, non Eoo tantum mari adiacens, verum et meridiano quod Indicum appellavimus. quae pars orienti est adversa, recto praetenditur spatio ad flexum et initio Indici maris |XVIII| |LXXV| colligit, deinde quae se flexit in meridiem, XXIIII. LXXV, ut Eratosthenes tradit, usque ad Indum amnem, qui est ab occidente finis Indiae. conplures autem totam eius longitudinem XL dierum noctiumque velifico navium cursu determinavere et a septentrione ad meridiem XXVIII.
passages.english: But where the peoples are clearly established, the Hemodi mountains rise and the people of the Indians begins, bordering not only the Eastern sea but also the southern one, which we have called the Indian. The part which faces the east stretches in a straight line to the bend and at the start of the Indian sea amounts to 1,875 [miles]; then the part which turns toward the south [amounts to] 2,475, as Eratosthenes records, as far as the river Indus, which is the boundary of India on the west. Many, however, have defined its whole length as forty days and nights of sailing for ships, and from north to south 2,800
passages.notes: The vertical bars mark the edition's sign for multiplication by 100,000 or 1,000 (here thousands of paces); "|XVIII| |LXXV|" is taken as 1,875 miles. The north–south figure continues in the next passage ("L???") and is damaged, so it is incomplete.

passages.original: Onesicritus, classis eius praefectus, elephantos ibi maiores bellicosioresque quam in India gigni scripsit, Megasthenes flumine dividi, incolasque Palaeogonos appellari, auri margaritarumque grandium fertiliores quam Indos. Eratosthenes et mensuram prodidit, longitudinis VII stadium, latitudinis V???, nec urbes esse, sed vicos DCCL . incipit ab Eoo mari inter ortum occasumque solis Indiae praetenta et quondam credita XX dierum navigatione a Prasiana gente distare, mox, quia papyraceis navibus armamentisque Nili peteretur, ad nostrarum navium cursus VII dierum intervallo taxata.
passages.english: Onesicritus, the commander of his fleet, wrote that elephants are born there larger and more warlike than in India; Megasthenes [wrote] that it is divided by a river, and that its inhabitants are called Palaeogoni, more productive of gold and large pearls than the Indians. Eratosthenes also gave its measurement, 7,000 stades in length, 5,000 in breadth, and [wrote] that there are no cities but 750 villages. It begins from the Eastern sea, stretching out in front of India between the rising and setting of the sun, and it was once believed to be twenty days' sailing distant from the Prasian people; later, because it was reached by papyrus boats with the rigging of the Nile, it was assessed at an interval of seven days by the course of our ships.
passages.notes: The breadth figure is damaged ("V???"); 5,000 is read from what survives. "His fleet" refers to Alexander the Great, named in the preceding context.

passages.original: sed in duos dividitur sinus. is qui ab oriente est Persicus appellatur, |XXV| circuitu, ut Eratosthenes tradit; ex adverso est Arabia, cuius |XV| longitudo. rursus altero ambitur sinu Arabico nominato. oceanum qui influit Azanium appellant. Persicum introitu V??? latitudinis, alii IIII fecerunt. ab eo ad intimum sinum recto cursu |XI|.XXV propemodum constat esse et situm eius humani capitis effigie.
passages.english: But it is divided into two gulfs. The one on the east is called the Persian, 2,500 [miles] in circuit, as Eratosthenes records; opposite is Arabia, whose length is 1,500. It is again surrounded by the other gulf, named the Arabian. The ocean which flows in they call the Azanian. Some have made the Persian [gulf] 5 [miles] wide at its entrance, others 4. From there to the innermost gulf in a straight course it is fairly well agreed to be 1,125 [miles], and its shape [to be] the likeness of a human head.
passages.notes: The entrance width is damaged ("V???"); the figure may have been larger. Bars indicate the edition's multiplier sign; figures read as hundreds of thousands of paces.

passages.original: Simili modo et de mensura eius varia prodidere, primus Dalion ultra Meroen longe subvectus, mox Aristocreon et Bion et Basilis, Simonides minor etiam quinquennio in Meroe moratus, cum de Aethiopia scriberet. nam Timosthenes, classium Philadelphi praefectus, sine mensura dierum LX a Syene Meroen iter prodidit, Eratosthenes DCXXV, Artemidorus DC, Sebosus ab Aegypti extremis |XVI|.LXXV, unde proxime dicti |XII|.L???. verum omnis haec finita nuper disputatio est, quoniam a Syene DCCCC.LXXV Neronis exploratores renuntiavere his modis: a Syene Hieran sycaminon LIII p., inde Tama LXXII regione Euonymiton Aethiopum, Primi CXX, Acinam LXIIII, Pitaram XXV, Tergedum CVI.
passages.english: In a similar way they have also recorded various things about its measurement: first Dalion, who travelled far upstream beyond Meroe, then Aristocreon and Bion and Basilis, and Simonides the Younger, who even stayed five years in Meroe when writing about Ethiopia. For Timosthenes, commander of the fleets of Philadelphus, recorded without a measurement the journey from Syene to Meroe as sixty days; Eratosthenes [gave] 625 [miles], Artemidorus 600, Sebosus from the farthest parts of Egypt 1,675, from which those last mentioned [gave] 1,250. But all this dispute has recently been ended, since Nero's explorers reported 975 [miles] from Syene, in these stages: from Syene to Hiera Sycaminos 53 miles, thence to Tama 72, in the region of the Euonymite Ethiopians; to Primi 120, to Acina 64, to Pitara 25, to Tergedum 106.
passages.notes: The figure "|XII|.L???" is damaged; 1,250 is read from what survives. "Those last mentioned" is ambiguous in the Latin.

passages.original: ab ea V dierum praenavigatione solitudines ad Aethiopas Hesperios et promunturium quod vocavimus Hesperu Ceras, inde primum circumagente se terrarum fronte in occasum ac mare Atlanticum. contra hoc quoque promunturium Gorgades insulae narrantur, Gorgonum quondam domus, bidui navigatione distantes a continente, ut tradit Xenophon Lampsacenus. penetravit in eas Hanno Poenorum imperator prodiditque hirta feminarum corpora, viros pernicitate evasisse; duarum Gorgadum cutes argumenti et miraculi gratia in lunonis templo posuit, spectatas usque ad Carthaginem captam. ultra has etiamnum duae Hesperidum insulae narrantur, adeoque omnia circa hoc incerta sunt, ut Statius Sebosus a Gorgonum insulis praenavigatione Atlantis dierum XL ad Hesperidum insulas cursum prodiderit, ab his ad Hesperu Ceras unius. nec Mauretaniae insularum certior fama est. paucas modo constat esse ex adverso Autololum a Iuba repertas, in quibus Gaetulicam purpuram tinguere instituerat.
passages.english: From it, after a voyage of five days along the coast, [there are] deserts as far as the Western Ethiopians and the promontory that we have called Hesperu Ceras, where the face of the land first turns round toward the west and the Atlantic sea. Opposite this promontory too the Gorgades islands are said to lie, once the home of the Gorgons, two days' sail from the mainland, as Xenophon of Lampsacus reports. Hanno, the Carthaginian commander, penetrated to them and reported that the women's bodies were hairy, [and that] the men had escaped by their swiftness; he placed the skins of two Gorgades in the temple of Juno as proof and as a marvel, and they were on view until Carthage was captured. Beyond these, two islands of the Hesperides are further said to lie, and everything about this is so uncertain that Statius Sebosus has reported the course from the islands of the Gorgons to the islands of the Hesperides as a voyage of forty days along Atlas, and from these to Hesperu Ceras as one [day]. Nor is the report of the islands of Mauretania any more certain. It is agreed only that there are a few opposite the Autololes, discovered by Juba, on which he had established the dyeing of Gaetulian purple.
passages.notes: "lunonis" read as Iunonis (Juno). "Hesperu Ceras" = Western Horn.

passages.original: Sexta comprehensio, qua continetur urbs Roma, amplectitur Caspias gentes, Caucasum, septentrionalia Armeniae, Apolloniam supra Rhyndacum, Nicomediam, Nicaeam, Cal- chadonem, Byzantium, Lysimacheam, Cherronesum, Melanem sinum, Abderam, Samothraciam, Maroneam, Aenum, Bessicam, Thraciam, Maedicam, Paeoniam, Illyrios, Durrachium, Canusium, Apuliae extuma, Campaniam, Etruriam, Pisas, Lunam, Lucam, Genuam, Liguriam, Antipolim, Massiliam, Narbonem, Tarraconem, Hispaniam Tarraconensem mediam et inde per Lusitaniam. gnomoni pedes VIII, umbrae VIII. longissima diei spatia horarum aequinoctialium XV addita VIIII parte unius horae aut, ut Nigidio placuit, quinta.
passages.english: The sixth zone, in which the city of Rome is contained, embraces the Caspian peoples, the Caucasus, the northern parts of Armenia, Apollonia above the Rhyndacus, Nicomedia, Nicaea, Chalcedon, Byzantium, Lysimachea, the Chersonese, the Black Gulf, Abdera, Samothrace, Maronea, Aenus, Bessica, Thrace, Maedica, Paeonia, the Illyrians, Dyrrachium, Canusium, the farthest parts of Apulia, Campania, Etruria, Pisa, Luna, Luca, Genua, Liguria, Antipolis, Massilia, Narbo, Tarraco, the middle of Hispania Tarraconensis, and thence through Lusitania. For a gnomon of 9 feet, the shadow is 8 feet. The longest days are 15 equinoctial hours, with the addition of a ninth part of one hour or, as Nigidius held, a fifth.
passages.notes: The text reads "gnomoni pedes VIII, umbrae VIII"; equal figures make little sense, and the gnomon figure is probably corrupt (perhaps IX). It is translated here as 9.

passages.original: super hos extrema in parte montium Trispithami Pygmaeique narrantur, ternas spithamas longitudine, hoc est ternos dodrantes, non excedentes , salubri caelo semperque vernante montibus ab aquilone oppositis, quos a gruibus infestari Homerus quoque prodidit. fama est insidentes arietum caprarumque dorsis armatos sagittis veris tempore universo agmine ad mare descendere et ova pullosque earum alitum consumere; ternis expeditionem eam mensibus confici; aliter futuris gregibus non resisti. casas eorum luto pinnisque et ovorum putaminibus construi. Aristoteles in cavernis vivere Pygmaeos tradit , cetera de iis ut reliqui. Cyrnos Indorum genus Isigonus annis centenis quadragenis vivere, item Aethiopas Macrobios et Seras existimat et qui Athon montem incolant, hos quidem, quia viperinis carnibus alantur;
passages.english: Above these, in the farthest part of the mountains, the Trispithami and Pygmies are said [to live], not exceeding three spans in height, that is, three times nine inches, in a healthy climate and perpetual spring, since the mountains shield them from the north; Homer too reported that they are harassed by cranes. The story is that in springtime, mounted on the backs of rams and goats and armed with arrows, they go down to the sea in a single column and consume the eggs and chicks of those birds; that this expedition is completed in three months; [and that] otherwise they could not withstand the future flocks. Their huts are built of mud and feathers and eggshells. Aristotle reports that the Pygmies live in caves; the rest about them [he reports] as the others do. Isigonus thinks that the Cyrni, a people of India, live 140 years, and likewise the Long-lived Ethiopians and the Seres and those who inhabit Mount Athos, the last indeed because they feed on vipers' flesh;

passages.original: tu qui corporis viribus fidis, tu qui fortunae munera amplexaris et te ne alumnum quidem eius existimas, sed partum, tu cuius imperatoria est mens , tu qui te deum credis aliquo successu tumens, tanti perire potuisti! atque etiam hodie minoris potes, quantulo serpentis ictus dente aut etiam, ut Anacreon poeta, acino uvae passae, ut Fabius Senator praetor, in lactis haustu uno pilo strangulatus. is demum profecto vitam aequa lance pensitabit, qui semper fragilitatis humanae memor fuerit.
passages.english: You who trust in the strength of your body, you who embrace the gifts of fortune and think yourself not even her nursling but her offspring, you whose mind is set on command, you who believe yourself a god, swollen with some success: you could perish at so slight a cost! And even today you can [perish] at a lesser one, from the tiny tooth of a snake's bite, or even, like the poet Anacreon, from a raisin, or, like Fabius Senator, a praetor, choked by a single hair in a draught of milk. He alone, surely, will weigh life in a fair balance who is always mindful of human frailty.

passages.original: in Creta terrae motu rupto monte inventum est corpus stans XLVI cubitorum , quod alii Orionis, alii Oti esse tradunt . Orestis corpus oraculi iussu refossum VII cubitorum fuisse monumentis creditur. iam vero ante annos prope mille vates ille Homerus non cessavit minora corpora mortalium quam prisca conqueri. Naevii Pollionis amplitudinem annales non tradunt, sed quia populi concursu paene sit interemptus , vice prodigii habitum. procerissimum hominum aetas nostra Divo Claudio principe Gabbaram nomine ex Arabia advectum novem pedum et totidem unciarum vidit.
passages.english: In Crete, when a mountain was split by an earthquake, a standing body of 46 cubits was found, which some say was Orion's, others Otus'. The body of Orestes, dug up at the command of an oracle, is believed from the records to have been 7 cubits. Indeed, nearly a thousand years ago that bard Homer never ceased to lament that the bodies of mortals were smaller than those of old. The annals do not record the size of Naevius Pollio, but because he was nearly killed by the crowding of the people, it was regarded as a portent. The tallest man our age has seen was one named Gabbara, brought from Arabia in the principate of the Deified Claudius, nine feet and as many inches [tall].

passages.original: at Vinnius Valens meruit in praetorio Divi Augusti centurio, vehicula vini culleis onusta, donec exinanirentur , sustinere solitus, carpenta adprehensa una manu retinere, obnixus contra nitentibus iumentis, et alia mirifica facere, quae insculpta monumento eius spectantur.Idem M. Varro: Rusticelius , inquit, Hercules appellatus mulum suum tollebat, Fufius Salvius duo centenaria pondera pedibus, totidem manibus et ducenaria duo umeris contra scalas ferebat. nos quoque vidimus Athanatum nomine prodigiosae ostentationis quingenario thorace plumbeo indutum cothurnisque quingentum pondo calciatum per scaenam ingredi.
passages.english: But Vinnius Valens, who served as a centurion in the praetorian guard of the Deified Augustus, used to hold up carts loaded with wine-skins until they were emptied, to stop wagons by catching hold of them with one hand, straining against the draught animals pulling the other way, and to do other marvellous things, which are seen carved on his tomb. The same M. Varro says: "Rusticelius, called Hercules, used to lift his mule; Fufius Salvius carried two hundred-pound weights on his feet, as many in his hands, and two two-hundred-pound weights on his shoulders, up a ladder." We too have seen a man named Athanatus, of marvellous display, walk across the stage wearing a lead breastplate of five hundred pounds and shod in boots of five hundred pounds.
passages.notes: "Wine-skins" renders culleus, a large leather sack and also a unit of measure.

passages.original: Oculorum acies vel maxime fidem excedentia invenit exempla . in nuce inclusam Iliadem Homeri carmen in membrana scriptum tradit Cicero. idem fuisse qui pervideret CXXXV passuum. huic et nomen M. Varro reddit: Strabonem vocatum; solitum autem Punico bello a Lilybaeo Siciliae promunturio, exeunte classe e Carthaginis portu, etiam numerum navium dicere.
passages.english: Keenness of sight has found examples that most exceed belief. Cicero reports that the Iliad, Homer's poem, written on parchment, was enclosed in a nutshell. He also [reports] that there was a man who could see clearly for 135 miles. Marcus Varro also gives his name: he was called Strabo; and [says] that in the Punic War he used to tell, from Lilybaeum, the promontory of Sicily, even the number of ships as the fleet left the harbour of Carthage.
passages.notes: "CXXXV passuum" presumably for 135 thousand paces (miles).

passages.original: itaque Alexander Magnus — etenim insignibus iudiciis optime citraque invidiam tam superba censura peragetur— inter spolia Darii Persarum regis unguentornc scrinio capto, quod erat auro, margaritis gemmisque pretiosum, varios eius usus amicis demonstrantibus, quando taedebat unguenti bellatorem et militia sordidum: immo Hercule, inquit, librorum Homeri custodiae detur, ut pretiosissimum humani animi opus quam maxime diviti opere servaretur. idem Pindari vatis familiae penatibusque iussit parci, cum Thebas raperet, Aristotelis philosophi patriam suam credidit tantaeque rerum claritati tam benignum testimonium miscuit.
passages.english: So Alexander the Great (for this so lofty assessment will be best carried out, and without odium, by distinguished verdicts), when among the spoils of Darius, king of the Persians, a casket for unguents had been captured, precious with gold, pearls and gems, and his friends were pointing out its various uses, since the warrior, soiled with campaigning, had no taste for unguent, said, "No, by Hercules, let it be given to the keeping of Homer's books," so that the most precious work of the human mind might be preserved in the richest workmanship possible. He also ordered that the family and household of the poet Pindar be spared when he was sacking Thebes; he believed the native city of the philosopher Aristotle to be his own, and mingled so kindly a testimony with such great glory of his deeds.
passages.notes: "unguentornc" read as unguentorum. The last clause about Aristotle's city (Stagira) is compressed; the sense may be that he restored it as if his own.

passages.original: De spatio atque longinquitate vitae homiuum non locorum modo situs, verum ettempora ac sua cuique sors nascendi incertum fecere. Hesiodus, qui primus aliqua de hoc prodidit, fabulose, ut reor, multa hominum aevo praeferens, cornici novem nostras attribuit aetates, quadruplum eius cervis, id triplicatum corvis, et reliqua fabulosius in phoenice ac Nymphis. Anacreon poeta Arganthonio Tartesiorum regi CL tribuit annos, Cinyrae Cypriorum decem annis amplius, Aegimio CC, Theopompus Epimenidi Gnosio CLVII;
passages.english: Concerning the span and length of human life, not only the situation of places but also periods and each person's lot of birth have made [it] uncertain. Hesiod, who first reported something about this, setting many [creatures] above the lifespan of men in a fabulous way, as I think, attributed to the crow nine of our generations, four times that to deer, three times that to ravens, and the rest still more fabulously for the phoenix and the Nymphs. The poet Anacreon assigns 150 years to Arganthonius, king of the Tartessians, ten years more to Cinyras, king of the Cypriots, 200 to Aegimius; Theopompus [assigns] 157 to Epimenides of Cnossus;

passages.original: Alia mortalitatis inconstantia: Homerus eadem nocte natos Hectorem etPolydamanta tradidit , tam diversae sortis viros. C. Mario Cn. Carbone III cos. a. d. V kal. Iunias M. Caelius Rufus et C. Licinius Calvus eadem die geniti sunt, oratores quidem ambo, sed tam dispari eventu. hoc etiam isdem horis nascentibus in toto mundo cotidie evenit, pariterque domini ac servi gignuntur, reges et inopes.
passages.english: Another [instance of] the inconstancy of mortal lot: Homer reported that Hector and Polydamas, men of such different fortune, were born on the same night. In the consulship of Gaius Marius and Gnaeus Carbo (his third), on the fifth day before the Kalends of June, Marcus Caelius Rufus and Gaius Licinius Calvus were born on the same day, both orators indeed, but with such unequal outcome. This also happens every day throughout the whole world to those born at the same hours, and masters and slaves, kings and paupers, are born alike.
passages.notes: "III" refers to Carbo's third consulship (82 BC).

passages.original: In primis autem miraculo sunt summaque frequentia mortes repentinae — hoc est summa vitae felicitas —, quas esse naturales docebimus . plurimas prodidit Verrius, nos cum dilectu modum servabimus. gaudio obiere praeter Chilonem, de quo diximus, Sophocles et Dionysius Siciliae tyrannus, uterque accepto tragicae victoriae nuntio, mater illa Cannensi filio incolume viso contra nuntium falsum;
passages.english: Above all, however, sudden deaths are a marvel, and very frequent ones; this is the supreme good fortune of life, and we shall show that they are natural. Verrius has recorded a great many; we shall keep to a limit and choose with care. Died of joy: besides Chilo, of whom we have spoken, Sophocles and Dionysius the tyrant of Sicily, each on receiving news of a victory in tragedy; and that mother who saw her son safe back from Cannae after a false report [of his death];

passages.original: Baebius Tamphilus , praetura et ipse functus, cum a puero quaesisset horas, Aulus Pompeius in Capitolio, cum deos salutasset, M'. uventius Thalna consul, cum sacrificaret , C. Servilius Pansa, cum staret in foro ad tabernam hora diei secunda in P. fratrem innixus, Baebius iudex, dum vadimonium differri iubet, M. Terentius Corax, dum tabellas scribit in foro. nec non et proximo anno, dum consular viro in aurem dicit, eques Romanus ante Apollinem eboreum qui est in foro Augusti, super omnes C. lulius medicus, dum inunguit, specillum per oculum trahens, A.
passages.english: Baebius Tamphilus, who had himself also held the praetorship, when he had asked a slave boy the time; Aulus Pompeius on the Capitol, when he had greeted the gods; Manius Juventius Thalna, consul, while he was sacrificing; Gaius Servilius Pansa, while standing in the forum at a shop at the second hour of the day, leaning on his brother Publius; Baebius, a judge, while ordering a court appearance to be postponed; Marcus Terentius Corax, while writing tablets in the forum; and also last year a Roman knight, while speaking into the ear of a man of consular rank, in front of the ivory Apollo which is in the Forum of Augustus; above all Gaius Julius, a physician, while applying ointment, drawing a probe through the eye; Aulus
passages.notes: A list of sudden deaths (the verb "died" is implied from the preceding context). "uventius" read as Iuventius, "lulius" as Iulius. The final "A." begins the name continued in the following passage (A. Manlius Torquatus).

passages.original: Litteras semper arbitror Assyrias fuisse, sed alii apud Aegyptios a Mercurio, ut Gellius, alii apud Syros repertas volunt, utrique in Graeciam attulisse e Phoenice Cadmum sedecim numero, quibus Troiano bello Palameden adiecisse quattuor hac figura ζυφχ, totidem post eum Simoniden melicum ψξωθ, quarum omnium vis in nostris recognoscitur .
passages.english: I have always thought that letters were Assyrian, but some hold that they were discovered among the Egyptians by Mercury, as Gellius does, others among the Syrians; both [say] that Cadmus brought them from Phoenicia into Greece, sixteen in number, to which Palamedes in the Trojan War added four, of this shape, ζ υ φ χ, and after him the lyric poet Simonides as many again, ψ ξ ω θ, the value of all of which is recognized in ours.
passages.notes: The Greek letters listed are as the edition prints them; the sets attributed to Palamedes and Simonides vary between sources and manuscripts.

passages.original: tegulas invenit Cinyra , Agriopae filius, et metalla aeris, utrumque in insula Cypro, item forcipem, martulum , vectem, incudem; puteos Danaus ex Aegypto advectus in Graeciam qua vocabatur Argos Dipsion; lapicidinas Cadmus Thebis aut, ut Theophrastus, in Phoenice; Thrason muros; turres, ut Aristoteles, Cyclopes , Tirynthii , ut Theophrastus ; Aegyptii textilia , inficere lanas Sardibus Lydi, fusos in lanificio Closter, filius Arachnae, linum et retia Arachne, fulloniam artem Nicias Megarensis, sutrinam Tychius Boeotius .
passages.english: Roof-tiles were invented by Cinyra, son of Agriopa, and copper mines, both on the island of Cyprus, and likewise the tongs, the hammer, the lever and the anvil; wells by Danaus, who came from Egypt into Greece, to the place that was called Thirsty Argos; stone quarries by Cadmus at Thebes, or, as Theophrastus says, in Phoenicia; walls by Thrason; towers by the Cyclopes, as Aristotle says, by the Tirynthians, as Theophrastus says; woven fabrics by the Egyptians, dyeing wool by the Lydians at Sardis, spindles for wool-working by Closter, son of Arachne, linen and nets by Arachne, the fuller's art by Nicias of Megara, shoemaking by Tychius of Boeotia.
passages.notes: 'martulum' taken as 'marculum' (hammer). 'Argos Dipsion' rendered 'Thirsty Argos'.

passages.original: fabricam materiariam Daedalus et in ea serram, asciam, perpendiculum, terebram, glutinum, ich- thyocollam; normam autem et libellam et tornum et clavem Theodorus Samius, mensuras et pondera Phidon Argivus aut Palamedes, ut maluit Gellius; ignem e silice Pyrodes Cilicis filius, eundem adservare ferula Prometheus; vehiculum cum quattuor rotis Phryges, mercaturas Poeni, culturas vitium et arborum Eumolpus Atheniensis, vinum aquae misceri Staphylus Sileni filius, oleum et trapetas Aristaeus Atheniensis, idem mella;
passages.english: Carpentry [was invented by] Daedalus, and within it the saw, the adze, the plumb-line, the auger, glue, and isinglass; but the square, the level, the lathe and the key by Theodorus of Samos; measures and weights by Phidon of Argos, or by Palamedes, as Gellius preferred; fire from flint by Pyrodes, son of Cilix, and keeping it in a fennel-stalk by Prometheus; the four-wheeled vehicle by the Phrygians, trade by the Carthaginians, the cultivation of vines and trees by Eumolpus of Athens, mixing wine with water by Staphylus, son of Silenus, oil and oil-mills by Aristaeus of Athens, and he also [discovered] honey;
passages.notes: 'ich- thyocollam' read as 'ichthyocollam' (fish-glue, isinglass).

passages.original: musicam Amphiors, fistulam et monaulum Pan Mercuri, obliquam tibiam Midas in Phrygia, geminas tibias Marsyas in eadem gente, Lydios modulos Amphion, Dorios Thamyras Thrax, Phrygios Marsyas Phryx, citharam Amphion, ut alii, Orpheus, ut alii, Linus. septem chordis primum cecinit III ad IIII primas additis Terpander, octavam Simonides addidit, nonam Timotheus. cithara sine voce cecinit Thamyris primus, cum cantu Amphion, ut alii, Linus.
passages.english: Music [was invented by] Amphion, the pan-pipe and the single pipe by Pan, son of Mercury, the transverse pipe by Midas in Phrygia, the double pipes by Marsyas in the same people, the Lydian modes by Amphion, the Dorian by Thamyras the Thracian, the Phrygian by Marsyas the Phrygian, the cithara by Amphion, or, as others say, by Orpheus, or, as others say, by Linus. Terpander first sang with seven strings, three being added to the first four; Simonides added the eighth, Timotheus the ninth. Thamyris first played the cithara without voice, Amphion with song, or, as others say, Linus.
passages.notes: 'Amphiors' read as 'Amphion'. The numerals 'III ad IIII' are understood as three added to the original four.

passages.original: ludos gymnicos in Arcadia Lycaon, funebres Acastus in Iolco,post eum Theseus in Isthmo , Hercules Olympiae; athleticam Pittheus , pilam lusoriam Gyges Lydus; picturam Aegyptii et in Graecia Euchir , Daedali cognatus, ut Aristoteli placet, ut Theophrasto, Polygnotus Atheniensis.
passages.english: Athletic games [were instituted] in Arcadia by Lycaon, funeral games by Acastus at Iolcus, after him by Theseus at the Isthmus, by Hercules at Olympia; athletics by Pittheus, the game of ball by Gyges the Lydian; painting by the Egyptians, and in Greece by Euchir, a kinsman of Daedalus, as Aristotle holds, or, as Theophrastus holds, by Polygnotus of Athens.

passages.original: Praedam ipsi in se expetendam sciunt solam esse in armis suis, quae Iua cornua appellat, Herodotus tanto antiquior et consuetudo melius dentes. quam ob rem deciduos casu aliquo vel senecta defodiunt. hoc solum ebur est; cetero et in his quoque, qua corpus intexit, vilitas ossea . quamquam nuper ossa etiam in laminas secari coepere paenuria: etenim rara amplitude iam dentium praeterquam ex India reperitur;
passages.english: They know that the only prize sought from them lies in their weapons, which Juba calls horns, but Herodotus, so much older, and common usage more properly [call] teeth. For this reason, when these have fallen out by some accident or through old age, they bury them. This alone is ivory; elsewhere, even in these, where the body covers them, [it is] cheap bone. Although lately even bones have begun to be cut into plates through scarcity: for a large size of tusks is now rarely found except from India;
passages.notes: 'Iua' read as 'Iuba' (King Juba). 'amplitude' read as 'amplitudo'.

passages.original: Decem annis gestare in utero vulgus existimat, Aristoteles biennio nec amplius quam [semel gignere pluresque quam] singulos, vivere ducenis annis et quosdam CCC. iuventa eorum a sexagesimo incipit. gaudent amnibus maxime et circa fluvios vagantur, cum alioqui nare propter magnitudinem corporis non possint.
passages.english: The common people think they carry their young in the womb for ten years, Aristotle for two years, and that they [give birth only once, and to no more than] one at a time, and that they live two hundred years and some three hundred. Their youth begins at sixty. They delight most of all in rivers and wander about near streams, although otherwise they cannot swim because of the size of their bodies.
passages.notes: The bracketed words are as marked by the edition, apparently a supplement; the text here is uncertain.

passages.original: magnitudo dentium videtur quidem in templis praecipua, sed tamen in extremis Africae, qua confinis Aethiopiae est, postium vicem in domiciliis praehere saepesque in his et pecorum stabulis pro palis elephantorum dentibus fieri Polybius tradidit auctore Gulusa regulo.
passages.english: The size of the tusks indeed seems outstanding in temples, but nevertheless Polybius has reported, on the authority of the chieftain Gulusa, that in the furthest parts of Africa, where it borders Ethiopia, they serve in place of door-posts in houses, and that fences in these and in the stalls of cattle are made with elephants' tusks for stakes.
passages.notes: 'praehere' read as 'praebere'.

passages.original: Aristoteles diversa tradit, vir quem in his magna secuturus ex parte praefandum reor. Alexandro Magno rege inflammato cupidine animalium naturas noscendi delegataque hac commentatione Aristoteli, summo in omni doctrina viro, aliquot milia hominum in totius Asiae Graeciaeque tractu parere iussa , omnium quos venatus, aucupia piscatusque alebant quibusque vivaria, armenta, alvaria, piscinae, aviaria in cura erant, ne quid usquam genitum ignoraretur ab eo.
passages.english: Aristotle reports differently, a man whom, since I shall follow him in large part in these matters, I think I should mention beforehand. King Alexander the Great, inflamed with a desire to know the natures of animals, having entrusted this study to Aristotle, a man supreme in all learning, ordered some thousands of men throughout the whole region of Asia and Greece to obey him, all those who lived by hunting, fowling and fishing, and those who had charge of game-parks, herds, beehives, fishponds and aviaries, so that nothing born anywhere should remain unknown to him.

passages.original: observatum ex duobus diversis generibus nata tertii generis fieri et neutri parentium esse similia eaque ipsa, quae sunt ita nata, non gignere in omni animalium genere; idcirco mulas non parere. est in annalibus nostris peperisse saepe, verum prodigii loco habitum. Theophrastus vulgo parere in Cappadocia tradit, sed esse id animal ibi sui generis. 20 mulae calcitratus inhibetur vini crebriore potu. in plurium Graecorum est monumentis cum equa muli coitu natum quod vocaverint ginnum , id est parvum mulum.
passages.english: It has been observed that offspring born of two different kinds are of a third kind and resemble neither parent, and that those very animals so born do not reproduce, in every kind of animal; for this reason mules do not bear young. It is recorded in our annals that they have often given birth, but this was held to be a portent. Theophrastus reports that they commonly bear young in Cappadocia, but that the animal there is of a kind of its own. A mule's kicking is checked by giving it wine to drink rather often. In the records of many Greeks it is stated that what is born of a mare mated with a mule they called a ginnus, that is, a little mule.
passages.notes: The stray '20' is a section number and has been omitted.

passages.original: togas rasas Phryxianasque Divi Augusti novissimis temporibus coepisse scribit Fenestella. crebrae papaveratae antiquiorem habent originem iam sub Lucilio poeta in Torquato notatae. praetextae apud Etruscos originem invenere . trabeis usos accipio reges; pictae vestes iam apud Homerum sunt iis, etinde triumphales natae. acu facere id Phryges invenerunt, ideoque Phrygioniae appellatae sunt. aurum intexere in eadem Asia invenit Attalus rex, unde nomen Attalicis. colores diversos picturae intexere Babylon maxime celebravit et nomen inposuit.
passages.english: Fenestella writes that smooth-shaven togas and Phryxian togas began in the last years of the Deified Augustus. Close-woven poppy-patterned togas have an older origin, being noted as early as the poet Lucilius, in [his lines on] Torquatus. Bordered togas (praetextae) had their origin among the Etruscans. I learn that kings wore the trabea; embroidered garments are already found in Homer, and from these the triumphal robes arose. The Phrygians discovered how to do this with the needle, and for that reason [such garments] are called Phrygionian. King Attalus, in the same Asia, discovered how to weave gold into cloth, whence the name Attalic [garments]. Weaving different colours into a picture was made most famous by Babylon, which gave it its name.
passages.notes: 'crebrae papaveratae' is obscure; probably close-woven togas of poppy-like (white or poppy-patterned) fabric. 'Phryxianae' of uncertain meaning (perhaps a shaggy or frieze cloth).

passages.original: plurimis vero liceis texere, quae polymita appellant, Alexandria instituit, scutulis dividere Gallia. Metellus Scipio tricliniaria Babylonica sestertium octingentis milibus venisse iam tune ponit in Catonis criminibus, quae Neroni principi quadragiens sestertio nuper stetere. Servi Tulli praetextae, quibus signum Fortunae ab eo dicatae coopertum erat, duravere ad Seiani exitum, mirumque fuit neque diffluxisse eas neque teredinum iniurias sensisse annis quingentis sexaginta.
passages.english: Weaving with very many leashes, [producing the cloth] they call polymita, was introduced by Alexandria; dividing [cloth] into checks, by Gaul. Metellus Scipio, among his charges against Cato, already states that Babylonian dining-couch covers had then been sold for 800,000 sesterces; these lately cost the emperor Nero four million sesterces. The bordered robes of Servius Tullius, with which the statue of Fortune dedicated by him was covered, lasted until the downfall of Sejanus, and it was a marvel that they had neither fallen to pieces nor suffered damage from moths in five hundred and sixty years.
passages.notes: 'liceis' read as 'liciis' (heddle-leashes). 'tune' read as 'tunc'. 'teredinum' properly wood-worms/moths.

passages.original: Suilli pecoris admissura a favonio ad aequinoctium vernum, aetas octavo mense, quibusdam in locis etiam quarto, usque ad octavum annum. partus bis anno, tempus utero quattuor mensum , numerus fecunditati ad vicenos , sed educare nequeunt tam multos. diebus X circa brumam statim dentatos nasci Nigidius tradit. implentur uno coitu, qui et geminatur propter facilitatem aboriendi. remedium, ne prima subatione neque ante flaccidas aures coitus fiat. mares non ultra trimatum generant. feminae senectute fessae cubantes coeunt.
passages.english: The mating of swine runs from the west wind to the spring equinox; the age [for breeding] is the eighth month, in some places even the fourth, and it continues up to the eighth year. They farrow twice a year; the time in the womb is four months; the number of the litter, for fertility, goes up to twenty, but they cannot rear so many. Nigidius records that those born in the ten days around the winter solstice are born with teeth already. They are impregnated by a single coupling, which is also repeated because they miscarry so easily. The remedy is that coupling should not take place at the first heat, nor before the ears droop. Males do not breed beyond three years. Females worn out with age couple lying down.
passages.notes: 'From the west wind': i.e. from the start of the favonius in early February.

passages.original: item in Syria angues circa Euphratis maxime ripas dormientes Syros non attingunt aut, etiamsi calcati momordere, non sentiuntur malefici , aliis cuiuscumque gentis infesti, avide et cum cruciatu exanimantes, quam ob rem et Syri non necant eos. contra in Latmo Cariae monte Aristoteles tradit a scorpionibus hospites non laedi, indi- genas interemi. sed reliquorum quoque animalium [et praeterea terrestrium] dicemus genera.
passages.english: Likewise in Syria, especially around the banks of the Euphrates, snakes do not touch Syrians who are asleep, or, even if they bite when trodden on, are not felt to be harmful, while to others of whatever nation they are deadly, killing eagerly and with torment; for which reason the Syrians do not kill them either. Conversely, Aristotle reports that on Latmus, a mountain of Caria, strangers are not harmed by scorpions, but natives are killed. But we shall also describe the kinds of the remaining animals [and moreover of land animals].
passages.notes: Bracketed words '[et praeterea terrestrium]' are marked by the edition as suspect.

passages.original: in eadem urbe Iaso Hegesidemus scribit et alium puerum Hermian nomine similiter maria perequitantem, cum repentinae procellae fluctibus exanimatus esset, relatum, delphinumque causam leti fatentem non reversum in maria atque in sicco expirasse . hoc idem et Naupacti accidisse Theophrastus tradit. nec modus exemplorum: eadem Amphilochi et Tarentini de pueris delphinisque narrant. quae faciunt ut credatur, Arionem quoque citharoedicae artis, interficere nautis in mari parantibus ad intercipiendos eius quaestus , eblanditum uti prius caneret cithara, congregatis cantu delphinis cum se iecisset in mare, exceptum ab uno Taenarum in litus pervectum.
passages.english: In the same city of Iasus, Hegesidemus writes, another boy too, named Hermias, similarly riding across the sea, when he had been drowned by the waves of a sudden storm, was brought back, and the dolphin, as if confessing itself the cause of his death, did not return to the sea and expired on dry land. Theophrastus reports that this same thing happened at Naupactus also. Nor is there any limit to examples: the people of Amphilochus and of Tarentum tell the same stories about boys and dolphins. These things make it credible that Arion too, a master of the art of singing to the lyre, when the sailors were preparing to kill him at sea in order to seize his earnings, having coaxed them into letting him first sing to his lyre, and dolphins having been gathered by the song, when he had thrown himself into the sea, was taken up by one and carried to the shore at Taenarum.
passages.notes: 'interficere' read as 'interficere eum' sense; 'expirasse' = 'exspirasse'.

passages.original: Murena quocumque mense parit, cum ceteri pisces stato pariant. ova eius citissime crescunt. in sicca litora elapsas vulgus coitu serpentium impleri putat. Aristoteles zmyrum vocat marem qui generet; discrimen esse quod murena varia et infirma sit, zmvrus unicolor et robustus dentesque et extra os habeat. in Gallia septentrionali murenis omnibus dextera in maxilla septenae maculae ad formam septentrionis aureo colore fulgent, dumtaxat viventibus , pariterque cum anima extinguuntur.
passages.english: The moray gives birth in any month, whereas the other fish spawn at a fixed time. Its eggs grow very quickly. Common people think that morays which have slipped out onto dry shores are impregnated by mating with snakes. Aristotle calls the male that does the begetting *zmyrus*; the difference, he says, is that the moray is mottled and weak, while the *zmyrus* is of one colour and sturdy, and has teeth that project even outside its mouth. In northern Gaul all morays have on the right jaw seven spots arranged in the shape of the Great Bear, gleaming with a golden colour, but only while they are alive, and they are extinguished together with their life.
passages.notes: 'zmvrus' is a scanning error for 'zmyrus'. 'Septentrio' (the seven stars of the Plough/Great Bear) puns on 'septenae' and 'septentrionali'.

passages.original: invenit in hoc animali documenta saevitiae Vedius Pollio, eques Romanus ex amicis Divi Augusti, vivariis earum inmergens damnata mancipia, non tamquam ad hoc feris terrarum non sufficientibus, sed quia in alio genere totum pariter homi- nem distrahi spectare non poterat. ferunt aceti gustu praecipue eas in rabiem agi. tenuissimum iis tergus, contra anguillis crassius, eoque verberari solitos tradit Verrius praetextatos et ob id multam iis dici non institutum.
passages.english: In this creature Vedius Pollio, a Roman knight and one of the friends of the deified Augustus, found the means for his cruelty, plunging condemned slaves into his ponds of them, not because the wild beasts of the land were insufficient for this, but because with another kind [of animal] he could not watch a whole man being torn apart all at once. They say that the taste of vinegar especially drives them into a frenzy. Their skin is very thin, whereas that of eels is thicker, and Verrius records that boys wearing the toga praetexta used to be beaten with it, and that for this reason it was not the custom to impose fines on them.
passages.notes: The animal is the moray eel (murena), from context.

passages.original: Aevi piscium memorandum nuper exemplum accepimus. Pausilypum villa est Campaniae haut procul Neapoli; in ea in Caesaris piscinis a Pollione Vedio coniectum piscem sexagensimum post annum expirasse scribit Annaeus Seneca, duobus aliis aequalibus eius ex eodem genere etiam tune viventibus. quae mentio piscinarum admonet , ut paulo plura dicamus hac de re prius quam digrediamur ab aquatilibus.
passages.english: We have recently received a memorable example of the lifespan of fish. Pausilypum is a villa in Campania not far from Naples; Annaeus Seneca writes that in it, in Caesar's fishponds, a fish put in by Vedius Pollio died after its sixtieth year, while two others of the same kind and of equal age were still living even then. This mention of fishponds prompts us to say a little more on this subject before we leave aquatic creatures.
