passages.original: Melanaë tos a Graecis dicta, eadem leporaria, minima magnitudine, viribus praecipua , colore nigricans, sola aquilarum fetus suos alit — ceterae , ut dicemus, fugant —, sola sine clangore, sine murmuratione. conversatur autem in montibus, secundi generis pygargus in oppidis et in campis, albicante cauda. tertii morphnos , quam Homerus et percnum vocat, aliqui et plangum et anatariam , secunda magnitudine et vi; huic vita circa lacus. Phemonoe, Apollinis dicta filia, dentes esse ei prodidit, mutae alias carentique lingua, eandem aquilarum nigerrimam, prominentiore cauda;
passages.english: The melanaetos, as it is called by the Greeks, also called the hare-eagle, smallest in size, outstanding in strength, blackish in colour, is the only one of the eagles that rears its young — the others, as we shall say, drive them away — and the only one without screaming or muttering. It lives in the mountains. The second kind, the pygargus [white-rump], lives in towns and plains, with a whitish tail. The third is the morphnos, which Homer also calls percnos, and some also plangus and duck-eagle, second in size and strength; its life is spent around lakes. Phemonoe, said to be the daughter of Apollo, stated that it has teeth, though otherwise mute and lacking a tongue, and that it is the blackest of the eagles, with a more prominent tail;

passages.original: cliviam quoque avem ab antiquis nominatam animadverto ignorari — quidam clamatoriam dicunt, Labeo prohibitoriam —, et apud Nigidium super appellatur avis, quae aquilarum ova frangat.
passages.english: I observe also that the bird called *clivia* by the ancients is unknown; some call it the 'shouting' bird, Labeo the 'forbidding' bird; and in Nigidius there is also named a bird that breaks the eggs of eagles.
passages.notes: *Clivia*: an augural bird of ill omen, not identifiable. 'Super appellatur' is odd Latin, perhaps corrupt; rendered 'there is also named'.

passages.original: maiore circumdatae multitudine resupinae pedibus repugnant collectaeque in artum rostro et unguibus totae teguntur. auxiliatur accipiter collegio quodam naturae bellumque partitur . noctuas sexagenis diebus hiemis cubare et novem voces habere tradit Nigidius.
passages.english: When surrounded by a larger crowd [of birds], they lie on their backs and fight back with their feet, and, drawn tightly together, they are entirely covered by beak and talons. The hawk comes to their aid through a kind of natural fellowship and shares the war. Nigidius records that owls lie dormant for sixty days of winter and have nine calls.

passages.original: deinde in una perfecta musica scientia: modulatus editur sonus et nunc continuo spiritu trahitur in longum, nunc variatur inflexo, nunc distinguitur conciso, copulatur intorto, promittitur revocato , infuscatur ex inopinato, interdum et secum ipse murmurat, plenus, gravis, acutus, creber, extentus, ubi visum est, vibrans, summus, medius, imus. breviterque omnia tam parvulis in faucibus, quae tot exquisitis tibiarum tormentis ars hominum excogitavit, non ut sit dubium hanc suavitatem praemonstratam efficaci auspicio, cum in ore Stesichori cecinit infantis. ac ne quis dubitet artis esse, plures singulis sunt cantus, nec iidem omnibus, sed sui cuique. certant inter se, palamque animosa contentio est. victa morte finit saepe vitam spiritu prius deficiente quam cantu.
passages.english: Next, in this one [bird] is the perfected science of music: the sound is uttered with modulation, and now it is drawn out long in one continuous breath, now varied by being inflected, now broken up by being cut short, linked by being twisted, prolonged by being recalled, darkened unexpectedly; sometimes too it murmurs to itself, full, deep, high, rapid, drawn out, and, when it pleases, quavering, highest, middle, lowest. In short, [there is] in so tiny a throat everything that human art has devised with the many elaborate mechanisms of pipes; so that there can be no doubt that this sweetness was foreshown by an effective omen when [a nightingale] sang on the lips of the infant Stesichorus. And so that no one may doubt that it is art, each has several songs, and not the same ones for all, but each its own. They compete with one another, and the contention is openly spirited. The loser often ends its life in death, its breath failing before its song.

passages.original: Alia ratio ficedulis, nam formam simul coloremque mutant. hoc nomen autumno habent, postea melancoryphi vocantur. sic et erithacus hieme, idem phoenicurus aestate. mutat et upupa, ut tradit Aeschylus poeta, obscena alias pastu avis, crista visenda plicatili, contrahens eam subrigensque per longitudinem capitis.
passages.english: The fig-peckers follow a different pattern, for they change both shape and colour together. They have this name in autumn; afterwards they are called melancoryphi [black-caps]. So too the erithacus in winter is the same bird as the phoenicurus [redstart] in summer. The hoopoe also changes, as the poet Aeschylus reports, a bird otherwise foul in its feeding, remarkable for its folding crest, which it draws down and raises along the length of its head.

passages.original: Vivere palumbes ad tricensimum annum, aliquas et ad quadragensimum, habemus auctores, uno tantum incommodo unguium — eodem et argumento senectae —, qui citra perniciem reciduntur. cantus omnibus similis atque idem trino conficitur versu praeterque in clausula gemitu, hieme mutis, a vere vocalibus. Nigidius putat, cum ova incubet sub tecto, nominatam palumbem relinquere nidos. pariunt autem post solstitium . columbae et turtures octonis annis vivunt.
passages.english: We have authorities that wood-pigeons live to their thirtieth year, some even to the fortieth, with only one trouble, in their claws (which is also the sign of old age), which are trimmed without harm. The song of all is alike and the same, made up of a threefold phrase and, besides, a moan at the close; they are mute in winter and vocal from spring. Nigidius thinks that when one is sitting on eggs under a roof, the wood-pigeon, if it is called by name, leaves the nest. They lay after the solstice. Doves and turtle-doves live eight years.
passages.notes: The Nigidius sentence is obscure; 'nominatam' taken as 'if addressed by name'.

passages.original: super tecta exaedificant turres iis nobilitatemque singularum et origines narrant, vetere iam exemplo. L. Axius eques Romanus ante bellum civile Pompeianum denariis CCCC singula paria venditavit, ut M. Varro tradit. quin et patriam nobilitavere in Campania grandissimae provenire existimatae.
passages.english: On their roofs they build towers for them and recount the pedigree and origins of each one, a practice now of long standing. Lucius Axius, a Roman knight, before the civil war with Pompey, sold single pairs for four hundred denarii, as Marcus Varro records. Indeed they have even brought renown to a homeland, those in Campania being thought to grow the largest.
passages.notes: Refers to pigeons, from context.

passages.original: nec Sirenes impetraverint fidem, adfirmet licet Dinon, Clitarchi celebrati auctoris pater, in India esse mulcerique earum cantu quos gravatos somno lacerent. qui credat ista, et Melampodi profecto aures lambendo dedisse intellectum avium sermonis dracones non abnuat vel quae Democritus tradit nominando aves quarum confuso sanguine serpens gignatur , quem quisquis ederit intellecturus sit alitum colloquia, quaeque de una ave galerita privatim commemorat, etiam sine his inmensa vitae ambage circa auguria.
passages.english: Nor would the Sirens win belief, though Dinon, father of the celebrated author Clitarchus, may affirm that they exist in India and that by their song they soothe people whom, once weighed down with sleep, they tear apart. Whoever would believe such things would surely not deny either that serpents by licking Melampus' ears gave him understanding of the speech of birds, or what Democritus reports, naming birds from whose mingled blood a serpent is produced, which whoever eats will understand the conversations of birds, and the things he records specifically about one bird, the crested lark—even without these, life is involved in immense perplexity concerning auguries.

passages.original: aquatilium rotunda, reliqua fere fastigio cacuminata. exeunt a rotundissima sui parte, dum pariuntur, molli putamine, sed protinus durescente quibuscumque emergunt portionibus. quae oblonga sint ova, gratioris saporis putat Horatius Flaccus. feminam edunt quae rotundiora gignuntur, reliqua marem. umbilicus ovis a cacumine inest, ceu gutta eminens in putamine .
passages.english: Those of aquatic creatures are round; the rest are mostly tapered to a point. They come out by their roundest part while being laid, with a soft shell, but one that hardens at once in whatever portions emerge. Horace Flaccus thinks that eggs that are oblong have the more pleasant taste. Those laid rounder produce a female, the rest a male. The navel of eggs is at the tip, like a drop standing out on the shell.

passages.original: ab eodem tempore plumescit , ita positus, ut caput supra dextrum pedem habeat, dextram vero alam supra caput. vitellus paulatim deficit. aves omnes in pedes nascuntur , contra quam reliqua animalia. quaedam gallinae omnia gemina ova pariunt et geminos interdum excludunt, ut Cornelius Celsus auctor est, alterum maiorem; aliqui negant omnino geminos excludi. plus vicena quina incubanda subici vetant. parere a bruma incipiunt. optima fetura ante vernum aequinoctium. post solstitium nata non implent magnitudinem iustam tantoque minus, quanto serius provenere.
passages.english: From the same time it grows feathers, lying so placed that it has its head above its right foot and its right wing above its head. The yolk gradually diminishes. All birds are born feet first, contrary to other animals. Some hens lay all their eggs double and sometimes hatch twins, as Cornelius Celsus states, one larger than the other; some deny that twins are ever hatched at all. They forbid putting more than twenty-five eggs under [a hen] for incubation. They begin laying from the winter solstice. The best brood is before the spring equinox. Those hatched after the summer solstice do not reach full size, and fall short the more, the later they were produced.

passages.original: in hominum genere maribus deverticula veneris, excogitata omnia scelere naturae , feminis vero abortus. quantum in hac parte multo nocentiores quam ferae sumus! viros avidiores veneris hieme, feminas aestate Hesiodus prodidit.
passages.english: In the human race, males have devised perversions of sex, all of them crimes against nature, and females abortions. How much more harmful than wild beasts we are in this respect! Hesiod has recorded that men are more eager for sex in winter, women in summer.

passages.original: Super cuncta est murium fetus, haut sine cunctatione dicendus, quamquam sub auctore Aristotele et Alexandri Magni militibus. generatio eorum lambendo constare, non coitu, dicitur. ex una genitos CXX tradiderunt , apud Persas vero praegnantes in ventre parentis repertas . et salis gustatu fieri praegnantes opinantur.
passages.english: Above all is the breeding of mice, which should not be stated without hesitation, even though it rests on the authority of Aristotle and of the soldiers of Alexander the Great. Their generation is said to come about by licking, not by intercourse. They have reported that 120 were born from one female, and that among the Persians pregnant females were found inside the belly of the mother. They also believe that they become pregnant by tasting salt.

passages.original: luporum minimi non texunt, maiores in terra, et cavernis exigua vestibula praepandunt. tertium eorundem genus erudita operatione conspicuum. orditur telas tantique operis materiae uterus ipsius sufficit, sive ita corrupta alvi natura stato tempore, ut Democrito placet, sive est quaedam intus lanigera fertilitas: tam moderato ungue, tam tereti filo et tam aequali deducit stamina, ipso se pondere usus. texere a medio incipit, circinato orbe subtemina adnectens, maculasque paribus semper intervallis, sed subinde crescentibus ex angusto dilatans indissolubili nodo inplicat.
passages.english: The smallest of the wolf-spiders do not weave; the larger ones weave on the ground and spread small porches in front of their holes. A third kind of the same is conspicuous for its skilled work. It begins its webs, and its own belly supplies the material for so great a work, whether because the nature of its bowel is so altered at a set time, as Democritus holds, or because there is some wool-producing fertility within: with so controlled a claw, so smooth a thread and so even does it draw out the warp, using its own weight. It begins weaving from the middle, attaching the woof in a circular round, and, widening the meshes from narrow at always equal intervals, but ones that grow steadily larger, it binds them with an indissoluble knot.

passages.original: his negatus aculeus, sed in quodam genere eorum grandi cornua praelonga , bisulca dentatis forcipibus in cacumine , cum libuit, ad morsum coeuntibus, infantium etiam remediis ex cervice suspenduntur; lucavos vocat hos Nigidius. aliud rursus eorum genus, qui e fimo ingentes pilas aversi pedibus volutant parvosque in iis contra rigorem hiemis vermiculos fetus sui nidulantur. volitant alii magno cum murmure aut mugitu, alii focos et prata crebris foraminibus excavant, nocturno stridore vocales.
passages.english: These are denied a sting, but in one large kind of them there are very long horns, two-pronged with toothed pincers at the tip, which close together to bite when it pleases; they are even hung from the neck as remedies for infants. Nigidius calls these *lucavi*. Again, another kind of them, which, facing backwards, roll huge balls of dung with their feet and lay in them small grubs, their offspring, as in a nest against the cold of winter. Others fly about with a great buzzing or bellowing; others hollow out hearths and meadows with many holes and are noisy with a shrill sound at night.
passages.notes: *Lucavi*: stag beetles (cf. lucanus).

passages.original: oculorum effigies inest, si quis praetentam detrahat membranam. et inter aves ardiolarum in geniere quos leucos vocant, altero oculo carere tradunt, optimi augurii, cum ad austrum volent septentrionemve : solvi enim pericula et metus narrant . Nigidius nec locustis, cicadis esse dicit. cocleis oculorum vicem cornicula bina praetemptatu inplent. nec lumbricis ulli sunt vermiumve generi.
passages.english: The likeness of eyes is present, if one draws off the membrane stretched over them. And among birds, of the kind of herons they call *leuci* ('white'), they report that they lack one eye, and are of the best omen when they fly toward the south or north, for they say it signifies release from dangers and fears. Nigidius says that neither locusts nor cicadas have [eyes]. In snails a pair of little horns fills the place of eyes by feeling ahead. Nor do earthworms or any kind of worm have any.
passages.notes: 'in geniere' read as 'in genere'. Nigidius sentence read as 'nec locustis [nec] cicadis'.

passages.original: Vocem non habere nisi quae pulmonem et arterias habeant, hoc est nisi quae spirent, Aristoteles putat. idcirco et insectis sonum esse, non vocem, intus inmeante spiritu et incluso sonante; alia murmur edere, ut apes, alia contractum stridorem, ut cicadas, receptum enim duobus sub pectore cavis spiritum, mobili occursante membrana intus, attritu eius sonare.
passages.english: Aristotle thinks that only those creatures have a voice which have a lung and windpipe, that is, only those that breathe. For this reason insects too have sound, not voice, the air passing in inside and sounding when enclosed; some give out a hum, like bees, others a compressed shrill, like cicadas, for the air taken into two cavities under the breast, with a movable membrane meeting it inside, sounds through its friction.

passages.original: inde Gabbam omnes petere solebant dierum viginti itinere et Palaestinen Syriam. postea Characem peti coeptum ac regna Parthorum ex ea causa, auctor est Iuba. mihi ad Persas etiam prius ista portasse quam in Syriam aut Aegyptum videntur Herodoto teste, qui tradit singula milia talentum annua turis pensitasse Arabas regibus Persarum. ex Syria revehunt styracem, acri odore eius in focis abigentes suorum fastidium. cetero non alia sunt ligni genera in usu quam odorata, cibosque Sabaei coquunt turis ligno, alii murrae, oppidorum vicorumque non alio quam ex aris fumo atque nidore.
passages.english: From there everyone used to make for Gabba, a journey of twenty days, and Palestinian Syria. Later Charax began to be the destination, and the kingdoms of the Parthians, for that reason, as Juba reports. To me it seems that they carried these goods to the Persians even earlier than to Syria or Egypt, on the testimony of Herodotus, who records that the Arabs paid a thousand talents of frankincense yearly to the kings of the Persians. From Syria they bring back storax, driving away their disgust at their own [scents] with its sharp smell on their hearths. Otherwise no kinds of wood are in use except fragrant ones, and the Sabaeans cook their food with frankincense wood, others with myrrh, the smoke and savour of their towns and villages being no different from that of altars.

passages.original: antea non fuisse chartarum usam: in palmarum foliis primo scriptitatum , dein quarundam arborum libris. postea publica monumenta plumbeis voluminibus, mox et privata linteis confici coepta aut ceris; pugillarium enim usum fuisse etiam ante Troiana tempora invenimus apud Homerum, illo vero prodente ne terram quidem ipsam, quae nunc Aegyptus, intellegitur , cum in Sebennytico et Saite eius nomo omnis charta nascatur, postea adaggeratam Nilo, si quidem a Pharo insula, quae nunc Alexandriae ponte iungitur, noctis dieique velifico navigi cursu terram afuisse prodidit. mox aemulatione circa bibliothecas regum Ptolemaei et Eumenis, supprimente chartas Ptolemaeo, idem Varro membranas Pergami tradit repertas. postea promiscue repatuit usus rei qua constat inmortalitas hominum.
passages.english: [He says that] before this there had been no use of paper: writing was done at first on palm leaves, then on the inner bark of certain trees. Afterwards public records began to be made on rolls of lead, and soon private ones too on linen or on wax; for we find in Homer that the use of writing-tablets existed even before the Trojan times, though by his account not even the land itself that is now understood as Egypt [existed then], since all paper grows in its Sebennytic and Saite nome, and [that land] was afterwards built up by silt from the Nile; for he related that the mainland was a day and a night's run of a sailing ship away from the island of Pharos, which is now joined to Alexandria by a bridge. Soon, through the rivalry over libraries between King Ptolemy and King Eumenes, when Ptolemy suppressed [the export of] paper, parchment was invented at Pergamum, as the same Varro reports. Afterwards the use of the material on which the immortality of human beings depends spread again indiscriminately.
passages.notes: 'usam' read as 'usum'. The infinitives depend on Varro's report from the preceding context.

passages.original: maritimo adflatu gaudent, roscida odere. nulla vitium minus Italiam amat, rara, parva, putrescens in ea, vino quoque quod genuit aestatem non exuperans; nec alia macro solo familiarior. Graecinus, qui alioqui Cornelium Celsum transcripsit, arbitratur non naturam eius repugnare Italiae, sed culturam avide palmites evocantium. ob id fertilitate sua absumi, si non praepinguis soli ubertas lassescentem sustineat. carbunculare negatur, magna dote, si verum est aliqua in vite caelo non esse ius.
passages.english: They delight in a sea breeze and hate dewy places. No vine likes Italy less: it is sparse, small and rotting there, and its wine too does not outlast the summer in which it was produced; nor is any other more at home in thin soil. Graecinus, who otherwise copied out Cornelius Celsus, judges that its nature is not hostile to Italy, but the cultivation of those who greedily call forth shoots; for that reason it is used up by its own fertility, unless the richness of a very fat soil supports it as it tires. It is said not to suffer from carbuncle, a great endowment, if it is true that in any vine the weather has no power.
passages.notes: carbunculare: a vine disease (blight) caused by heat or weather.

passages.original: Pariana gaudent Pisae, Mutina Perusinia nigro acino, intra quadriennium albescente vino. mirum ibi cum sole circumagi uvam quae ob id streptis vocatur, et in Italia Gallicam placere, trans Alpis vero Picenam. dixit Vergilius Thasias et Mareotidas et Lageas compluresque externas, quae non reperiuntur in Italia.
passages.english: Pisa delights in the Parian grape, Mutina in the Perusinian, with a black berry, its wine turning white within four years. It is remarkable that there a grape turns round with the sun, which for that reason is called streptis ('twisting'), and that in Italy the Gallic grape is favoured, but beyond the Alps the Picene. Virgil spoke of Thasian, Mareotic and Lagean grapes and many foreign ones which are not found in Italy.

passages.original: quas suspendas duracinas, Aminnias maiores, vel ad fabrum ferrarium pro passis hae recte servantur. nec sunt vetustiora de illa re Latinae linguae praecepta. tam prope ab origine rerum sumus. Aminneam proxime dictam Varro Scantianam vocat.
passages.english: "Those you hang up [should be] the hard-fleshed and the larger Aminnian; or these are rightly kept at the blacksmith's [forge] as raisins." Nor are there older precepts on that subject in the Latin language; so near are we to the origin of things. The Aminnian just mentioned Varro calls the Scantian.
passages.notes: The quotation continues Cato's precepts from the preceding context. 'At the blacksmith's' presumably refers to drying the grapes by the heat of the smithy.

passages.original: digna opera quae in Caecubis Setinisque agris proficeret, quando et postea saepenumero septenos culleos singula iugera, hoc est amphoras centenas quadragenas, musti dedere! ac ne quis victam in hoc antiquitatem arbitretur , idem Cato denos culleos redire ex iugeribus scripsit, efficacibus exemplis non maria plus temerata conferre mercatori, non in Rubrum litus Indicumve merces petitas quam sedulum ruris larem.
passages.english: Worthy labour, to succeed in the Caecuban and Setine lands, since afterwards too single iugera often yielded seven cullei of must, that is 140 amphorae! And lest anyone think antiquity was surpassed in this, the same Cato wrote that ten cullei came from each iugerum, showing by effective examples that the sea, violated the more, does not bring more to a merchant, nor wares sought on the Red or Indian shore, than a diligent farm household.
passages.notes: Context suggests the 'digna opera' refers to the vineyard work of Acilius Sthenelus/Remmius Palaemon; 'idem Cato' is abrupt in this extract.

passages.original: neque enim fabulosa aut de origine eius varie prodita consectamur, praeterquam Aristaeum primum omnium in eadem gente mel miscuisse vino, suavitate praecipua utriusque naturae sponte provenientis . Maroneum vicies tanto addito aquae miscendum Homerus prodidit. durat etiam nunc vis in eadem terra generi rigorque indomitus, quippe cum Mucianus ter consul ex iis qui nuperrime prodidere sextarios singulos octonis aquae misceri compererit praesens in eo tractu, esse autem colore nigrum, odoratum, vetustatepinguescere .
passages.english: For we do not pursue the fabulous or the varied accounts given of its origin, except that Aristaeus was the first of all, in the same people, to mix honey with wine, both substances being of exceptional sweetness and arising spontaneously. Homer recorded that Maronean wine was to be mixed with twenty times as much water added. Even now the strength of the kind persists in the same land and its untamed hardness, since Mucianus, three times consul, one of those who wrote most recently, found when present in that district that single sextarii are mixed with eight of water, and that it is black in colour, fragrant, and grows richer with age.
passages.notes: 'vetustatepinguescere' read as 'vetustate pinguescere'.

passages.original: tria eorum genera: decima parte aquae addita quam musti expressa sit et ita nocte ac die madefactis vinaceis rursusque prelo subiectis; alterum, quo modo Graeci factitavere, tertia parte eius quod expressum sit addita aquae expressoque decocto ad tertias partes. tertium est faecibus vini expressum, quod faecatum Cato appellat. nullum ex his plus quam annui usus.
passages.english: There are three kinds of them: one in which water is added amounting to a tenth of the must pressed out, and the skins are thus soaked for a night and a day and put under the press again; the second, as the Greeks have been accustomed to make it, by adding water to a third of what has been pressed out and boiling down what is pressed out to a third; the third is pressed from the lees of wine, which Cato calls faecatum. None of these is for use beyond a year.

passages.original: Iulius Caesar censores anno urbis conditae DCLXV edixerunt, ne quis vinum Graecum, Aminniumque octonis aeris singula quadrantalia venderet. haec enim verba sunt. tanta vero Graeco vino gratia erat, ut singulae potiones in convictu darentur. quibus vinis auctoritas fuerit sua iuventa, M. Varro his verbis tradit: L. Lucullus puer apud patrem numquam lautum convivium vidit, in quo plus semel Graecum vinum daretur: ipse cum rediit ex Asia, milia cadum congiarium divisit amplius centum. C. Sentius, quem praetorem vidimus, Chium vinum suam domum inlatum dicebat tum primum, cum sibi cardiaco medicus dedisset: Hortensius super X cadum heredi reliquit.
passages.english: [... and] Julius Caesar, as censors, in the 665th year from the founding of the city, issued an edict that no one should sell Greek and Aminnian wine at eight *asses* per *quadrantal* [a measure of about 26 litres]. For these are the words. And so great was the esteem for Greek wine that it was served only one cup at a time at a banquet. What prestige these wines had in his youth M. Varro relates in these words: "Lucius Lucullus as a boy never saw at his father's house a sumptuous banquet at which Greek wine was served more than once; he himself, when he returned from Asia, distributed more than a hundred thousand jars as a largesse. Gaius Sentius, whom we have seen as praetor, used to say that Chian wine was brought into his house for the first time when the doctor had given it to him for a heart complaint. Hortensius left more than ten thousand jars to his heir."
passages.notes: The opening is garbled by the passage break: the context shows the consuls were P. Licinius Crassus and L. Julius Caesar. 'Super X' presumably stands for 10,000 (X with a bar).

passages.original: similiter hyssopites e Cilicio hyssopo unciis tribus in duos congios musti coiectis aut tusis in vinum. fiunt utraque et alio modo, circa radices vitium sato. sic et elleboriten fieri ex veratro nigro Cato docet. sic fit et scammonites , mira vitium natura saporem alienum in se trahendi, quare et salicem redolent Patavinorum in palustribus vindemiae. sic et elleborum seritur in Thaso aut cucumis silvester aut scammonia, quod vinum phthorium vocatur, quoniam abortus facit.
passages.english: Similarly hyssop wine [is made] from Cilician hyssop, three ounces being thrown into two congii of must, or [the hyssop] crushed into wine. Both [kinds] are also made in another way, by sowing [the plant] around the roots of the vines. In this way too, Cato teaches, hellebore wine is made from black hellebore. In this way scammony wine is also made, since vines have a wonderful natural capacity for drawing a foreign flavour into themselves; this is why the vintages of the Patavians in the marshlands even smell of willow. In this way also hellebore is sown in Thasos, or wild cucumber or scammony; this wine is called *phthorium* ["destroyer"], because it causes abortions.
passages.notes: "coiectis" read as "coniectis".

passages.original: Genera earum tria dixit Vergilius, orchites et radios et posias, nec desiderare rastros aut falces ullamve curam. sine dubio et in iis solum maxime caelumque refert. verum tamen et tondentur, cum et vites, atque etiam interradi gaudent.
passages.english: Virgil named three kinds of them, the orchites, the radius and the posia, and [said] that they need neither rakes nor pruning-hooks nor any care. Without doubt in their case too soil and climate matter most. But nevertheless they are also pruned, at the same time as the vines, and they even benefit from being thinned out.
passages.notes: The subject ("them") is olives, as the following context shows.

passages.original: error hominum falsus existimantium maturitatis initium quod est vitii proximum, deinde quod oleum crescere olivae came arbitrantur, cum sucus omnis in corpus abeat lignumque intus grandescat. ergo tum maxime rigantur; quod ubi cura multisve imbribus accidit , oleum absumitur nisi consecuta serenitate quae corpus extenuet. omnino enim, ut Theophrasto placet, et olei causa calor est, quare in torcularibus etiam ac cellis multo igni quaeritur. tertia est culpa in parsimonia, quoniam propter inpendium decerpendi expectatur ut decidant olivae. qui medium temperamentum in hoc servant, perticis decutiunt cum iniuria arborum sequentisque anni damno.
passages.english: [There is] a mistake made by people who wrongly think that the beginning of ripeness is what is in fact closest to a fault; next, that they suppose the oil increases with the flesh of the olive, when all the juice passes into the body [of the fruit] and the woody stone grows larger inside. Therefore it is then that they are watered most; and when this happens through care or through heavy rains, the oil is used up, unless fine weather follows to thin down the body [of the fruit]. For in general, as Theophrastus holds, heat is also the cause of oil, which is why it is sought with plenty of fire even in the presses and storerooms. A third error lies in thrift, since to save the cost of picking, people wait for the olives to fall. Those who keep a middle course in this knock them down with poles, injuring the trees and causing loss in the following year.
passages.notes: "came" read as "carne".

passages.original: odor est iis cotoneorum, magnitude quae Scaudianis, color rubens . ac ne quis sic ambitum valuisse claritatis e familia putet, sunt et Sceptiana ab inventore libertino, insignia rotunditate . Cato adicit Quiriniana et quae tradit in doliis condi Scantiana. omnium autem nuperrime adoptata sunt parva gratissimi saporis, quae Petisia nominantur. patrias nobilitavere Amerina et Graecula. cetera e causis traxere nomen: germanitatis cohaerentia gemella, numquam singula in fetu, colore syrica, cognatione melapia, mustea a celeritate mitescendi, quae nunc melimela dicuntur a sapore melleo, orbiculata a figura orbis in rotunditatem circumacti 5 —haec in Epiro primum provenisse argumento sunt Graeci, qui Epirotica vocant —, mammarum effigie orthomastia, condicione castrati seminis quae spadonia appellant Belgae.
passages.english: They have the smell of quinces, the size of the Scaudian [apples], and a reddish colour. And lest anyone think that ambition for fame has had such force only through [noble] family, there are also Sceptian [apples], named from their inventor, a freedman, remarkable for their roundness. Cato adds Quirinian apples, and Scantian, which he records are preserved in jars. But the most recent of all to be adopted are small ones of very pleasant flavour, which are named Petisian. The Amerine and the Graecula have made their native lands famous. The rest have taken their names from [various] causes: the twin apples from their brotherly cohesion, never [growing] singly on the tree; the Syrian from their colour; the melapia from their kinship [with the pear]; the must-apples from the speed of their ripening, which are now called *melimela* [honey-apples] from their honeyed taste; the orbiculata from their shape, a circle turned into a round — the Greeks are evidence that these first grew in Epirus, since they call them Epirotic —; the orthomastia from their likeness to breasts; and those which the Belgae call spadonia from their condition of seedlessness, as if castrated.
passages.notes: Stray "5" omitted; "magnitude" read as "magnitudo".

passages.original: patriae nomina habent serissima omnium Amerina, Picentina, Numantina , Alexandrina, Numidiana, Graeca et in iis Tarentina, Signina, quae alii a colore testacea appellant, sicut onychina, purpurea, ab odore myrapia, laurea, nardina, tempore hordearia , collo ampullacea, et Coriolana, Bruttia gentilitatis, cucurbitina, acidula suci. incerta nominum causa est barbaricis, Veneriis quae colorata dicunt, regiis quae minimo pediculo sessilia, patriciis, vocimis, viridibus oblongisque. praeterea dixit volema Vergilius a Catone sumpta, qui et sementiva et mustea nominat.
passages.english: Names from their native land are borne by the latest of all, the Amerine, Picentine, Numantine, Alexandrine, Numidian, Greek and, among these, Tarentine [pears]; the Signine, which others call *testacea* from their [brick-]colour, as also the onyx-pears and purple pears; from their smell the myrapia, laurel- and nard-pears; from their season the barley-pears; from their neck the flask-pears; and the Coriolan and Bruttian from family; the gourd-pears and the sourish ones from their juice. The reason for the names is uncertain in the case of the barbarian pears; the Venus-pears, which they call coloured; the royal ones, which sit on a very short stalk; the patrician; the *vocima*; and the green and oblong ones. Besides these Virgil spoke of *volema*, taken from Cato, who also names seed-time pears and must-pears.
passages.notes: "vocimis" unidentified.

passages.original: sunt praeterea eaedem serotinae et praecoces, biferae, alba ac nigra, cum messe vindemiaque maturescentes . serotinae et a corio appellatae duro, ex Chalcidicis quarundam trifero proventu. Tarenti tantum praedulces nascuntur, quas vocant onas . Cato de ficis ita memorat: Ficos mariscas in loco cretoso aut aperto serito, in loco autem crassiore aut stercorato Africanas et Herculaneas, Sacontinas, hibernas, Tellanas atras pediculo longo. postea tot subiere nomina atque genera, ut vel hoc solum aestimantibus appareat mutatam esse vitam. sunt et hibernae quibusdam provinciis, uti Moesiae, sed artis, non naturae. parvarum genusarborum post autumnum fimo contegunt, deprehensasque in his hieme grossos, quae mitiore caelo refossae cum arbore atque in lucem remissae novossoles aliosque, quam quibus vixere, avide tamquam iterum natae accipiunt et curl venientium flore maturescunt, alieno praecoces anno, in tractu vel gelidissimo .
passages.english: There are besides the same [figs] late and early, two-crop, white and black, ripening with the harvest and the vintage. Late ones also named from their hard skin; among the Chalcidian some with a triple yield. At Tarentum alone very sweet ones grow, which they call *onae*. Cato records this about figs: "Plant marisca figs in chalky or open ground, but in richer or manured ground the African and Herculanean, Saguntine, winter, and black Tellane with a long stalk." Since then so many names and kinds have come in that, even to those judging by this alone, it is evident that life has changed. There are also winter figs in certain provinces, such as Moesia, but by art, not nature. They cover a kind of small tree with dung after autumn, and the unripe figs caught on them by winter, when the weather turns milder, are dug up again with the tree and brought back into the light, and eagerly take in new suns, other than those under which they lived, as if born a second time, and ripen with the blossom of the coming [crop], early in someone else's year, even in a very cold region.
passages.notes: "curl" read as "cum"; "Sacontinas" taken as Saguntine; "onas" uncertain.

passages.original: Sed a Catone appellata iam tum Africana admonet Africae ad ingens docimentum usi eo pomo. namque perni ciali odio Carthaginis flagrans nepotumque securitatis anxius, cum clamaret omni senatu Carthaginem delendam, adtulit quodam die in curiam praecocem ex ea provincia ficum ostendensque patribus : Interrogo vos, inquit, quando hanc pomum demptam putetis ex arbore.
passages.english: But the African [fig], already so named by Cato, reminds [us] of Africa, for he used that fruit as a tremendous demonstration. For burning with deadly hatred of Carthage and anxious for the security of his descendants, when he was crying out in every senate [session] that Carthage must be destroyed, he brought one day into the senate-house an early fig from that province, and showing it to the fathers said: "I ask you, when do you think this fruit was picked from the tree?"

passages.original: generosissima quibus circa pediculos tenera folia. quartum genus torminale appellant, remedio tantum probabile, adsiduum proventu minimumque pomo, arbore dissimile, foliis paene platani . non ferunt ante trimatum ex ullo genere. Cato et sorva condi sapa tradit.
passages.english: The finest are those which have tender leaves around the stalks. The fourth kind they call *torminale* [colic-sorb], to be commended only as a remedy, constant in yield and smallest in fruit, unlike [the others] in its tree, with leaves almost [like those] of the plane. No kind bears before its third year. Cato records that sorbs too are preserved in boiled-down must.

passages.original: Cato tria genera myrti prodidit, nigram, candidam , coniugulam, fortassis a coniugiis, ex illo Cluacinae genere. nunc et alia distinctio sativae aut silvestris et in utraque latifoliae, in silvestri propria oxymyrsinae. sativarum genera topiarii faciunt Tarentinam folio minuto, nostratem patulo, hexasticham densissimo, senis foliorum versibus .
passages.english: Cato recorded three kinds of myrtle, black, white, and conjugal, perhaps from marriages, of the kind belonging to Cluacina. Now there is also another distinction, of cultivated or wild, and in both a broad-leaved [kind], and peculiar to the wild the *oxymyrsine*. Of the cultivated ones the ornamental gardeners make [these] kinds: the Tarentine with small leaf, ours with spreading leaf, and the hexasticha with very dense leaf, in six rows of leaves.

passages.original: Laurus triumphis proprie dicatur, vel gratissima domibus, ianitrix Caesarum pontificumque. sola et domos exornat et ante limina excubat. duo eius genera tradidit Cato , Delphicam et Cypriam. Pompeius Len a e u s adiecit quam mustacem appellavit, quoniam mustaceis subiceretur: hanc esse folio maximo flaccidoque et albicante ; Delphicam aequali colore viridiorem, maximis bacis atque e viridi rubentibus ac victores Delphis coronare ut triumphantes Romae;
passages.english: The laurel is properly dedicated to triumphs, and is most welcome in homes, doorkeeper of the Caesars and the pontiffs. It alone both adorns houses and keeps watch before their thresholds. Cato recorded two kinds of it, the Delphic and the Cyprian. Pompeius Lenaeus added one which he called *mustax*, because it was placed under must-cakes: [he says] this has a very large, limp, whitish leaf; the Delphic, of even colour, is greener, with very large berries, reddish out of green, and with it victors are crowned at Delphi, as those who triumph are at Rome;

passages.original: Ilicis duo genera. ex his in Italia folio non multum ab oleis distant milaces a quibusdam Graecis dictae; in provinciis aquifoliae sunt ilices. glans utriusque brevior et gracilior, quam Homerus aculon appellat eoque nomine a glande distinguit. masculas ilices negant ferre.
passages.english: There are two kinds of holm-oak. Of these, the ones in Italy, which differ little from olives in leaf, are called *milaces* by some Greeks; in the provinces the holm-oaks are holly-leaved. The acorn of both is shorter and slenderer; Homer calls it *akylos* and by that name distinguishes it from the acorn. They say that male holm-oaks do not bear.
passages.notes: Greek *akylos* (Latin 'aculon') is the acorn of the holm-oak.

passages.original: Glans fagea suem hilarem facit, carnem cocibilem ac levem et utilem stomacho; iligna suem angustam, nitidam, strigosam; ponderosam querna, diffusam, gravissima et ipsa glandium atque dulcissima. proximam huic cerream tradit Nigidius, nec ex alia solidiorem carnem, sed duram. iligna temptari sues, nisi paulatim detur. hanc novissimam cadere. fungosam carnem fieri aesculo, robore, subere.
passages.english: Beech mast makes a pig lively, its flesh easy to cook, light and good for the stomach; holm-oak acorns make a pig slim, sleek and lean; the common-oak acorn makes it heavy and spread out, being itself the heaviest and sweetest of acorns. Nigidius reports that next to this comes the Turkey-oak acorn, and that no other gives firmer flesh, but it is tough. [He says] that pigs are made ill by holm-oak acorns unless they are given gradually, and that this acorn is the last to fall. The flesh becomes spongy from the winter oak, the hard oak and the cork oak.
passages.notes: The identifications of the oak species (aesculus, robur, cerrus) are uncertain.

passages.original: postea tota arbor succiditur et medulla eius uritur. sic et in Syria terelhintho detrahunt cortices, ibi quidem et e ramis ac radicibus, cum resina damnetur ex his partibus. in Macedonia laricem masculam urunt, feminae radices tantum. Theopompus scripsit in Apolloniatarum agro picem fossilem, non deteriorem Macedonica, inveniri. pix optima ubique ex apricis aquilonis situ, ex opacis horridior virusque praeferens, frigida hieme deterior ac minus copiosa et decolor.
passages.english: Afterwards the whole tree is cut down and its pith is burned. In this way too in Syria they strip the bark from the terebinth, there indeed also from the branches and roots, although resin from these parts is held to be poor. In Macedonia they burn the male larch, but only the roots of the female. Theopompus wrote that in the territory of the Apolloniates mineral pitch is found, no worse than the Macedonian. The best pitch everywhere comes from sunny places with a northern aspect; from shady places it is rougher and has an unpleasant smell; in a cold winter it is worse, less plentiful and discoloured.
passages.notes: 'terelhintho' read as 'terebintho'.

passages.original: utraque autem immittitur in perticas asseresve amputation ramorum , qui XIII anno denariis singulis veneunt, quaestuosissima in satus ratione silva, vulgoque dotem filiae antiqui plantaria ea appellabant. huic patria insula Creta, quamquam Cato Tarentinam eam appellat, credo, quod primum eo venerit. et in Aenaria succisa regerminat; sed in Creta quocumque in loco terram moverit quispiam, nisu naturali haec gignitur protinusque emicat, illa vero etiam non appellato solo ac sponte maximeque in Idaeis montibus et quos Albos vocant summisque in his, unde numquam nives absunt, plurima, quod miremur, alibi non nisi in tepore proveniens et nutricem magno opere fastidiens.
passages.english: Both kinds, moreover, are grown into poles or stakes by lopping the branches, and these sell at a denarius apiece in the thirteenth year, making it the most profitable woodland in the planting reckoning; and the ancients commonly called these plantations a daughter's dowry. Its native land is the island of Crete, although Cato calls it Tarentine, I believe because it first came there. On Aenaria too it shoots again when cut down; but in Crete, wherever anyone has turned the soil, this one is produced by a natural impulse and springs up at once, while that one grows even from ground not tilled, and of its own accord, especially on the mountains of Ida and those they call the White Mountains, and most abundantly on their summits, where the snow is never absent; which is remarkable, since elsewhere it grows only in warmth and greatly dislikes a nurse.
passages.notes: The subject appears to be the cypress (from context); 'amputation' read as 'amputatione'. The contrast 'haec… illa' presumably refers to the two kinds just mentioned; the sense of 'nutricem… fastidiens' (dislikes tending/a nurse-tree) is uncertain.

passages.original: diebus VII proximis, quibus luna plena fuerit, optime eximitur. omnino caveto ni quam materiem doles neve caedas neve tangas nisi siccam, neve gelidam neve rorulentam . —Tiberius item et in capillo tondendo servavit interlunia . M. Varro adversus defluvia praecipit observandum id a pleniluniis.—
passages.english: "[Timber] is best taken out during the seven days after the moon has been full. Above all take care not to hew, cut or touch any timber unless it is dry, and not when it is frosty or dewy." Tiberius likewise observed the interlunar days in cutting his hair. M. Varro advises that, against hair falling out, this be observed from the full moon onwards.
passages.notes: The quotation is from Cato, as the preceding context shows. Varro's advice presumably means cutting hair in the waning moon.

passages.original: nec non ex ipsis vitibus causas mutuantur in frigidis praecoces serendo, ut maturitas antecedat algorem, quae poma vitesque rorem oderint, contra ortus, ut statim auferat sol, quae ament, ad occasus vel etiam ad septentriones, ut diutius eo fruantur. ceteri fere rationem naturae secuti in aquilonem obversas vites et arbores poni suasere. odoratiorem etiam fieri talem fructum Democritus putat.
passages.english: They also borrow principles from the vines themselves: in cold places they plant early-ripening kinds, so that ripeness may come before the frost; fruit trees and vines that dislike dew [they plant] facing the sunrise, so that the sun may remove it at once; those that like it, facing the west or even the north, so that they may enjoy it longer. Most others, following the logic of nature, have advised that vines and trees be set facing the north wind. Democritus thinks that fruit of this kind also becomes more fragrant.

passages.original: intellegere modo libeat dictam mira significatione teneram , et quidquid optari debet, in eo vocabulo invenietur. illa temperatae ubertatis, illa mollis facilisque culturae, nec madida nec sitiens. illa post vomerem nitescens, qualem fons ingeniorum Homerus in armis a deo caelatam dixit addiditque miraculum nigrescentis, quamvis fieret ex auro. illa quam recentem exquirunt inprobae alites vomerem comitantes corvique aratoris vestigia ipsa rodentes. reddatur hoc in loco luxuriae quoque sententia et aliqua in propositum certe. Cicero, lux doctrinarum altera, Meliora, inquit, unguenta sunt quae terram, quam quae crocum sapiunt. hoc enim maluit dixisse quam redolent. ita est profecto, illa erit optima quae unguenta sapiet. quod si admonendi sumus, qualis sit terrae odor ille qui quaeritur, contingit saepe etiam quiescente ea sub occasum solis, in quo loco arcus caelestes deiecere capita sua, et cum a siccitate continua immaduit imbre.
passages.english: Only let us be willing to understand it, [soil] called 'tender' with remarkable significance, and whatever ought to be wished for will be found in that word. That soil is of moderate richness, of soft and easy cultivation, neither soaked nor thirsty. That soil gleams after the ploughshare, such as Homer, the fountainhead of genius, said was engraved by a god on the armour, and he added the marvel of its turning black although it was made of gold. That soil is the one which, freshly turned, the shameless birds seek out as they follow the ploughshare, and the crows pecking at the very footsteps of the ploughman. Let a remark about luxury also be given in this place, and one certainly to some extent to the purpose. Cicero, the second light of learning, says: 'Ointments that taste of earth are better than those that taste of saffron.' For he preferred to say this rather than 'smell of.' So it is indeed: that soil will be best which tastes of ointments. But if we must be told what that odour of earth is which is sought, it often occurs even when the earth is at rest, towards sunset, in a place where rainbows have let down their ends, and when after continuous drought it has been moistened by rain.

passages.original: Fimi plures differentiae, ipsa res antiqua. iam apud Homerum regius senex agrum ita laetificans suis manibus reperitur. Augeas rex in Graecia excogitasse traditur , divulgasse vero Hercules in Italia, quae regi suo Stercuto Fauni filio ob hoc inventum inmortalitatem tribuit .
passages.english: There are several differences of manure, and the thing itself is ancient. Already in Homer an old king is found enriching his field in this way with his own hands. King Augeas is said to have devised it in Greece, and Hercules to have spread it in Italy, which granted immortality to its king Stercutus, son of Faunus, for this invention.

passages.original: Cato: Stercus unde facias, stramenta, lupinum , paleas, fabalia ac frondis iligneam quernea m. ex segete evellito ebulum, cicutam et circum salicta herbam altam ulvamque. eam substernito ovibus, bubusque frondem putidam. -Vinea si macra erit, sarmenta sua comburito et indidem inarato. idemque: Ubi saturus eris frumentum, oves ibi delectato.
passages.english: Cato: 'You can make manure from straw, lupins, chaff, bean-stalks, and holm-oak and oak leaves. Pull up from the cornfield danewort and hemlock, and around the willow-beds tall grass and sedge. Spread this as litter for the sheep, and rotten leaves for the oxen.' 'If a vineyard is poor, burn its own prunings and plough them in on the spot.' And likewise: 'Where you are going to sow grain, fold sheep there.'
passages.notes: 'delectato' is probably for 'dilectato'/'stabulato' (pen); sense 'fold' given.

passages.original: in sulco repastinato palmi altitudine vicenae fere acervatim *seruntur*, mense Martio. eaedem et propagine*, triumphalis talea tantum. myrti genera omnia in Campania bacis seruntur, Romae propagine. Tarentinam Democritus et alio modo seri docet, grandissimis bacarum tusis leviter, ne grana frangantur,..... eaque intrita restem circumlini atque ita seri. parietem fore... densitatis , ex quo virgulae differantur. sic et spinas saepis causa serunt, tomice moris spinarum circumlita.
passages.english: They are sown in a trench dug over to a palm's depth, about twenty in a heap, in the month of March. The same kinds [are grown] also by layering, the triumphal [laurel] only by cutting. All kinds of myrtle are sown from berries in Campania, at Rome by layering. Democritus teaches that the Tarentine is also sown another way: the largest berries are pounded lightly, so that the seeds are not broken, [...] a rope is smeared with this paste and sown thus. A hedge will be formed [...] of density, from which the shoots may be transplanted. In this way they also sow thorns for a hedge, smearing a cord of rush with a paste of thorn-berries.
passages.notes: The text has lacunae (marked by dots) after 'frangantur' and in 'parietem fore... densitatis'; translated as far as legible. 'tomice' taken as a rope of rush; 'moris' as blackberries/thorn-berries.

passages.original: ficus si in scilla—bulborum hoc genus est— seratur, ocissime ferre traditur pomum neque vermiculationi obnoxium, quo vitio carent et reliqua poma similiter sata. radicum filis magnam adhibendam curam, ut exemptas appareat, non evolsas, quis dubitet? qua ratione et reliqua confessa omittimus, sicuti terram circa radices festuca cospissandam, quod Cato primum in ea re esse censet, plagam quoque a trunco oblini fimo et foliis praeligari praecipiens.
passages.english: If a fig is planted in a squill (this is a kind of bulb), it is said to bear fruit very quickly and not liable to worms; other fruits planted in the same way are also free of this fault. Who would doubt that great care must be taken of the fibres of the roots, so that they appear taken out, not torn up? For which reason we also omit the other points that are acknowledged, such as that the earth around the roots should be packed down with a rammer, which Cato judges the first thing in this matter, instructing also that the wound at the trunk be smeared with manure and bound round with leaves.
passages.notes: 'exemptas' for 'exempta' and 'cospissandam' for 'conspissandam'; 'festuca' here a rammer.

passages.original: rubi namque curvati gracilitate et simul proceritate nimia defigunt rursus in terram capita iterumque nascuntur ex sese repleturi omnia, ni resistat cultura, prorsus ut possint videri homines terrae causa geniti. ita pessima atque execranda res propaginem tamen docuit ac viviradicem. eadem autem natura et hederis. Cato propagari praeter vitem tradit ficum, oleam, punicam, malorum genera omnia, laurus , pruna, myrtum, nuces abellanas et Praenestinas, platanum .
passages.english: For brambles, bent by their slenderness and at the same time excessive length, fix their tips back in the earth and are born again from themselves, ready to fill everything if cultivation did not resist, so that men might seem to have been born altogether for the sake of the earth. Thus a most wretched and accursed thing nevertheless taught layering and the rooted cutting. Ivies too have the same nature. Cato records that besides the vine the following are propagated by layering: the fig, olive, pomegranate, all kinds of apple, laurels, plums, myrtle, Abellan and Praenestine nuts, and the plane.

passages.original: ergo amputatis omnibus ramis, ne sucum avocent, nitidissima in parte quaque praecipua cernatur hilaritas, exempta scutula ita, ne descendat ulta corticem ferrum, inprimitur ex alia cortex par cum sui germinis mamma, sic conpage densata, ut cicatrici locus non sit et statim fiat unitas, nec umorem nec adflatum recipiens; nihilominus tamen et luto munire et vinculo melius. hoc genus non pridem repertum volunt qui novis moribus favent, sed iam et apud veteres Graecos invenitur et apud Catonem, qui oleam ficumque sic inseri iussit, mensura etiam praefinita secundum reliquam diligentiam suam: cortices scalpro excidi quattuor digitorum longitudine et trium latitudine atque ita coagmentari et ilia sua intrita oblini, eadem ratione ut in malo.
passages.english: So, all the branches having been cut off so that they do not draw away the sap, in the sleekest part, where the greatest vigour is seen, a small patch is removed in such a way that the blade does not go below the bark, and a matching piece of bark from another [tree], with its bud, is pressed in, fitted so closely that there is no room for a scar and a union forms at once, admitting neither moisture nor air; nevertheless it is better also to protect it with clay and a binding. Those who favour new ways claim that this method was discovered not long ago, but it is found already among the ancient Greeks and in Cato, who ordered the olive and fig to be grafted thus, even prescribing the measurements in keeping with his usual care: the bark is to be cut out with a knife four fingers long and three wide, then fitted together and smeared with that paste of his, in the same way as for the apple.
passages.notes: 'ulta' read as 'ultra'. 'ilia sua intrita' read as 'illa sua intrita' (his paste).

passages.original: <7> Est etiamnum nova inserendi ratio, ne quid sciens quidem praeteream, quod usquam invenerim, Columellae excogitata, ut adfirmat ipse, qua vel diversae insociabilesque arborum naturae copulentur, ut fici atque oleae. iuxta hanc seri ficum iubet non ampliore intervallo , quam ut contingi large possit ramo oleae quam maxime sequaci atque oboedituro, eumque omni interim tempore edomari meditatione curvandi.
passages.english: There is, moreover, a new method of grafting (so that I may not knowingly pass over anything I have found anywhere), devised by Columella, as he himself asserts, by which even different and incompatible natures of trees may be joined, such as the fig and the olive. He directs that a fig be planted beside an olive at no greater distance than allows it to be reached easily by a branch of the olive that is as pliant and obedient as possible, and that this branch be meanwhile trained the whole time by practice in bending.

passages.original: <20> Cato de omni cultura vitium ita praecipit: Quam altissimam vineam facito alligatoque recte, dum ne nimium constringas. hoc modo eam curato: capita vitium per sementim ablaqueato. vineam putatam circumfodito, arare incipito, ultro citroque sulcos perpetuos ducito. vites teneras quam primum propagato, sicoccato: veteres quam minimum castrato; potius, si opus erit, deicito biennioque post praecidito. vitem novellam resecari tum erit tempus, ubi valebit.
passages.english: Cato gives these instructions on the whole cultivation of vines: "Make the vineyard as tall as possible, and tie it up properly, provided you do not bind it too tightly. Tend it in this way: during the sowing season dig round the heads of the vines. When the vineyard has been pruned, dig around it, begin to plough, and draw continuous furrows back and forth. Propagate young vines by layering as soon as possible, in this way; castrate the old ones as little as possible; rather, if need be, lay them down and two years later cut them back. It will be time to cut back a young vine when it is strong."
passages.notes: "sicoccato" is evidently a corruption of "sic occato" or similar; translated as "in this way" (Cato's text has "sic propagato"), though "occato" (harrow) may be intended.

passages.original: Olea praeter vermiculationem, quam aeque ac ficus sentit, clavum etiam patitur, sive fungum placet dici vel patellam. haec est solis exustio. nocere tradit Cato et museum rubrum. nocet plerumque vitibus atque oleis et nimia fertilitas. scabies communis omnium est. inpetigo et, quae adgnasci solent, cocleae peculiaria ficorum vitia, nec ubique. sunt enim quaedam aegritudines et locorum.
passages.english: The olive, besides worm-infestation, which it suffers just as the fig does, also suffers from the 'nail', or 'fungus' or 'little dish' if one prefers to call it that. This is a scorching by the sun. Cato records that red moss is also harmful. Excessive fruitfulness too often harms vines and olives. Scab is common to all. Impetigo, and the snails that usually grow on them, are diseases peculiar to figs, and not everywhere; for there are some diseases that belong also to places.
passages.notes: "museum" read as "muscum" (moss), a scanning error.

passages.original: <6> Vitibus praeter vermiculationem et siderationem morbus peculiaris articulatio tribus de causis: una vi tempestatium germinibus ablatis, altera, ut notavit Theophrastus , in supinum excisis, tertia culturae imperitia laesis. omnes enim earum iniuriae in articulis sentiuntur. siderationis genus est et his deflorescentibus roratio, aut cum acini, priusquam crescant, decocuntur in callum.
passages.english: Vines, besides worm-infestation and blight, have a peculiar disease, 'jointing', from three causes: first, when the buds have been carried off by violent storms; second, as Theophrastus noted, when they have been cut facing upwards; third, when they have been damaged by unskilled cultivation. For all injuries to them are felt at the joints. A kind of blight is also a 'bedewing' while they are shedding their blossom, or when the grapes, before they grow, are hardened into a callus.

passages.original: Iuniorum e familia Bubulcum nominarunt, qui bubus optime utebatur. quin et in sacris nihil religiosius confarreationis vinculo erat, novaeque nuptae farreum praeferebant. agrum male colere censorium probrum iudicabatur, atque, ut refert Cato, cum virum bonum laudantes bonum agricolam bonumque colonum dixissent, amplissime laudasse existimabantur. hinc et locupletes dicebant loci, hoc est agri, plenos. pecunia ipsa a pecore appellabatur.
passages.english: In the family of the Junii they named one Bubulcus, who handled oxen best. Indeed, in religious rites too nothing was more sacred than the bond of *confarreatio* [marriage by the offering of spelt], and new brides carried a spelt cake before them. To cultivate land badly was judged a matter for censorial reproof, and, as Cato reports, when people praising a good man had called him a good farmer and a good husbandman, they were thought to have praised him most highly. Hence also they called the rich *locupletes*, that is, 'full of place', meaning of land. Money itself (*pecunia*) was named from cattle (*pecus*).

passages.original: quasdam obcaecari et in alias dirigi maiores patentioresque et, si sit occasio, silice vel glarea sterni, ora autem earum binis utrimque lapidibus statuminari et alio superintegi. silvae extirpandae rationem Democritus prodidit, lupini flore in suco cicutae uno die macerato sparsisque radicibus.
passages.english: [It is useful that] some [ditches] be blinded and others directed into larger and more open ones, and, if there is opportunity, that they be laid with flint or gravel, while their mouths be propped with two stones on each side and covered with another on top. Democritus has handed down a method for clearing a wood: the flower of lupine steeped for one day in hemlock juice and sprinkled on the roots.
passages.notes: The opening clause depends on the construction in the preceding context ("utilissimum est").

passages.original: Sed non ante supra dictum geniculorum numerum conceptus est spicae, qui ut spem sui fecit, iiii aut V tardissime diebus florere incipiunt totidemque aut paulo pluribus deflorescunt, hordea vero, cum tardissime, diebus VII. Varro quater novenis diebus fruges absolvi tradit et mense nono meti.
passages.english: But the ear is not conceived before the number of joints stated above, and once it has given promise of itself, [the grains] begin to flower at the latest in four or five days, and lose their flower in as many or a few more days; barley, however, at the latest in seven days. Varro reports that the crops are completed in four times nine days and are reaped in the ninth month.

passages.original: Antiquissimum in cibis hordeum, sicut Atheniensium ritu Menandro auctore apparet et gladiatorum cognomine , qui hordearii vocabantur. polentam quoque Graeci non aliunde praeferunt. pluribus fit haec modis. Graeci perfusum aqua hordeum siccant nocte una ac postero die frigunt, dein molis frangunt.
passages.english: Barley is the most ancient among foods, as appears from the custom of the Athenians, on Menander's authority, and from the nickname of gladiators, who were called *hordearii* ['barley-men']. The Greeks too prefer polenta made from nothing else. It is made in several ways. The Greeks soak barley in water, dry it for one night, and the next day roast it, then break it in mills.

passages.original: Aegyptus similaginem conficit e tritico suo nequaquam Italicae parem. qui zea utuntur non habent far. est et haec ltaliae, in Campania maxime, semenque appellatur . hoc habet nomen res praeclara, ut mox docebimus, propter quam Homerus ζείδωρος ἄρουρα dixit, non, ut aliqui arbitrantur, quoniam vitam donaret. amylum quoque ex ea fit priore crassius; haec sola differentia est. ex omni genere durissimum far et contra hiemes firmissimum . patitur frigidissimos locos et minus subactos vel aestuosos sitientesque.
passages.english: Egypt makes fine flour from its own wheat, by no means equal to the Italian. Those who use zea do not have spelt. This too belongs to Italy, especially in Campania, and is called 'seed'. This name belongs to an excellent thing, as we shall shortly show, on account of which Homer spoke of 'zeidoros aroura' [zea-giving ploughland], not, as some think, because it gave life. Starch too is made from it, coarser than the former; this is the only difference. Of every kind, spelt is the hardiest and most resistant to winters. It tolerates very cold places and less worked ones, or hot and thirsty ones.
passages.notes: "ltaliae" read as "Italiae".

passages.original: Pistores Romae non fuere ad Persicum usque bellum annis ab urbe condita super DLXXX. ipsi panem faciebant Quirites, mulierumque id opus maxime erat, sicut etiam nunc in plurimis gentium. artoptas iam Plautus appellat in fabula, quam Aululariam inscripsit, magna ob id concertatione eruditorum, an is versus poetae sit illius, certumque fit Atei Capitonis sententia cocos tum panem lautioribus coquere solitos, pistoresque tantum eos, qui far pisebant, nominatos.
passages.english: There were no bakers at Rome until the war with Perseus, more than 580 years after the founding of the city. The citizens made bread themselves, and this was chiefly the work of women, as it still is among most peoples. Plautus already names *artoptae* [bread-bakers] in the play he entitled the Aulularia, which has caused much dispute among scholars whether that line is that poet's; and it becomes certain from the opinion of Ateius Capito that cooks at that time used to bake bread for the wealthier, and that only those who pounded spelt were called *pistores*.

passages.original: Apud antiquos erat pabuli genus, quod Cato ocinum vocat, quo sistebant alvom bubus. id erat e pabuli segete viride desectum, antequam generaret. Sura Mamilius aliter id interpretatur et tradit fabae modios x, viciae II, tantundem erviliae in iugero autumno misceri et seri solitos, melius et avena Graeca, cui non cadit semen, admixta.
passages.english: Among the ancients there was a kind of fodder which Cato calls *ocinum*, with which they checked the bowels of oxen. It was cut green from a fodder crop before it produced seed. Mamilius Sura interprets it differently and records that 10 modii of bean, 2 of vetch and the same amount of chickling were customarily mixed and sown per iugerum in autumn, and better still with Greek oats, whose seed does not fall, mixed in.

passages.original: <3> Aratione per traversum iterata occatio sequitur , ubi res poscit, crate vel rastro, et sato semine iteratur haec quoque, ubi consuetudo patitur, crate contenta vel tabula aratro adnexa—quod vocant lirare — operiente semina; ni operiantur, quae primum appellata, deliratio est. quarto seri sulco Vergilius existimatur voluisse, cum dixit optimam esse segetem, quae bis soles, bis frigora sensisset. spissius solum, sicut plerumque in Italia, quinto sulco seri melius est, in Tuscis vero nono. at fabam et viciam non proscisso serere sine damno conpendium operae est.
passages.english: When the ploughing has been repeated crosswise, harrowing follows, where the situation requires it, with a hurdle or a rake; and after the seed has been sown this too is repeated, where custom allows, being content with a hurdle or a board attached to the plough, which covers the seeds; this they call *lirare* [to ridge]. If the seeds are not covered, this is what was first called *deliratio* [going out of the furrow]. Virgil is thought to have meant that sowing should be done at the fourth ploughing, when he said that the best crop is the one that has felt the sun twice and the cold twice. Denser soil, as is generally found in Italy, is better sown at the fifth ploughing, and in Etruria indeed at the ninth. But to sow beans and vetch on land that has not been broken up is a saving of labour without loss.
passages.notes: *sulcus* here means a ploughing, not a single furrow. The pun on *lirare/deliratio* (origin of 'delirium') cannot be kept in English.

passages.original: idque, ne nobis tantum putemus accidere, et reliqua fallit animalia sagaciora circa hoc, ut quo vita eorum constet, aestivasque alites praeposteri aut praeproperi rigores necant, hibernas aestus. ideo Vergilius errantium quoque siderum rationem ediscendam praecipit, admonens observandum frigidae Saturni stellae transitum. sunt qui certissimum veris indicium arbitrentur ob infirmitatem animalis papiliones. sed eo ipso anno, cum commentaremur haec, notatum est, proventum eorum ter repetito frigore extinctum advenasque volucres a.
passages.english: And this, lest we think it happens only to us, also deceives the other animals, which are keener in this matter, since their life depends on it: untimely or premature frosts kill the summer birds, and [untimely] heat the winter ones. For this reason Virgil also directs that the system of the wandering stars be learned, warning that the passage of the cold star of Saturn must be watched. There are some who think that butterflies, because the creature is so frail, are the surest sign of spring. But in the very year in which we were writing these notes, it was observed that their brood was wiped out by cold returning three times, and that the migrant birds, which on
passages.notes: The passage breaks off mid-sentence; the final 'a.' appears to begin a date ('a[nte] d[iem] VI kal. Febr.', 27 January) continued in the following text.

passages.original: minus hoc in reliquis mirum, quos diversi excusaverint tractus. eorum, qui in eadem regione dissedere , unam discordiam ponemus exempli gratia: occasum matutinum vergiliarum Hesiodus—nam huius quoque nomine exstat astrologia—tradidit fieri, cum aequinoctium autumni conficeretur, Thales xxv die ab aequinoctio , Anaximander XXXI, Euctemon XLIIIII Eudoxus XLVIII. nos sequimur observationem Caesaris maxime; haec erit Italiae ratio. dicemus autem et aliorum placita, quoniam non unius terrae, sed totius naturae interpretes sumus, non auctoribus positis—id enim verbosum est —, sed regionibus.
passages.english: This is less surprising in the rest, whom the different regions [they observed] may excuse. Of those who disagreed within the same region we shall set down one disagreement by way of example. Hesiod (for an astronomy also survives under his name) recorded that the morning setting of the Pleiades occurs when the autumn equinox is completed; Thales [put it] on the 25th day after the equinox, Anaximander on the 31st, Euctemon on the 44th, Eudoxus on the 48th. We follow above all the observation of Caesar; this will be the reckoning for Italy. But we shall also state the views of others, since we are interpreters not of one land but of the whole of nature, setting them down not by authors (for that would be wordy) but by regions.
passages.notes: 'XLIIIII' read as 44.

passages.original: Ex his unum hoc erit idem et lino ac papaveri serendo. Cato de papavere ita tradit: Virgas et sarmenta, quae tibi usioni supererunt, in segete comburito. ubi eas combusseris, ibi papaver serito. silvestre in miro usu est melle decoctum ad faucium remedia, visque somnifera etiam sativo. et hactenus de hiberna semente.
passages.english: Of these, this one [time] will also be the same for sowing flax and poppy. Cato writes thus about the poppy: 'Burn the twigs and vine-cuttings that are left over from your use in the cornfield. Where you have burnt them, sow poppy there.' The wild poppy, boiled down with honey, is remarkably useful as a remedy for the throat, and the cultivated kind too has a sleep-inducing power. So much for the winter sowing.

passages.original: Verum ut pariter omnis culturae quoddam breviarium peragatur, eodem tempore conveniet arbores stercorare, adcumulare item vineas—sufficit in iugerum opera—et, ubi patietur loci ratio, arbusta ac vineas putare, solum seminariis bipalio praeparare, incilia aperire, aquam de agro pellere, torcular lavare et recondere. a kal. Novemb. gallinis ova supponere nolito, donec bruma conficiatur . in eum diem ternadena subicito aestate tota, hieme pauciora, non tamen infra novena. Democritus talem futuram hiemem arbitratur, qualis fuerit brumae dies et circa eum terni; item solstitio aestatem. circa brumam plerisque bis septeni halcyonum feturae ventorum quiete molliunt caelum. sed et in his et in aliis omnibus ex eventu significationum intellegi sidera debebunt , non ad dies utique praefinitos expectari tempestatum vadimonia.
passages.english: But so that a kind of summary of all cultivation may be gone through alongside, at the same time it will be proper to manure trees, likewise to heap earth around vines (one day's labour is enough for a iugerum), and, where the nature of the place allows, to prune tree-trained and other vines, to prepare the soil for nurseries with the double-spade, to open the drainage channels, to drive water off the land, and to wash and put away the press. From the first of November do not set eggs under hens until the winter solstice is over. Up to that day put thirteen under each throughout the summer, fewer in winter, but not under nine. Democritus thinks that the winter will be like the day of the solstice and the three days around it, and likewise the summer [like] the summer solstice. Around the winter solstice, according to most, twice seven days of the halcyons' breeding soften the sky with a calm of the winds. But both in these and in all other matters the stars must be understood from the outcome of their signs, and the appointed appearances of storms are not to be expected on fixed days in any case.
passages.notes: *vadimonia* (legal term: sureties for appearance in court) used figuratively of weather.

passages.original: <3> Cato verna opera sic definit: scrobes fieri, seminaria.... propagari, in locis crassis et umidis ulmos, ficos, poma, oleas seri, prata stercorari luna sitiente; quae rigua non erunt, a flatu favoni defendi et purgari, herbas malas radicitus erui, ficos interputari, seminaria fieri et vetera sarciri: haec antequam vineam fodere incipias.
passages.english: Cato defines the spring tasks thus: trenches are to be made, nurseries .... layered; in rich and moist places elms, figs, fruit trees and olives are to be planted; meadows manured when the moon is waning; those which are not irrigated to be protected from the west wind and cleared; bad weeds pulled up by the roots; figs thinned by pruning; nurseries made and old ones repaired: [do] these before you begin to dig the vineyard.
passages.notes: Lacuna after 'seminaria' marked in the edition. *luna sitiente* ('thirsty moon') taken as waning or dry moon; sense uncertain.

passages.original: herba optima in prato trifoli, proxima graminis, pessima nummuli siliquam etiam diram ferentis. invisa et equisaeti est, a similitudine equinae saetae. secandi tempus, cum spica deflorescere coepit atque roborari. secandum, antequam inarescat. Cato: fenum, inquit, ne sero seces: prius quam se- men maturum sit. quidam pridie rigant. ubi non sunt rigua, noctibus roscidis secari melius. quaedam partes Italiae post messem secant. <5> Fuit hoc quoque maioris inpendii apud priores, Creticis tantum transmarinisque cotibus notis nec nisi oleo aciem falcis excitantibus;
passages.english: The best plant in a meadow is clover, next is grass; worst is *nummulus* [moneywort], which also bears a dreadful pod. Also hated is horsetail, [named] from its likeness to a horse's hair. The time for cutting is when the ear has begun to shed its flower and to harden. It must be cut before it dries out. Cato says: 'Do not cut hay late; [cut it] before the seed is ripe.' Some water it the day before. Where there is no irrigation, it is better cut on dewy nights. Some parts of Italy cut it after the harvest. This too was a greater expense among our predecessors, since only Cretan and other overseas whetstones were known, and they sharpened the sickle's edge only with oil;
passages.notes: Identification of *nummulus* uncertain.

passages.original: Etenim praedicta ventorum ratione, ne saepius eadem dicantur, transire convenit ad reliqua tempestatum praesagia, quoniam et hoc placuisse Vergilio magno opere video, siquidem in ipsa messe saepe concurrere proelia ventorum damnosa imperitis refert. tradunt eundem Democritum metente fratre eius Damaso ardentissimo aestu orasse, ut reliquae segeti parceret raperetque desecta sub tectum, paucis mox horis saevo imbre vaticinatione adprobata. quin immo et harundinem non nisi inpendente pluvia seri iubent et fruges insecuturo imbre.
passages.english: For, now that the system of the winds has been set out, so that the same things are not said too often, it is proper to pass on to the other forecasts of weather, since I see that this too greatly pleased Virgil, for he reports that during the harvest itself battles of the winds often clash, ruinous to the inexperienced. They say that this same Democritus, when his brother Damasus was reaping in very burning heat, begged him to spare the rest of the crop and to hurry what had been cut under cover, and a few hours later his prophecy was proved by a savage rainstorm. Indeed they even direct that reeds be planted only when rain is impending, and crops when a shower is about to follow.

passages.original: cornu superius acuminatum septentrionale m atque rigidum illum praesagit ventum, inferius austrum, utraque erecta noctem ventosam. si quartam orbis rutilus cinget, et ventos et imbres praemonebit. apud Varronem ita est: Si quarto die luna erit directa, magnam tempestatem in mari praesagiet, nisi si coronam circa se habebit et eam sinceram, quoniam illo modo non ante plenam lunam hiematurum ostendit. si plenilunio per dimidium pura erit, dies serenos significabit;
passages.english: The upper horn pointed and stiff foretells the north wind; the lower [horn so], the south wind; both upright, a windy night. If a red ring surrounds [the moon] on the fourth [day], it will warn of both winds and rain. In Varro it is as follows: "If on the fourth day the moon is upright, it will foretell a great storm at sea, unless it has a halo around it, and that a clear one, since in that case it shows there will be no stormy weather before the full moon. If at the full moon it is clear over half [its disc], it will signify fine days;
passages.notes: 'septentrionale m' read as 'septentrionem'.

passages.original: Cadurci, Caleti, Ruteni, Bituriges ultimique hominum existimati Morini, immo vero Galliae universae vela texunt, iam quidem et transrhenani hostes, nec pulchriorem aliam vestem eorum feminae novere . qua admonitione succurrit quod M. Varro tradit, in Serranorum familia gentilicium esse feminas lintea veste non uti. in Germania autem defossae atque sub terra id opus agunt. similiter etiam in Italiae regione Aliana inter Padum Ticinumque amnes, ubi a Saetabi tertia in Europa lino palma;
passages.english: The Cadurci, Caleti, Ruteni, Bituriges and the Morini, thought the remotest of men, indeed the whole of Gaul, weave sailcloth, and now even our enemies beyond the Rhine, and their women know no finer garment. This reminder brings to mind what M. Varro reports, that in the family of the Serrani it is a family custom for the women not to wear linen clothing. In Germany, moreover, they do this work in pits dug underground. Similarly too in the Alian district of Italy, between the rivers Po and Ticino, where [the linen] holds third prize in Europe after that of Saetabis;
passages.notes: The location of the 'Aliana' district is uncertain.

passages.original: <3> Hortorum Cato praedicat caules. hinc primum agricolae aestimabant prisci et sic statim faciebant iudicium , nequam esse in domo matrem familias—etenim haec cura feminae dicebatur —, ubi indiligens esset hortus , quippe e carnario aut macello vivendum esse.
passages.english: Of garden produce Cato praises cabbages. From this [the garden] the farmers of old first made their assessment, and at once judged that the mistress of a household was worthless (for this was said to be a woman's charge) where the garden was neglected, since then one would have to live from the meat-store or the market.
