passages.notes: *hinc* may refer to the garden generally rather than cabbages.

passages.original: forte primo natum ita audio unum, mox semine ex illo genus factum, melopeponas vocant. non pendent hi, sed humi rotundantur, colore aureo. mirum in his praeter figuram coloremque et odorem , quod maturitatem adepti, quamquam non pendentes, statim a pediculo recedunt. Columella suum tradit commentum , ut toto anno contingant, fruticem rubi quam vastissimum in apricum locum transferre et recidere duum digitorum relicta stirpe circa vernum aequinoctium. ita in medulla rubi semine cucumeris insito terra minuta fimoque circumaggeratas resistere frigori radices.
passages.english: I hear that one first happened to grow like this by chance, and soon from its seed a variety was produced; they call them *melopepones* [apple-melons]. These do not hang, but grow round on the ground, golden in colour. Remarkable in them, besides shape, colour and smell, is that once they reach ripeness, though not hanging, they at once come away from the stalk. Columella gives his own device for having them all year round: transplant a bramble bush, as large as possible, into a sunny spot and cut it back around the spring equinox, leaving a stump of two fingers; then, with cucumber seed inserted into the pith of the bramble and fine earth and dung heaped around, the roots withstand the cold.

passages.original: Proxima hinc est bulborum natura, quos Cato in primis serendos praecipit celebrans Megaricos. verum nobilissima est scilla, quamquam medicamini nata exacuendoque aceto. nec ulli amplitudo maior, sicuti nec vis asperior. duo genera medicae, masculae albis foliis, feminae nigris.
passages.english: Next after this is the nature of bulbs, which Cato instructs should be sown among the first, praising those of Megara. But the most famous is the squill, although it grows for medicine and for sharpening vinegar. No [bulb] has greater size, just as none has harsher potency. There are two medicinal kinds, the male with white leaves, the female with dark.

passages.original: <1> Olus caulesque, quibus nune principatus hortorum, apud Graecos in honore fuisse non reperio, sed Cato brassicae miras canit laudes, quas in medendi loco reddemus. genera eius facit: extentis foliis, caule magno, alteram crispo folio, quam apiacam vocant, tertiam minutis caulibus, lenem, teneram minimeque probat. brassica toto anno seritur, quoniam et toto secatur, utilissime tamen ab aequinoctio autumni, transferturque, cum v foliorum est.
passages.english: Cabbage and cabbage-stalks, which now hold first place in gardens, I do not find to have been held in honour among the Greeks, but Cato sings wondrous praises of cabbage, which we shall report in the section on medicine. He makes [these] kinds of it: [one] with spreading leaves and a large stalk; a second with curly leaf, which they call *apiaca*; a third with small stalks, smooth and tender, and this he approves least. Cabbage is sown all year round, since it is also cut all year round, but most profitably from the autumn equinox, and it is transplanted when it has five leaves.
passages.notes: 'nune' read as 'nunc'.

passages.original: Sed praecipue olusatrum mirae naturae est. hipposelinum Graeci vocant, alii zmyrnium. e lacrima caulis sui nascitur. seritur et radice. sucum eius qui colligunt, murrae saporem habere dicunt, auctorque est Theophrastus murra sata natum. hipposelinum veteres praeceper unt in locis incultis, lapidosis iuxta maceriam seri—nun et repastinato seritur et a favonio post aequinoctium autumnum —, quippe cum capparis quoque seratur sic, siccis maxime, area ideo fossainclusa ripisque undique circumstructis lapide;
passages.english: But above all alexanders (*olusatrum*) is of a wonderful nature. The Greeks call it *hipposelinum*, others *zmyrnium*. It grows from the tear [i.e. gum] of its own stalk. It is also sown from the root. Those who collect its juice say it has the taste of myrrh, and Theophrastus is the authority that it was born from sown myrrh. The ancients instructed that *hipposelinum* be sown in uncultivated, stony places next to a dry-stone wall—now it is also sown in dug-over ground and from the time of the west wind [Favonius] after the autumn equinox—since the caper too is sown in this way, especially in dry places, the bed therefore being enclosed by a trench and banked round on all sides with stone;
passages.notes: Scanning errors corrected ('praeceper unt', 'nun', 'fossainclusa'). 'autumnum' is odd; Favonius normally blows after the spring season, and the text may be confused here.

passages.original: Medius ad haec et sanguinem excreantibus coctos dari iubet, et puerperis ad lactis copiam augendam, Hippocrates capitis mulierum defluvia perfricari raphanis , et super umbilicum inponi contra tormenta volvae. reducunt et cicatrices ad colorem. semen quoque ex aqua inpositum sistit ulcera, quae phagedaenas vocant. Democritus venerem hoc cibo stimulari putat, ob id fortassis voci nocere aliqui tradiderunt. folia, quae in oblongis dumtaxat nascuntur, excitare oculorum aciem dicuntur. ubi vero acrior raphani medicina admota sit, hysopum dari protinus imperant;
passages.english: Medius in addition to this orders them [radishes] to be given boiled to those spitting blood, and to women after childbirth to increase the supply of milk; Hippocrates [orders] women's falling hair to be rubbed with radishes, and [them] to be placed above the navel against griping of the womb. They also bring scars back to [normal] colour. The seed too, applied in water, checks the ulcers they call *phagedaenae* [eating sores]. Democritus thinks sexual desire is stimulated by this food; perhaps for this reason some have recorded that it harms the voice. The leaves, which grow only on the long kinds, are said to sharpen the eyesight. But when a too harsh dose of radish has been administered, they direct that hyssop be given at once;
passages.notes: 'Medius' is uncertain; possibly a corruption of a physician's name (e.g. Meges or Mnesitheus).

passages.original: Philistio in lacte coquit et ad stranguriam dat radicis uncias quattuor, ex aqua hydropicis, similiter et opisthotonicis et pleuriticis et comitialibus. habentes ear feriri a serpentibus negantur aut, qui ante gustaverint, non laedi; percussis inponitur cum axungia. folia contra cruditates manduntur. Orpheus amatorium inesse staphylino dixit, fortassis quoniam venerem stimulari hoc cibo certum est. ideo conceptus adiuvari aliqui prodiderunt. ad reliqua et sativa pollet, efficacior tamen silvestris magisque in petrosis nata. semen sativae quoque contra scorpionum ictus ex vino aut posca salutare est.
passages.english: Philistio boils it in milk and gives four ounces of the root for strangury; in water for dropsy, similarly also for opisthotonus, pleurisy and epilepsy. Those who carry it are said not to be struck by snakes, or those who have tasted it beforehand not to be harmed; for those bitten it is applied with lard. The leaves are chewed against indigestion. Orpheus said that there is a love-charm in the *staphylinus* [wild carrot], perhaps because it is certain that sexual desire is stimulated by this food. Hence some have recorded that conception is aided. For other purposes the cultivated kind is also potent, but the wild is more effective, and more so that grown in rocky places. The seed of the cultivated kind too is salutary against scorpion stings, taken in wine or *posca* [vinegar-water].
passages.notes: 'ear' read as 'eam'.

passages.original: ac, ne contra araneos mures venenati morsus valere miremur, aconitum, quod alio nomine pardalianches vocatur, debellat, item hyoscyamum , canum morsus, in quae vulnera cum melle inponitur . ad serpentium quidem ictus tostum cum restibus suis efficacissime ex oleo inlinitur, adtritisque corporum partibus, vel si in vesicas intumuerint. quin et suffito eo evocari secundas partus existimat Hippocrates, cinere eius cum oleo capitis ulcera manantia sanitati restituens. suspiriosis coctum, aliqui crudum id dedere; Diocles hydropicis cum centaurio aut in fico duplici ad evacuandam alvum, quod efficacius praestat viride cum coriandro in mero potum;
passages.english: And, lest we should wonder that it is effective against shrew-mice and venomous bites, it overcomes aconite, which by another name is called *pardalianches*, likewise henbane, [and] dogs' bites, on which wounds it is applied with honey. For snakebites indeed it is most effectively smeared on roasted with its own strings [of bulbs], in oil, and on chafed parts of the body, or if they have swelled into blisters. Indeed Hippocrates thinks that the afterbirth is drawn out by fumigation with it, and with its ash in oil he restores running sores of the head to health. For asthmatics some have given it cooked, some raw; Diocles [gave it] for dropsy with centaury or in a split fig to empty the bowels, which it does more effectively green, drunk with coriander in neat wine;
passages.notes: The subject is garlic (from context).

passages.original: Silvestris sive erraticae inmenso plus effectus laudat Cato, adeo ut aridae quoque farinae in olfactorio collectae vel odore tantum naribus rapto vitia earum graveolentiamque sanari adfirmet. hanc alii petraeam vocant, inimicissimam vino, quam praecipue vitis fugiat aut, si non possit fugere, moriatur.
passages.english: Cato praises the wild or 'wandering' [cabbage] as having immensely greater effect, so much so that he asserts that even of the dried powder gathered in a smelling-box, or merely by its odour drawn up into the nostrils, their disorders and foul smell are cured. Others call this the 'rock' [cabbage], most hostile to wine, which the vine especially shuns or, if it cannot shun it, dies.

passages.original: praeterea oculis inlitum cum melle, ita ut subinde foveantur ferventi suco decocti, aliisque membrorum epiphoris per se tritum aut cum pane vel polenta inpositum mire auxiliatur. pisces quoque, si aegrotent in piscinis, apio viridi recreantur. verum apud eruditos non aliud erutum terra in maiore sententiarum varietate est. distinguitur sexu. Chrysippus feminam esse dicit crispioribus foliis et duris, crasso caule, sapore acri et fervido; Dionysius... nigriorem, brevem, radicis ..., vermiculos gignentem; ambo neutrum ad cibos admittendum, immo omnino nefas, namque id defunctorum epulis feralibus dicatum esse—visus quoque claritati inimicum —[caule feminae vermiculos gigni] ideoque eos, qui ederint, sterilescere, mares feminasve;
passages.english: Moreover, smeared on the eyes with honey, provided they are bathed from time to time with the hot juice of the decoction, and for fluxes of other limbs, pounded by itself or applied with bread or barley-meal, it helps wonderfully. Fish too, if they are sick in fishponds, are revived by green celery. But among the learned no other thing dug from the earth is the subject of greater variety of opinion. It is distinguished by sex. Chrysippus says the female has curlier and hard leaves, a thick stalk, and a sharp, hot taste; Dionysius [says it is] darker, short, with root ..., producing little worms; both [say] that neither is to be admitted as food, indeed that it is altogether sinful, for it is dedicated to the funeral feasts of the dead—it is also hostile to clearness of sight—[little worms are produced in the stalk of the female] and therefore those who have eaten it become sterile, males or females;
passages.notes: The text is lacunose after 'Dionysius' and after 'radicis'. The bracketed clause is an editorial deletion or transposition in the edition.

passages.original: dederunt et lethargicis ex aceto olfaciendum et comitialibus bibendum decoctae sucum in cyathis IIII; ante accessiones, quarum frigus intolerabile est, alsiosisque et crudam in cibo. urinam quoque vel cruentam pellit, feminarum etiam purgationes secundasque et iam emortuos partus, ut Hippocrati videtur, ex vino dulci nigro pota. itaque inlitam et vulvarum causa et suffire iubet. Diodes et cardiacis inponit ex aceto et melle cum farina hordeacia et contra ileum decocta farina in oleo velleribus collecta.
passages.english: They have also given it to the lethargic to smell in vinegar, and to epileptics to drink the juice of the decoction, four *cyathi*; before attacks whose chill is intolerable, and to those sensitive to cold, also raw in food. It expels urine too, even bloody, also women's menstrual purgings and the afterbirth and already dead fetuses, as Hippocrates holds, drunk in sweet dark wine. Therefore he also prescribes it smeared on and as a fumigation for disorders of the womb. Diocles also applies it to cardiac patients in vinegar and honey with barley meal, and against ileus the meal boiled in oil and gathered up in fleeces.
passages.notes: The plant is probably pennyroyal or a similar herb (from context). 'Diodes' in the context is likely Diocles.

passages.original: voci suco utilis, sub certamine dumtaxat, qui et gargarizatur uva tumente adiecta ruta et coriandro ex lacte; utilis et contra tonsillas cum alumine, linguae asperae cum melle et convulsis intus per se vitiisque pulmonis. singultus et vomitiones sistit cum suco granati, ut Democritus monstrat. recentis sucus narium vitia spiritu subductus emendat; ipsa trita choleras, in aceto quidem pota, sanguinis fluctiones intus, ileum etiam inposita cum polenta et si mammae tendantur.
passages.english: [It is] useful for the voice through its juice, at least during a contest; this is also gargled for a swollen uvula, with rue and coriander added, in milk; [it is] useful also for the tonsils with alum, for a rough tongue with honey, and by itself for internal convulsions and lung disorders. It stops hiccups and vomiting with pomegranate juice, as Democritus shows. The juice of the fresh [plant], drawn up by breathing, corrects nasal disorders; the [plant] itself pounded [checks] choleras, and drunk in vinegar, internal haemorrhages; applied with barley meal [it helps] ileus too, and if the breasts are distended.
passages.notes: The verb governing 'choleras' is implied. The plant is probably mint.

passages.original: Blitum iners videtur ac sine sapore aut acrimonia ulla, unde convicium feminis apud Menandrum faciunt mariti. stomacho inutile est. ventrem adeo turbat, ut choleram faciat aliquis. dicitur tamen adversus scorpiones potum e vino prodesse, clavis pedum inlini, item lienibus et temporum dolori ex oleo. Hippocrates menstrua sisti eo cibo putat.
passages.english: Blite seems sluggish and without flavour or any sharpness, which is why husbands in Menander use it as a term of abuse for their wives. It is bad for the stomach. It so disturbs the bowels that in some people it causes cholera. It is said, however, that taken in wine it is beneficial against scorpions, and that it is applied to corns of the feet, and likewise, with oil, to the spleen and to pain in the temples. Hippocrates thinks that menstruation is checked by eating it.

passages.original: De floribus..... supra dictis scripsit Theophrastus apud Graecos; ex nostris autem inscripsere aliqui libros anthologicon, flores vero persecutus est nemo, quod equidem inveniam. nec nos nunc scilicet coronas nectemus —id enim frivolum est—, sed de floribus quae videbuntur digna memorabimus.
passages.english: On the flowers mentioned above, Theophrastus wrote among the Greeks; among our own writers, some have given books the title Anthologicon, but nobody, so far as I can find, has dealt with flowers. Nor shall we now, of course, weave garlands, for that is a trivial matter, but we shall record those things about flowers that seem worth recording.
passages.notes: The dots after 'floribus' mark a lacuna or editorial omission in the edition.

passages.original: germinat omnis primo inclusa granoso cortice, quo mox intumescente et in virides alabastros fastigato paulatim rubescens dehiscit ac sese pandit, in calice medio staminis conplexa luteos apices. usus eius in coronis prope minimus est. oleo maceratur, idque iam a Troianis temporibus Homero teste. praeterea in unguenta transit, ut diximus. medicas per se artes praebet. emplastris atque collyriis inseritur mordaci subtilitate, mensarum etiam deliciis perunguendis, minime noxia carie.
passages.english: Every [rose] first buds enclosed in a granular husk; this soon swells and tapers into green buds, and, gradually reddening, it splits open and spreads itself out, embracing in the middle of its cup the yellow tips of the stamens. Its use in garlands is almost the least [of its uses]. It is steeped in oil, and this [was done] already from Trojan times, as Homer testifies. Besides this it passes into unguents, as we have said. By itself it furnishes medical remedies. It is put into plasters and eye-salves because of its biting fineness, and also into the delicacies with which tables are anointed, its decay being very little harmful.
passages.notes: The closing phrases ('mensarum etiam deliciis perunguendis, minime noxia carie') are obscure; the sense of 'carie' (decay, or perhaps the dried powdered rose) is uncertain.

passages.original: Troianis temporibus iam erat honos ei; hos certe flores Homerus tris laudat loton, crocum, hyacinthum.
passages.english: Already in Trojan times it was held in honour; at any rate Homer praises these three flowers: the lotus, the crocus and the hyacinth.

passages.original: Ceterae eiusdem generis folio differunt: asphodelus oblongum et angustum habet, scilla latum et tractabile , gladiolus simile nomini. asphodelus manditur et semine tosto et bulbo, set hoc in cinere tosto, dein sale et oleo addito, praeterea tuso cum ficis, praecipua voluptate , ut videtur Hesiodo. tradunt et ante portas villarum satum remedio esse contra veneficiorum noxiam. asphodeli mentionem et Homerus fecit. radix eius napis modicis similis est, neque alia numerosior LXXX simul acervatis saepe bulbis.
passages.english: The others of the same kind differ in leaf: the asphodel has a long, narrow one, the squill a broad and pliable one, the gladiolus one like its name. The asphodel is eaten both with its seed roasted and as a bulb, but this [is] roasted in ashes, then with salt and oil added, or else pounded with figs, with particular enjoyment, as Hesiod seems to think. They also report that, planted in front of the gates of country houses, it is a remedy against the harm of poisonings. Homer too made mention of the asphodel. Its root is like a moderate-sized turnip, and no other [plant] has more numerous [roots], with bulbs often heaped together eighty at once.
passages.notes: 'veneficiorum' may mean sorcery as well as poisoning.

passages.original: praeterea a celebratis auctoribus contra omnia venena pro antidoto sufficere xxv grana eius, quod minyanthes ex eo appellavimus, tradi, multa alia praeterea in remediis eius adscribi. sed me contra sententias eorum gravissimi viri auctoritas movet, Sophocles enim poeta venenatum id dicit, Simos quoque ex medicis, decocti aut contriti sucum infusum corpori easdem uredines facere, quas si percussis a serpente inponatur. ergo non aliter utendum eo quam contra venena censuerim.
passages.english: [I know] also that it is reported by celebrated authorities that twenty-five grains of it, of the kind which we have therefore called minyanthes, suffice as an antidote against all poisons, and that many other remedial properties are attributed to it besides. But the authority of a most weighty man moves me against their opinions: for the poet Sophocles says that it is poisonous, and so too Simos among the physicians, [saying] that the juice of it boiled or crushed, poured on the body, produces the same burning as on those struck by a serpent if it is applied. Therefore I should judge that it should not be used except against poisons.
passages.notes: 'minyanthes' is the name of a kind of trefoil; the sentence about Simos is somewhat confused in the Latin.

passages.original: orthopnoicis prodest cum melle et thoracem purgat eodem ecligmate et lateri medetur cum semine lini. addunt hysopum et piperis aliquid . inlinitur lieni, difficilem ventrem tostum cibo emollit. Hippocrates vulvam purgari poto eo pronuntiat, dolore levari tosto acetabuli mensura, dulci poto et inposito cum suco malvae, intestinorum animalia pelli cum hydromelite et sale, defluvia capitis semine inlito cohonestari. articulariis morbis et podagricis plurimi cum oleo vetere aut folia cum ursino adipe trita inponunt.
passages.english: With honey it is good for those suffering from orthopnoea, and the same electuary clears the chest, and with linseed it heals the side. Some add hyssop and a little pepper. It is applied to the spleen; roasted and taken as food it softens a constipated belly. Hippocrates declares that the womb is cleansed when it is drunk; that pain is relieved by an acetabulum's measure roasted, drunk in sweet wine and applied with mallow juice; that intestinal worms are expelled with hydromel and salt; and that the falling of hair is remedied by applying the seed. For diseases of the joints and gout very many apply it with old oil, or the leaves pounded with bear's fat.
passages.notes: 'cohonestari' (literally 'made seemly') is taken as 'remedied'. The plant is not named in the passage.

passages.original: Loton qui arborem putant tantum esse, vel Homero auctore coargui possunt. is enim inter herbas subnascentes deorum voluptati loton primam nominavit. folia eius cum melle oculorum cicatrices, argema, nubeculas discutiunt.
passages.english: Those who think the lotus is only a tree can be refuted on Homer's authority alone. For among the herbs springing up for the pleasure of the gods he named the lotus first. Its leaves with honey disperse scars of the eyes, argema [a kind of ulcer], and films.

passages.original: Asphodelum de clarissimis herbarum, ut quod heroion aliqui appellaverint, Hesiodus et in silvis nasci dixit, Dionysius marem ac feminam esse. defectis corporibus et phthisicis constat bulbos eius cum tisana decoctos aptissime dari, panemque ex his cum farina subactis saluberrimum esse. Nicander et contra serpentes ac scorpiones vel caulem, quem anthericum vocavimus, vel semen vel bulbos dedit in vino tribus drachmis substravitque somno contra hos metus.
passages.english: Asphodel is among the most famous of plants, so much so that some have called it *heroion*; Hesiod said it grows also in woods, Dionysius that it is male and female. It is agreed that its bulbs, boiled with barley gruel, are very suitably given to the emaciated and consumptive, and that bread made from them kneaded with flour is most wholesome. Nicander also prescribed, against snakes and scorpions, either the stalk, which we have called *anthericus*, or the seed or the bulbs, in wine, at three drachmas, and spread it beneath the sleeper against these dangers.

passages.original: Xenocrates et lichenas, psoras, lepras radice in aceto decocta tolli dicit, item suco cum hyoscyamo et pice liquida alarum quoque et feminum vitia; et capillum crispiorem fieri, raso prius capite, si radice ea fricetur, Simos lapides renium in vino decocta potaque eximi. Hippocrates semine ad impetus lienis dari censet. iumentorum quoque ulcera ac scabiem radix inlita aut decoctae sucus ad pilum reducit. mures eadem fugantur, caverna praeclusa moriuntur.
passages.english: Xenocrates says that lichens, itch and leprous sores are removed by the root boiled in vinegar, and likewise by the juice with henbane and liquid pitch [are removed] disorders of the armpits and thighs; and that the hair becomes curlier, the head first being shaved, if it is rubbed with that root; Simos [says] that stones of the kidneys are expelled by it boiled in wine and drunk. Hippocrates advises that the seed be given for attacks of the spleen. The root applied, or the juice of a decoction, also restores the hair over sores and scab of draught animals. Mice are put to flight by it, and when their hole is blocked [with it] they die.

passages.original: sucus quoque eius bibitur, stomacho perquam commendatus et urinae calculisque et harenis pellendis et vesicae pruritibus. extenuat et lienis, iocineris reniumque pituitas. semen menses feminarum adiuvat bilemque a partu siccat. datur et contra profluvia geniturae viris. Chrysippus et conceptionibus earn putat conferre multum. bibitur in vino ieiunis. inlinitur et contra venena marinorum, sicut Petrichus in carmine suo significat.
passages.english: Its juice is also drunk, being highly recommended for the stomach, for the urine, for expelling stones and gravel, and for itching of the bladder. It also thins phlegm of the spleen, liver and kidneys. The seed aids women's menstruation and dries up bile after childbirth. It is also given to men against discharges of semen. Chrysippus thinks it contributes much to conception as well. It is drunk in wine by those fasting. It is also applied against the venoms of sea creatures, as Petrichus indicates in his poem.
passages.notes: 'earn' is a scanning error for 'eam'. The plant is presumably the caucalis of the preceding context.

passages.original: Estur et soncos—ut quem Theseo apud Callimachum adponat Hecale—uterque, albus et niger. lactucae similes ambo, nisi spinosi essent, caule cubitali, anguloso, intus cavo, sed qui fractus copioso lacte manet. albus, cui e lacte nitor, utilis orthopnoicis lactucarum modo ex embammate.
passages.english: The sow-thistle (soncos) is also eaten, such as Hecale in Callimachus serves to Theseus; both kinds, the white and the black. Both are like lettuce, except that they are prickly, with a stem a cubit long, angular, hollow inside, but which when broken runs with abundant milk. The white, which has a sheen from its milk, is useful for those with orthopnoea, in the manner of lettuces, [taken] in a dressing.

passages.original: multi senectam longam mulsi tantum intrita toleravere, neque alio ullo cibo, celebri Pollionis Romili exemplo. centensimum annum excedentem eum divus Augustus hospes interrogavit, quanam maxime ratione vigorem illum animi corporisque custodisset. at ille respondit: intus mulso, foris oleo. Varro regium cognominatum arquatorum morbum tradit, quoniam mulso curetur.
passages.english: Many have endured a long old age on nothing but bread soaked in honeyed wine, with no other food, as in the famous example of Pollio Romilius. When he was over a hundred years old, the deified Augustus, as his guest, asked him by what means above all he had preserved such vigour of mind and body. And he replied: "Honeyed wine within, oil without." Varro reports that jaundice is called the 'royal disease' because it is treated with honeyed wine.

passages.original: Myrtus sativa candida minus utilis medicinae quam nigra. semen eius medetur sanguinem excreantibus, item contra fungos in vino potum. odorem oris commendat vel pridie commanducatum; ita apud Menandrum Synaristosae hoc edunt. datur et dysintericis idem denarii pondere in vino. ulcera difficilia in extremitatibus corporis sanat cum vino subfervefactum. inponitur lippitudini cum polenta et cardiacis in mamma sinistra et contra scorpionis ictum in mero et ad vesicae vitia, capitis dolores, aegilopas, antequam suppurent, item tumoribus, exemptisque nucleis in vino vetere tritum eruptionibus pituitae.
passages.english: The cultivated white myrtle is less useful in medicine than the black. Its seed is a remedy for those spitting blood, and likewise, taken in wine, against [poisonous] mushrooms. It makes the breath of the mouth pleasant even if chewed the day before; so in Menander the women of the Synaristosae eat it. The same is also given to dysentery patients in wine, at the weight of a denarius. Warmed with wine, it heals stubborn ulcers on the extremities of the body. It is applied with pearl-barley for inflammation of the eyes, and on the left breast for heart complaints, and in neat wine against the sting of the scorpion, and for disorders of the bladder, headaches, and lachrymal fistulas before they suppurate, likewise for swellings; and with the kernels removed, pounded in old wine, for eruptions of phlegm.
passages.notes: Synaristosae: Menander's comedy 'The Women at Lunch'.

passages.original: Genista quoque vinculi usum praestat, floris apibus gratissimi. dubito an haec sit quam Graeci auctores sparton appellavere, cum ex ea lina piscatoria apud eos factitari docuerim, et numquid hanc designaverit Homerus , cum dixit navium sparta dissoluta. nondum enim fuisse Hispanum Africanumve spartum in usu certum est et, cum fierent sutiles naves, lino tamen, non sparto umquam sutas. semen eius, quod Graeci eodem nomine appellant, in folliculis passiolorum modo nascens purgat hellebori vice drachma et dimidia pota in aquae mulsae cyathis IIII ieiunis.
passages.english: Broom also serves the purpose of a binding, and its flower is very pleasing to bees. I doubt whether this is what the Greek authors called sparton, since I have shown that among them fishing lines were commonly made of it, and whether Homer meant this when he said the ships' sparta had come loose. For it is certain that Spanish or African esparto was not yet in use, and that, when sewn ships were made, they were nevertheless sewn with flax, never with esparto. Its seed, which the Greeks call by the same name, growing in little pods like those of kidney beans, purges in place of hellebore when a drachma and a half is drunk in four cyathi of honey-water on an empty stomach.

passages.original: in vino potae sistunt alvum. radix decocta et inlita extrahit infixa corpori, utilissima et luxatis tumoribusque. aquifolia arbor in domo aut villa sata veneficia arcet. flore eius aquam glaciari Pythagoras tradit; item baculum ex ea factum in quodvis animal emissum, etiamsi citra ceciderit defectu mittentis, ipsum per sese cubito propius adlabi; tam praecipuam naturam inesse arbori .—Taxi arboris fumus necat mures.
passages.english: Drunk in wine, they check the bowels. The root, boiled and applied, draws out things lodged in the body, and is very useful also for dislocations and swellings. The holly tree, planted in a house or country-house, wards off sorcery. Pythagoras records that water is frozen by its flower; likewise that a staff made from it, when thrown at any animal, even if it falls short through the weakness of the thrower, glides of its own accord a cubit nearer; so outstanding a nature is in the tree. The smoke of the yew tree kills mice.
passages.notes: 'they' presumably refers to the holly berries mentioned in the preceding context.

passages.original: Coracesia et calicia Pythagoras aquam glaciari tradit, quarum mentionem apud alios non reperio, nec apud eum alia de his. idem Minyada appellat et nomine alio Corinthiam, cuius decocto in aqua suco protinus sanari ictus serpentium, si foveantur, dicit.
passages.english: Pythagoras records that water is frozen by coracesia and calicia, of which I find no mention in other writers, nor anything else about them in him. He also names a Minyas, by another name Corinthia, by whose juice, boiled in water, he says snake bites are healed at once if they are bathed with it.
passages.notes: The plants coracesia, calicia and Minyas are unidentified.

passages.original: Democriti certe chirocmeta esse constat. at in his ille post Pythagoram Magorum studiosissimus quanto portentosiora tradit! ut aglaophotim herbam, quae admiratione hominum propter eximium colorem acceperit nomen , in marmoribus Arabiae nascentem Persico latere, qua de causa et marmaritim vocari; hac Magos uti, cum velint deos evocare.
passages.english: It is at any rate agreed that the Chirocmeta are by Democritus. But in these how much more prodigious are the things he reports, he who after Pythagoras was most devoted to the Magi! For instance, the plant aglaophotis, which received its name from men's admiration of its exceptional colour, growing in the marble quarries of Arabia on the Persian side, for which reason it is also called marmaritis; the Magi use it when they wish to summon the gods.
passages.notes: Chirocmeta: a work attributed to Democritus, whose authenticity Pliny elsewhere questions.

passages.original: durat tamen tradita persuasio in magna parte vulgi, veneficiis et herbis id cogi eamque unam feminarum scientiam praevalere. certe quid non repleverunt fabulis Colchis Media aliaeque, in primis Itala Circe dis etiam adscripta? unde arbitror natum, ut Aeschylus e vetustissimis in poetica refertam Italiam herbarum potentia proderet, multique Circeios, ubi habitavit illa, magno argumento etiam nunc durante in Marsis, a filio eius orta gente, quoniam esse domitores serpentium constat.
passages.english: Yet the inherited belief persists among a great part of the common people that this [i.e. drawing down the moon] is compelled by sorcery and herbs, and that this one science of women is supreme. Certainly, what have Colchian Medea and other women not filled with fables, above all Italian Circe, who was even enrolled among the gods? From this, I think, it arose that Aeschylus, one of the most ancient in poetry, declared Italy full of the power of herbs, and many [said the same of] Circeii, where she lived, strong evidence of this still remaining even now among the Marsi, a people sprung from her son, since it is established that they are tamers of snakes.
passages.notes: The thing 'compelled' is inferred from the preceding context about eclipses of the moon; the text is elliptical.

passages.original: herbas certe Aegyptias a regis uxore traditas Helenae suae plurimas narrat ac nobile illud nepenthes oblivionem tristitiae veniamque adferens et ab Helena utique omnibus mortalibus propinandum. primus autem omnium, quos memoria novit, Orpheus de herbis curiosius aliqua prodidit. post eum Musaeus et Hesiodus polium herbam in quantum mirati sint diximus. Orpheus et Hesiodus suffitiones commendavere. Homerus et alias nominatim herbas celebrat, quas suis locis dicemus. ab eo Pythagoras clarus sapientia primus volumen de effectu earum composuit , Apollini, Aesculapio et in totum dis immortalibus inventione et origine adsignata;
passages.english: He certainly tells of very many Egyptian herbs given by the king's wife to his Helen, and that famous nepenthes, bringing forgetfulness of sorrow and pardon, and which Helen was to offer to all mortals. But first of all those whom memory knows, Orpheus published some rather careful things about herbs. After him, Musaeus and Hesiod—we have said how much they admired the herb polium. Orpheus and Hesiod recommended fumigations. Homer also celebrates other herbs by name, which we shall speak of in their places. After him Pythagoras, famed for wisdom, was the first to compose a volume on their effects, assigning their discovery and origin to Apollo, Aesculapius, and in general to the immortal gods;

passages.original: Xanthus historiarum auctor in prima earum tradit, occisum draconis catulum revocatum ad vitam a parente herba, quam balim nominat, eademque Tylonem, quem draco occiderat, restitutum saluti. et luba in Arabia herba revocatum ad vitam hominem tradit. dixit Democritus, credidit Theophrastus esse herbam, cuius contactu inlatae ab alite, quam retulimus, exiliret cuneus a pastoribus arbori adactus. quae etiamsi fide carent, admirationem tamen implent coguntque confiteri multum esse quod vero supersit.
passages.english: Xanthus, the writer of histories, records in the first [book] of them that a young serpent which had been killed was brought back to life by its parent with a herb which he names balis, and that by the same [herb] Tylon, whom a serpent had killed, was restored to health. Juba too records that in Arabia a man was brought back to life by a herb. Democritus stated, and Theophrastus believed, that there is a herb at whose touch, when it is brought by the bird we have mentioned, a wedge driven into a tree by shepherds leaps out. Even if these things lack credibility, they nevertheless fill [us] with wonder and compel [us] to admit that much of truth remains.
passages.notes: 'luba' read as Juba (scanning error). The bird is the woodpecker, mentioned earlier in the work.

passages.original: Clarissima herbarum est Homero teste quam vocari a dis putat moly, et inventionem eius Mercurio adsignat contraque summa veneficia demonstrationem. nasci eam hodie circa Pheneum et in Cyllene Arcadiae tradunt specie illa Homerica, radice rotunda nigraque, magnitudine cepae, folio scillae, effodi autem non difficulter.
passages.english: The most famous of herbs, on Homer's testimony, is the one he thinks is called moly by the gods, and he assigns its discovery to Mercury and [to him also] the showing [of its use] against the strongest sorceries. They say that today it grows around Pheneus and on Cyllene in Arcadia, of that Homeric appearance, with a round black root the size of an onion, the leaf of a squill, and that it is dug up without difficulty.

passages.original: Tertia est centauris cognomine triorchis. qui eam secat, rarum est ut non vulneret sese. haec sucum sanguineum emittit. Theophrastus defendi eam inpugnarique colligentes tradit a triorche accipitrum genere, unde et nomen accepit. inperiti confundunt haec omnia et primo generi adsignant.
passages.english: The third is the centaury surnamed *triorchis*. Whoever cuts it rarely fails to wound himself. It gives off a blood-red juice. Theophrastus records that it is defended, and those gathering it are attacked, by the *triorchis*, a kind of hawk, from which it also took its name. The unskilled confuse all these and assign them to the first kind.

passages.original: frater is fuit Musae, a quo divum Augustum conservatum indicavimus . iidem fratres instituere a balineis frigida multa corpora adstringere ; antea non erat mos nisi calida tantum lavari, sicut apud Homerum etiam invenimus. sed Iubae volumen quoque extat de ea herba et clarum praeconium. invenit eam in monte Atlante, specie thyrsi, foliis acanthinis. vis tanta est, ut e longinquo sucus excipiatur incisa conto;
passages.english: He was the brother of Musa, by whom, as we have pointed out, the deified Augustus was saved. These same brothers introduced the practice of bracing the body with plenty of cold water after the baths; before that it was the custom to bathe only in hot water, as we find even in Homer. But there is also a volume by Juba on this plant, and a famous eulogy of it. He found it on Mount Atlas, with the appearance of a thyrsus and leaves like acanthus. Its potency is so great that the juice is collected from a distance, [the plant] being cut open with a pole;

passages.original: Eadem vis crethmo ab Hippocrate admodum laudatae. est autem inter eas quae eduntur silvestrium herbarum; hanc certe apud Callimachum adponit rustica illa Hecale. species quae elatae hortensiae. caulis unus palmum altus; semen fervens, odoratum ceu libanotidis, rotundum; siccatum rumpitur. habet intus nucleum candidum , quem aliqui cachrym vocant. folia pinguia albicant veluti olivae, crassiora et salsa gustu;
passages.english: The same property belongs to crethmos, which was highly praised by Hippocrates. It is, moreover, among the wild plants that are eaten; this at least is what that country woman Hecale serves in Callimachus. Its appearance is that of the tall garden kind. It has a single stem a palm high; the seed is hot, fragrant like that of libanotis, and round; when dried it bursts. Inside it has a white kernel, which some call *cachrys*. The leaves are fleshy and whitish like those of the olive, but thicker, and salty to the taste;
passages.notes: 'quae elatae hortensiae' is obscure; perhaps a plant name has fallen out of the text.

passages.original: in totum quidem Graeci, cum concitationem hanc volunt significare, satyrion appellant, sic et crataegin cognominantes et thelygonon et arrhenogonon, quarum semen testibus simile est. tithymalli quoque ramorum medullam habentes ad venerem proniores fieri dicuntur. prodigiosa sunt quae circa hoc tradit Theophrastus , auctor alioqui gravis, septuageno coitu durasse libidinem contactu herbae, cuius nomen genusque non posuit. — Sideritis adalligata varices minuit et sine dolore praestat.
passages.english: In general, indeed, the Greeks, when they wish to denote this stimulation, use the name satyrion, and they likewise give the names crataegis, thelygonon and arrhenogonon to plants whose seed resembles testicles. Those who have the pith of the branches of tithymallus are also said to become more inclined to sex. Prodigious are the things that Theophrastus, otherwise a weighty authority, reports on this subject: that through contact with a plant, whose name and kind he did not give, desire lasted through seventy acts of intercourse. Sideritis, tied on as an amulet, reduces varicose veins and keeps them free of pain.

passages.original: daucum et menses et secundas potu facillime pellit, ladanum suffitu corrigit volvas, dolori earum exulceratisque inponitur. emortua scamonium pellit potum vel adpositum. menses ciet hypericum utrumque adpositum, ante alia vero, ut Hippocrati videtur, crethmos e vino semine vel radicis cortice, trahit et secundas, succurrit et strangulationibus ex aqua pota; item radix e geranio peculiariter secundis inflationibusque volvarum conveniens.
passages.english: Daucum, taken in drink, very readily brings on both menstruation and the afterbirth; ladanum as a fumigation corrects [disorders of] the womb, and is applied for pain and ulceration there. Scammony, drunk or applied, expels a dead fetus. Both kinds of hypericum, applied, bring on menstruation, but above all, as Hippocrates holds, crethmos in wine, [using] the seed or the bark of the root; it also draws out the afterbirth, and drunk in water it relieves suffocation [of the womb]; likewise the root of geranium is especially suited for the afterbirth and for flatulence of the womb.

passages.original: Solanum Graeci στρύχνον vocant, ut tradit Cornelius Celsus. huic vis reprimendi refrigerandique .— Smyrnion caulem habet apii, folia latiora et maxime circa stolones multos, quorum a sinu exiliunt, pinguia et ad terram infracta, odore medicato cum quadam acrimonia iucundo, colore in luteum languescente , capitibus caulium orbiculatis ut apii, semine rotundo nigroque ;
passages.english: The Greeks call solanum *strychnon*, as Cornelius Celsus records. It has a repressive and cooling property. Smyrnion has the stem of celery, and broader leaves, chiefly around its many shoots, from whose fold they spring; they are fleshy and bent down to the ground, with a medicinal smell that is pleasant with a certain pungency, and a colour fading into yellow; the heads of the stems are round like those of celery, and the seed is round and black;

passages.original: in augurum certe disciplina constat neque diras neque ulla auspicia pertinere ad eos, qui quamque rem ingredientes observare se ea negaverint, quo munere divinae indulgentiae maius nullum est. quid? non et legum ipsaruin in duodecim tabulis verba sunt: qui fruges excantass it, et alibi: qui malum carmen incantassit ? Verrius Flaccus auctores ponit, quibus credat in obpugnationibus ante omnia solitum a Romanis sacerdotibus evocari deum, cuius in tutela id oppidum esset, promittique illi eundem aut ampliorem apud Romanos cultum. et durat in pontificum disciplina id sacrum, constatque ideo occultatum , in cuius dei tutela Roma esset, ne qui hostium simili modo agerent.
passages.english: Certainly in the discipline of the augurs it is established that neither curses nor any auspices concern those who, when undertaking any matter, have declared that they do not observe them, and no gift of divine indulgence is greater than this. What? Are there not also, in the Twelve Tables of the laws themselves, the words: "whoever has charmed away crops," and elsewhere: "whoever has chanted an evil spell"? Verrius Flaccus cites authorities whom he trusts, [saying] that in sieges it was customary, before anything else, for the god under whose protection that town was to be called out by the Roman priests, and for the same or more ample worship among the Romans to be promised to him. And this rite endures in the discipline of the pontiffs, and it is agreed that for this reason it has been kept secret under the protection of which god Rome is, so that none of [our] enemies might act in a similar way.
passages.notes: 'ipsaruin' read as 'ipsarum'; 'excantass it' as 'excantassit'.

passages.original: neque est facile dictu, externa verba atque ineffabilia abrogent fidem validius an Latina et inopinata , quae inridicula videri cogit animus semper aliquid inmensum exspectans ac dignum deo movendo, immo vero quod numini imperet. dixit Homerus profluvium sanguinis vulnerato femine Ulixen inhibuisse carmine, Theophrastus ischiadicos sanari, Cato prodidit luxatis membris carmen auxiliare, M. Varro podagris. Caesarem dictatorem post unum ancipitem vehiculi casum ferunt semper, ut primum consedisset, id quod plerosque nunc facere scimus, carmine ter repetito securitatem itinerum aucupari solitum.
passages.english: Nor is it easy to say whether foreign and unpronounceable words undermine belief more strongly, or Latin and unexpected ones, which the mind forces us to regard as ridiculous, since it is always expecting something immense and worthy of moving a god, or rather of commanding a divinity. Homer said that Ulysses stopped the flow of blood from a wound in his thigh by a charm; Theophrastus that sufferers from sciatica are cured [so]; Cato published a charm helpful for dislocated limbs, Marcus Varro one for gout. They say that the dictator Caesar, after a single dangerous accident with his carriage, was always accustomed, as soon as he had taken his seat, to seek safety on his journeys by repeating a charm three times, something we know most people do now.

passages.original: probabilius id facit hasta velitaris evulsa corpori hominis, si terrain non attigerit; eosdem enim inlata effectus habet. sic et sagittas corpori eductas, si terrain non attigerint, subiectas cubantibus amatorium esse Orpheus et Archelaus scribunt, quin et comitialem morbum sanari cibo e care ferae occisae eodem ferro, quo homo interfectus sit. quorundam partes medicae sunt, sicuti diximus de Pyrrhi regis pollice, et Elide solebat ostendi Pelopis os ulnamque eam eburneam adfirmabant.—(Naevos in facie tondere religiosum habent etiam nunc multi).—
passages.english: This is done more plausibly by a light-armed soldier's spear pulled out of a man's body, if it has not touched the ground; for when brought [into the house] it has the same effect. So too Orpheus and Archelaus write that arrows drawn out of a body, if they have not touched the ground, placed under people lying in bed act as a love charm; and further, that epilepsy is cured by eating the flesh of a wild animal killed with the same iron by which a man was slain. Parts of some individuals are medicinal, as we have said of King Pyrrhus' thumb; and at Elis the bone of Pelops used to be shown, and they asserted that his shoulder-blade was of ivory. (Many even now regard it as a religious scruple to shave moles on the face.)
passages.notes: 'terrain' read as 'terram', and 'care' as 'carne' (scanning errors). 'ulnam' strictly 'forearm', but the Pelops legend concerns the shoulder.

passages.original: si quod animal aurem intraverit et inspuatur, exire. inter amuleta est editae quemque urinae inspuere, similiter in calciamentum dextri pedis, priusquam induatur, item cum quis transeat locum, in quo aliquod periculum adierit. Marcion Zmyrnaeus, qui de simplicibus effectibus scripsit, rumpi scolopendras marinas sputo tradit, item rubetas aliasque ranas, Ofilius serpentes, si quis in hiatum earum expuat, Salpe torporem sedari quocumque membro stupente, si quis in sinum expuat aut si superiores palpebras saliva tangat.cur non et haec credamus rite fieri, extranei interventu aut, si dormiens spectetur infans, a nutrice terna adspui in os?
passages.english: [They believe] that if some creature has entered the ear and one spits into it, it comes out. Among amulets is [the practice] of each person spitting on the urine he has passed, likewise into the shoe of the right foot before it is put on, and also when one passes a place where one has met some danger. Marcion of Smyrna, who wrote on the effects of simples, records that sea scolopendras burst from spittle, and likewise toads and other frogs; Ofilius [says the same of] snakes, if one spits into their open mouths; Salpe [says] that numbness is relieved in any limb that is benumbed if one spits into one's bosom or touches the upper eyelids with saliva. Why should we not also believe that these things are rightly done: that when a stranger comes in, or if an infant is looked at while asleep, the nurse spits three times into its mouth?
passages.notes: 'Zmyrnaeus' = of Smyrna. Some editions read 'adspui' as spitting at/toward the mouth; the sense of the final clause is somewhat uncertain.

passages.original: Sanguine ipsius hominis ex quacumque parte emisso efficacissime anginam inlini tradunt Orpheus et Archelaus, item ora comitiali morbo conlapsorum, exurger e enim protinus; quidam, si pollices pedum pungantur eaeque guttae referantur in faciem, aut si virgo dextro pollice attingat, hac coniectura censentes virgines carnes edendas.
passages.english: Orpheus and Archelaus record that quinsy is most effectively treated by smearing it with the blood of the person himself, let from any part, and likewise the mouths of those who have collapsed in an epileptic fit, for they get up at once; some [say this happens] if the big toes are pricked and those drops are brought to the face, or if a virgin touches [them] with her right thumb, concluding from this that virgin flesh should be eaten.
passages.notes: 'exurger e' read as 'exurgere'. The final inference is obscure; the text may be corrupt.

passages.original: sicut totius corporis valetudini in varietate victus inobservata. Hippocrates tradit non prandentium celerius senescere exta ; verum id remediis cecinit, non epulis, quippe multo utilissima est temperantia in cibis. L. Lucullus hanc de se praefecturam servo dederat, ultimoque probro manus in cibis triumphali seni deiciebatur vel in Capitolio epulanti, pudenda re servo suo facilius parere quam sibi.
passages.english: just as, for the health of the whole body, [lies] in variety of diet left unregulated. Hippocrates records that the internal organs of those who do not take a midday meal age faster; but he pronounced this for remedies, not for banquets, since moderation in food is by far the most beneficial thing. Lucius Lucullus had given a slave this supervision over himself, and, to his utter disgrace, the old man who had triumphed had his hand pulled back from the food even when dining on the Capitol, a shameful thing, finding it easier to obey his own slave than himself.
passages.notes: The opening clause is incomplete; the preceding sentence is missing.

passages.original: Sternumenta pinna gravedinem emendant et si quis mulae nares, ut tradunt, osculo attingat, sternumenta et singultum. ad hoc Varro suadet palmam alterna manu scalpere; plerique anulum e sinistra in longissimum dextrae digitum transferre, in aquam ferventem manus mergere. Theophrastus senes laboriosius sternuere dicit.
passages.english: Sneezing brought on with a feather relieves heaviness in the head, and if someone touches a mule's nostrils with a kiss, as they report, [it stops] sneezing and hiccups. For this Varro advises scratching the palm with the other hand; most people [advise] moving a ring from the left hand to the longest finger of the right, [or] plunging the hands into hot water. Theophrastus says that old men sneeze with more difficulty.
passages.notes: The opening sentence is elliptical; 'sternumenta et singultum' presumably depends on an implied verb such as 'stops'.

passages.original: ideo haec in consiliis ducum potestatiumve fieri vetuere maiores velut omnem actum inpedientia, vetuere vero et sacris votisve simili modo interesse; capita autem aperiri aspectu magistratuum non venerationis causa iussere, sed, ut Varro auctor est, valetudinis, quoniam firmiora consuetudine ea fierent.—Cum quid oculo inciderit , alterum conprimi prodest, cum aqua dextrae auriculae , sinistro pede exultari capite in dextrum umerum devexo, invicem e diversa aure;
passages.english: For this reason our ancestors forbade these things to be done at councils of generals or men in authority, as hindering every proceeding; and they forbade [anyone] to attend sacrifices or vows in a similar posture. They ordered heads to be uncovered at the sight of magistrates, not for the sake of veneration but, as Varro is our authority, for the sake of health, since heads would become stronger by the habit. When something has fallen into an eye, it helps to press the other one shut; when water [has got into] the right ear, [it helps] to hop on the left foot with the head tilted toward the right shoulder, and the reverse for the opposite ear;
passages.notes: 'auriculae' read with an implied verb ('has entered'); the sentence is elliptical.

passages.original: si sit odor gravior, ut plerunmque fit longis vitiis, diluto melle lana includitur. et contra regium morbum in oculis relictum instillatur cum elaterio. peculiariter valet potum contra venena, quae data sint e marino lepore, bupresti aut etiam, ut Aristoteles tradit, dorycnio, et contra insaniam , quae facta sit hyoscyami potu. podagris quoque iubent inlini cum cicuta, alii cum oesypo et adipe anserino , qualiter et vulvarum doloribus inponitur. alvum etiam sistit potu, ut Rabirius scribit, et menses ciet.
passages.english: If the smell is rather offensive, as usually happens with long-standing complaints, wool soaked in diluted honey is inserted. And against jaundice that has remained in the eyes it is dropped in with elaterium. It is especially effective when drunk against poisons given from the sea-hare, the buprestis, or even, as Aristotle reports, dorycnium, and against madness caused by drinking henbane. For gout too they prescribe smearing it on with hemlock, others with oesypum and goose fat, in the way it is also applied for pains of the womb. Drunk, it also checks the bowels, as Rabirius writes, and promotes menstruation.
passages.notes: The subject is woman's milk (from context). 'plerunmque' read as 'plerumque'. Oesypum is the grease of unwashed wool.

passages.original: vis eius maxima contra accipitrum genus. detrahere enim supervolantem ad se traditur et voluntarium praebere lacerandum ceteris animalibus. caput eius et guttur, si roboreis lignis accendantur, imbrium et tonitruum concursus facere Democritus narrat, item iocur in tegulis ustum. reliqua ad veneficia pertinentia quae dicit, quamquam falsa existimantes , omittemus, praeterquam ubi inrisu coarguent eum : dextro oculo, si viventi eruatur, albugines oculorum cum lacte caprino tolli, lingua adalligata pericula puerperii;
passages.english: Its power is greatest against the hawk family. For it is said to drag down to itself a hawk flying over it and to offer it up of its own accord to be torn apart by other animals. Democritus relates that its head and throat, if burned on oak wood, produce a gathering of rainstorms and thunder, and likewise its liver burned on roof tiles. The other things he says relating to sorcery we shall omit, though we judge them false, except where they will refute him by [provoking] ridicule: that with the right eye, if it is gouged out of the living animal, white spots of the eyes are removed with goat's milk; that the tongue, tied on [as an amulet], [removes] the dangers of childbirth;
passages.notes: The animal is the chameleon (from context). 'inrisu coarguent eum' is awkward; sense taken as 'they convict him through the laughter they arouse'.

passages.original: tune eaM revocavit in lucem Hippocrates, genitus in insula Coo in primis clara ac valida et Aesculapio dicata. is, cum fuisset mos, liberatos morbis scribere in templo eius dei quid auxiliatum esset, ut postea similitudo proficeret, exscripsisse ea traditur atque, ut Varro apud nos credit, templo cremato iis instituisse medicinam hanc, quae clinice vocatur. nec fruit postea quaestus modus, quoniam Prodicus, Selymbriae natus, e discipulis eius instituit quam vocant iatralipticen et unctoribus quoque medicorum ac mediastinis vectigal invenit.
passages.english: Then Hippocrates recalled it into the light, born on the island of Cos, an island especially famous and powerful and dedicated to Aesculapius. Since it had been the custom for those freed from diseases to write in the temple of that god what had helped them, so that a similar case might later benefit, he is said to have copied these out and, as Varro among us believes, after the temple was burned, to have founded with them this medicine which is called 'clinical'. Nor was there any limit afterwards to the profit, since Prodicus, born at Selymbria, one of his pupils, founded what they call iatraliptice [healing by anointing], and found a source of income even for the anointers and the drudges of the physicians.
passages.notes: 'eaM' read as 'eam' (medicine); 'fruit' read as 'fuit'.

passages.original: Est et formicarum genus venenatum, non fere in Italia. solipugas Cicero appellat, salpugas Baetica. his cor vespertilionis contrarium omnibusque formicis.
passages.english: There is also a venomous kind of ant, hardly found in Italy. Cicero calls them solipugae, Baetica salpugae. The heart of a bat is an antidote to these and to all ants.

passages.original: Alopecias replet fimi pecudum cinis cum oleo cyprio et melle, item ungularum muli vel mulae ex oleo myrteo, praeterea, ut Varro noster tradit, nurinum fimum, quod ille muscerdas appellat, aut muscarum capita recentia prius folio ficulneo asperatas. alii sanguine muscarum utuntur, alii x diebus cinerem earum inlinunt cum cinere chartae vel nucum ita, ut sit tertia portio e muscis;
passages.english: Ash of sheep's dung with Cyprus oil and honey fills out bald patches (alopecia), and likewise [ash] of the hooves of a male or female mule in myrtle oil; furthermore, as our Varro records, mouse dung, which he calls muscerdae, or fresh heads of flies, [applied after the patches have] first been roughened with a fig leaf. Others use the blood of flies, others for ten days smear on their ash with ash of paper or of nuts, so that a third portion is from the flies;
passages.notes: 'nurinum' read as 'murinum'. 'asperatas' refers to the bald patches.

passages.original: senectus serpentium fervente testa usta instillatur rosaceo admixta, contra omnia quidem vitia efficax, sed contra graveolentiam praecipue ac, si purulenta sint, ex aceto, melius cum felle caprino vel bubulo aut testudinis marinae —vetustior anno eadem membrana non prodest, nec imbre perfusa, ut aliqui putant —, aranei sanies cum rosaceo aut per se in lana vel cum croco, gryllus cum sua terra effossus et inlitus. magnam auctoritatem huic animali perhibet Nigidius, maiorem Magi, quoniam retro ambulet terramque terebret, stridat noctibus. venantur eum formica circumligata capillo in cavernam eius coniecta, efflato prius pulvere, ne sese condat; ita formicae conplexu extrahitur.
passages.english: The slough of snakes, burned on a hot potsherd and mixed with rose oil, is dropped [into the ears], effective indeed against all ailments, but especially against foul smell, and, if they are full of pus, [it is given] in vinegar, better with the gall of a goat or ox or sea turtle — this same skin is no use when more than a year old, nor when soaked by rain, as some think —; [also] the juice of a spider with rose oil, or by itself in wool, or with saffron; and a cricket dug up with its earth and smeared on. Nigidius attributes great authority to this creature, the Magi greater, because it walks backwards, bores into the earth, and chirps at night. They hunt it by throwing into its hole an ant tied around with a hair, the dust having first been blown away so that it does not hide itself; thus it is drawn out clinging to the ant.

passages.original: Sine dubio illic orta in Perside a Zoroastre, ut inter auctores convenit. sed unus hic fuerit an postea et alius, non satis constat. Eudoxus, qui inter sapientiae sectas clarissimam utilissimamque eam intellegi voluit, Zoroastren hunc sex milibus annorum ante Platonis mortem fuisse prodidit; sic et Aristoteles. Hermippus, qui de tota ea arte diligentissime scripsit et viciens c milia versuum a Zoroastre condita indicibus quoque voluminum eius positis explanavit, praeceptorem, a quo institutum diceret, tradidit Agonacen, ipsum vero quinque milibus annorum ante Troianum bellum fuisse.
passages.english: Without doubt it arose there, in Persia, from Zoroaster, as the authorities agree. But whether he was the only one, or whether there was also another later, is not sufficiently established. Eudoxus, who wanted it to be understood as the most famous and useful of the schools of wisdom, stated that this Zoroaster lived six thousand years before the death of Plato; so too did Aristotle. Hermippus, who wrote most carefully about that whole art and expounded two million verses composed by Zoroaster, even adding tables of contents of his volumes, reported that the teacher by whom he said he was instructed was Agonaces, and that [Zoroaster] himself lived five thousand years before the Trojan War.
passages.notes: 'It' is magic (the art of the Magi). 'viciens c milia' = 2,000,000 verses.

passages.original: nec postea quisquam dixit, quonam modo venisset Telmesum, religiosissimam urbem, quando transisset ad Thessalas matres, quarum cognomen diu optinuit in nostro orbe, aliena genti Troianis utique temporibus Chironis medicinisn medicis V2R1d. contentae et solo Marte fulminanti. miror equidem Achillis populis famam eius in tantum adhaesisse, ut Menander quoque, litterarum subtilitati sine aemulo genitus, Thessalam cognominaret famulam complexam ambages feminarum detrahentium lunam. Orphea putarem e propinquo artem primum intulisse ad vicina usque superstitionis ac medicinae provectum, si non expers sedes eius tota Thrace magices fuisset.
passages.english: Nor did anyone afterwards say how it had come to Telmessus, a most religious city, or when it passed over to the Thessalian mothers, whose name it long bore in our part of the world, though it was foreign to that people, who at least in Trojan times were content with the medicines of Chiron and with Mars alone as their thunderer. I am indeed amazed that its fame clung so strongly to the people of Achilles that even Menander, born without rival for literary subtlety, called [his play] 'The Thessalian Woman', containing the tricks of women who draw down the moon. I would have thought that Orpheus first brought the art in from nearby, having advanced to the neighbouring [domain] of superstition from medicine, were it not that all Thrace, his homeland, had been without magic.
passages.notes: Text contains an intruded apparatus note ('medicinisn medicis V2R1d.'), omitted; read 'Chironis medicinis contentae'. 'famulam' is likely corrupt for 'fabulam' (play), translated so. 'ad vicina usque superstitionis ac medicinae provectum' is obscure.

passages.original: alii fimum drachma una in lactis caprini vel ovilli vel passi cyathis III ante accessiones; sunt qui totas censeant devorandas. aspidis cutem pondere sexta parte denarii cum piperis pari modo Parthorum gentes in remedium quartanae bibunt. Chrysippus philosophus tradidit phryganion adalligatum remedio esse quartanis. quod esset animal, neque ille descripsit nec nos invenimus qui novisset; demonstrandum tamen fuit a tam gravi auctore dictum, si cuius cura efficacior esset inquirendi. cornicis carnes esse et nidum inlinere in longis morbis utilissimum putant. —Et in tertianis fiat potestas experiendi , quoniam miserias copia spei delectat, anne aranei , quem lycon vocant, tela cum ipso in spleniolo resinae ceraeque inposita utrisque temporibus et fronti prosit, aut ipse calamo adalligatus, qualiter et aliis febribus prodesse traditur, item lacerta viridis adalligata viva in eo vase, quod capiat, quo genere et recidivas frequenter abigi adfirmant.
passages.english: Others [give] the dung, one drachma in three cyathi of goat's or sheep's milk or raisin wine, before the attacks; there are some who think they should be swallowed whole. The Parthian peoples drink the skin of an asp, in the weight of a sixth of a denarius, with an equal amount of pepper, as a remedy for quartan fever. The philosopher Chrysippus reported that the phryganion tied on [as an amulet] is a remedy for quartan fevers. What animal it was he did not describe, nor have we found anyone who knew it; yet it had to be pointed out, since it was said by so weighty an authority, in case anyone's diligence in inquiry should prove more successful. They think that eating the flesh of a crow and smearing on its nest is most useful in long illnesses. In tertian fevers too let there be opportunity of testing, since an abundance of hope comforts the wretched, whether the web of the spider they call lycos, together with the spider itself, applied in a small plaster of resin and wax to both temples and the forehead, helps, or the spider itself tied on in a reed, in which way it is said to help other fevers as well; likewise a green lizard tied on alive in a vessel that holds it, a method by which they assert that relapses too are often driven off.
passages.notes: Phryganion is unidentified, as Pliny himself says.

passages.original: in eadem provincia ophion, cervis tantum pilo similis nec alibi nascens. iidem auctores sirulugum nec quale esset animal nec ubi nasceretur tradiderunt. fuisse quidem non dubito, cum et medicinae ex eo sint demonstratae . M. Cicero tradit animalia biuros vocari, qui vites in Campania erodant.
passages.english: In the same province [there is] the ophion, resembling deer only in its hair and found nowhere else. The same authors reported the sirulugus, but neither what sort of animal it was nor where it was found. That it did exist I do not doubt, since remedies from it have also been recorded. Marcus Cicero records that there are animals called biuri which gnaw the vines in Campania.
passages.notes: The sirulugus and biuri are unidentified.

passages.original: purgat hic corpora, tertianas febres discutit, calculorum vitia. eadem aqua igne admoto turbida fit ac postremo rubescit. Leucogaei fontes inter Puteolos et Neapolim oculis et vulneribus medentur. Cicero in admirandis posuit Reatinis tantum paludibus ungulas iumentorum indurari.
passages.english: This [water] purges the body and dispels tertian fevers and complaints of stones. The same water, when fire is applied, becomes cloudy and finally turns reddish. The Leucogaean springs between Puteoli and Naples heal eyes and wounds. Cicero, in his 'Marvels', recorded that only in the marshes of Reate are the hooves of draught animals hardened.

passages.original: In Boeotia ad Trophonium deum iuxta flumen Hercynnum e duobus fontibus alter memoriam, alter oblivionem adfert, inde nominibus inventis. in Cilicia apud oppidum Cescum rivus fluit Nuus, ex quo bibentium subtiliores sensus fieri M. Varro tradit, at in Cea insula fontem esse, quo hebetes fiant, Zamae in Africa, ex quo canorae voces.— Vinum taedio venire iis, qui ex Clitorio lacu biberint, ait Eudoxus, set Theopompus inebriari fontibus iis, quos diximus, Mucianus Andri e fonte Liberi patris statis diebus septenis eius dei vinum fluere, si auferatur e conspectu templi, sapore in aquam transeunte, Polyclitus Lipari iuxta Solos Ciliciae ungui, Theophrastus hoc idem in Aethiopia eiusdem nominis fonte, Lycos in Indis Oratis fontem esse, cuius aqua lucernae luceant;
passages.english: In Boeotia at [the shrine of] the god Trophonius, near the river Hercynnus, of two springs one brings memory, the other forgetfulness, and their names were found from this. In Cilicia near the town of Cescum flows a stream, the Nuus, from which the senses of those who drink become sharper, as Marcus Varro records, but [he says] that on the island of Cea there is a spring by which men become dull, and at Zama in Africa one from which voices become melodious. Eudoxus says that those who have drunk from the Clitorian lake come to loathe wine, and Theopompus that they become drunk from the springs we have mentioned; Mucianus [says] that on Andros, from the spring of Father Liber, on fixed days, seven [in number], the wine of that god flows, [but] if it is carried out of sight of the temple, the taste turns into water; Polyclitus [says] that at Liparis near Soli in Cilicia people anoint themselves [from a spring], Theophrastus [says] the same of a spring of the same name in Ethiopia; Lycos [says] that among the Indian Oratae there is a spring with whose water lamps burn;
passages.notes: 'set' read as 'sed'. 'Oratis' identification uncertain.

passages.original: quod et circa Danuvii exortum audivi, done veniatur ad fontem alveo adpositum, ubi finitur id genus piscium, ideoque ibi caput amnis eius intellegit fama. hoc idem et in Lydia in stagno Nympharum tradunt. in Arcadia ad Pheneum aqua profluit e saxis Styx appellata, quae ilico necat, ut diximus, sed esse pisces parvos in ea tradit Theophrastus, letales et ipsos, quod non in alio genere mortiferorum fontium. necare aquas Theopompus et in Thracia apud Cichros dicit, Lycos in Leontinis tertio die quam quis biberit, Varro ad Soracten in fonte, cuius sit latitudo quattuor pedum; sole oriente eum exundare ferventi similem; aves, quae degustaverint, iuxta mortuas iacere.
passages.english: This I have heard also concerning the source of the Danube: until one comes to a spring beside the channel, where that kind of fish ends, and therefore report understands that to be the head of that river. They record the same also in Lydia, in the pool of the Nymphs. In Arcadia near Pheneus a water called the Styx flows from the rocks, which kills at once, as we have said, but Theophrastus records that there are small fish in it, themselves also deadly, which is not [the case] in any other kind of deadly spring. Theopompus says that waters kill also in Thrace near the Cichri; Lycos [says] at Leontini [they kill] on the third day after one has drunk; Varro [mentions] near Soracte a spring four feet wide; that at sunrise it overflows like something boiling, and birds that have tasted it lie dead beside it.
passages.notes: 'done' read as 'donec'. The opening refers to a context lost before this passage (fish found in a river's waters).

passages.original: illi quidem et lignum referre arbitrantur. quercus optima, ut quae per se cinere sincero vim salis reddat, alibi corylus laudatur. ita infuso liquore salso arbor etiam in salem vertitur. quicumque ligno confit sal niger est. Apud Theophrastum invenio Umbros harundinis et iunci cinerem decoquere aqua solitos, done exiguum superesset umoris. quin et e muria salsamentorum recoquitur iterumque consumpto liquore ad naturam suam redit, vulgo e menis iucundissimus.
passages.english: They think indeed that the kind of wood also matters. Oak is best, since by itself its pure ash yields the quality of salt; elsewhere hazel is praised. Thus when salty liquid is poured on, even the wood turns into salt. All salt made with wood is black. In Theophrastus I find that the Umbrians used to boil down the ash of reeds and rushes in water until only a little moisture remained. Moreover, salt is also boiled again from the brine of salted fish, and when the liquid is used up again it returns to its own nature; that from the mena-fish is commonly the most pleasant.
passages.notes: 'done' read as 'donec'; 'menis' = mena, a small fish.

passages.original: Mihi videntur mira et quae Ovidius prodidit piscium ingenia in eo volumine, quod halieuticon inscribitur : scarum inclusum nassis non fronte erumpere nec infestis viminibus caput inserere, sed aversum caudae ictibus crebris laxare fores atque ita retrorsum repere, quem luctatum eius si forte alius scarus extrinsecus videat, adprehensa mordicus cauda adiuvare nisus erumpentis;
passages.english: To me the instincts of fish that Ovid recorded in the volume entitled Halieuticon also seem remarkable: that the parrot-wrasse, when shut in a wicker trap, does not break out head first or thrust its head between the hostile osiers, but turning round loosens the door with repeated blows of its tail and so creeps out backwards; and that if another parrot-wrasse happens to see its struggle from outside, it seizes the tail in its teeth and helps the efforts of the one breaking out;
passages.notes: scarus is usually taken as the parrot-wrasse or parrotfish; the identification is not certain.

passages.original: Ranarum marinarum ex vino et aceto decoctarum sucus contra venena bibitur, et contra ranae rubetae venenum et contra salamandras vel e fluviatilibus; si carnes edantur iusve decoctarum sorbeatur, prosunt et contra leporem marinum et contra serpentes supra dictos, contra scorpiones ex vino. Democritus quidem tradit, si quis extrahat ranae viventi linguam, nulla alia corporis parte adhaerente, ipsaque dimissa in aquam inponat supra cordis palpitationem mulieri dormienti, quaecumque interrogaverit , vera responsuram.
passages.english: The juice of sea-frogs boiled down in wine and vinegar is drunk against poisons, both against the poison of the bramble-toad and against salamanders, or [the juice] of river frogs [may be used]; if their flesh is eaten or the broth of them boiled is sipped, they are also beneficial against the sea-hare and against the serpents mentioned above, and against scorpions [when taken] in wine. Democritus indeed records that if someone pulls the tongue out of a living frog, with no other part of the body adhering to it, and after letting the frog go back into the water, places [the tongue] over the beating of the heart of a sleeping woman, she will answer truthfully whatever he asks.
passages.notes: 'vel e fluviatilibus' is elliptical; it may mean that river frogs serve as well.

passages.original: Omnium piscium fluviatilium marinorumque adipes liquefacti sole admixto melle oculorum claritati plurimum conferunt, item castoreum cum melle. callionymi fel cicatrices sanat et carnes oculorum supervacuas consumit . nulli hoc piscium copiosius, ut existumavit Menander quoque in comoediis. idem piscis et uranoscopos vocatur ab oculo, quem in capite habet. et coracini fel excitat visum, et marini scorpionis rufi cum oleo vetere aut melle Attico incipientes suffusiones discutit;
passages.english: The fats of all river and sea fish, melted in the sun and mixed with honey, contribute greatly to clearness of the eyes, as does castoreum with honey. The gall of the callionymus heals scars and eats away superfluous flesh of the eyes. No fish has this [gall] in greater quantity, as Menander too supposed in his comedies. The same fish is also called uranoscopos ['sky-gazer'] from the eye which it has on [the top of] its head. The gall of the coracinus also stimulates the sight, and that of the red sea-scorpion, with old oil or Attic honey, disperses incipient cataracts;

passages.original: ii quoque, qui ob legationem acceperant aureos, in publico tantum utebantur iis, intra domos vero ferreis, quo argumento etiam nunc sponsae muneris vice ferreus anulus mittitur, isque sine gemma. equidem nec Iliacis temporibus ullos fuisse anulos video. nusquam certe Homerus dicit, cum et codicillos missitatos epistularum gratia indicet et conditas arcis vestes ac vasa aurea argenteaque et eas colligatas nodi, non anuli, nota. sortiri quoque contra provocationes duces non anulis tradit, fabricae etiam deum fibulas et alia muliebris cultus, sicut inaures, in primordio factitasse, sine mentione anulorum.
passages.english: Those too who had received gold [rings] for an embassy used them only in public, but at home iron ones; for which reason even now an iron ring is sent to a betrothed woman as a gift, and that without a gem. For my part I do not see that there were any rings even in the Trojan times. Homer certainly never mentions them, though he shows that tablets were sent for the purpose of letters, and that clothes and gold and silver vessels were stored in chests and tied up with the mark of a knot, not of a ring. He also records that the leaders drew lots in response to challenges not with rings, and that the god of the forge in the beginning made brooches and other articles of women's adornment, such as earrings, without mention of rings.

passages.original: iam alii pondera eorum ostentant. aliis plures quam unum gestare labor est, alii bratteas infercire leviore materia propter casum tutius gemmarum sollicitudini putant, alii sub gemmis venena cludunt, sicut Demosthenes summus Graeciae orator, anulosque mortis gratia habent. denique vel plurima opum scelera anulis fiunt. quae fuit illa vita priscorum , qualis innocentia, in qua nihil signabatur! nunc cibi quoque ac potus anulo vindicantur a rapina.
passages.english: Now others show off their weight. For others it is a burden to wear more than one; others think it safer, given the anxiety over gems, to stuff the gold leaf with lighter material in case they fall; others shut poisons under their gems, as did Demosthenes, the greatest orator of Greece, and keep rings for the sake of death. In short, even the greatest crimes of wealth are committed with rings. What a life that was of the ancients, what innocence, in which nothing was sealed! Now even food and drink are protected from theft by a ring.
passages.notes: 'bratteas infercire leviore materia propter casum tutius' is difficult; sense may be that hollow gold settings are filled with lighter material, thought safer against loss/dropping.

passages.original: iam Midas et Croesus inrinitum possederant, iam Cyrus devicta Asia pondo XXIIII invenerat praeter vasa aurumque factum et in eo solium, platanum, vitem. qua victoria argenti D??? talentorum reportavit et craterem Semiramidis, cuius pondus xv talentorum colligebat. talentum Aegyptium pondo LXXX patere M. Varro tradit. iam regnaverat in Colchis Saulaces Aeetae subolis, qui terram virginem nactus plurimum auri argentique eruisse dicitur in Suanorum gente, et alioqui velleribus aureis incluto regno. et illius aureae camarae, argenteae trabes et columnae atque parastaticae narrantur victae Sesostri, Aegypti regi tam superbo , ut prodatur annis quibusque sorte reges singulos e subiectis iungere ad currum solitus atque ita triumphare!
passages.english: Already Midas and Croesus had possessed boundless [gold]; already Cyrus, having conquered Asia, had found 24,000 pounds besides vessels and wrought gold, and in it a throne, a plane tree, and a vine. By that victory he carried off 500,000 talents of silver and the mixing bowl of Semiramis, whose weight amounted to 15 talents. Marcus Varro records that the Egyptian talent amounts to 80 pounds. Already Saulaces, a descendant of Aeetes, had reigned in Colchis, who, having come upon virgin earth, is said to have dug up very much gold and silver in the territory of the Suani, a kingdom otherwise famous for golden fleeces. And his golden vaults, and silver beams, columns and pilasters, are said [to have been seized when he was] conquered by Sesostris, king of Egypt, a man so arrogant that it is related that every year he used to yoke to his chariot kings chosen by lot from among his subjects, one at a time, and so celebrate his triumph!
passages.notes: 'inrinitum' read as 'infinitum'. The silver figure is garbled ('D???'); probably 500,000. 'XXIIII' likely 24,000 pounds (thousands implied). The yoking of kings 'singulos' is somewhat unclear.
