passages.original: super cetera non robigo ulla, non aerugo, non aliud ex ipso, quod consumat bonitatem minuatve pondus. iam contra salis et aceti sucos, domitores rerum, constantia superat omnia, superque netur ac texitur lanae modo vel sine lana. tunica aurea triumphasse Tarquinium Priscum Verrius docet; nos vidimus Agrippinam Claudi principis, edente eo navalis proelii spectaculum, adsidentem et indutam paludamento aureo textili sine alia materia. Attalicis vero iam pridem intexitur , invento regum Asiae.
passages.english: Beyond everything else, [gold has] no rust, no verdigris, nothing else coming from itself that consumes its goodness or lessens its weight. Further, against the juices of salt and vinegar, the conquerors of things, it surpasses all things in steadfastness, and moreover it is spun and woven like wool, or without wool. Verrius teaches that Tarquinius Priscus celebrated a triumph in a golden tunic; we have seen Agrippina, [wife] of the emperor Claudius, when he was presenting the spectacle of a naval battle, sitting beside him dressed in a military cloak woven of gold without any other material. Into Attalic [fabrics] it has long been woven, an invention of the kings of Asia.

passages.original: ubicumque quinta argenti portio est, electrum vocatur. scobes hae reperiuntur in canaliensi. fit et cura electrum argento addito. quod si quintam portionem excessit, incudibus non resistit. vetusta et electro auctoritas Homero teste, qui Menelai regiam auro, electro, argento, ebore fulgere tradit. Minervae templum habet Lindos insulae Rhodiorum, in quo Helena sacravit calicem ex electro; adicit historia, mammae suae mensura.
passages.english: Wherever the proportion of silver is one fifth, it is called electrum. These grains are found in the canaliensis [gold]. Electrum is also made artificially by adding silver. If it exceeds a fifth part, it does not withstand the anvil. Electrum too has ancient prestige, as Homer witnesses, who records that the palace of Menelaus gleamed with gold, electrum, silver and ivory. Lindos, in the island of the Rhodians, has a temple of Minerva in which Helen dedicated a cup of electrum; the story adds [that it was made] to the measure of her breast.
passages.notes: canaliensi presumably refers to 'channel' gold mentioned earlier in the book.

passages.original: Auctoritatem colori fuisse non miror. iam enim Troianis temporibus rubrica in honore erat Homero teste, qui naves ea commendat, alias circa pigmenta picturasque rarus. milton vocant Graeci miniumque cinnabarim . unde natus error inscitia nominum. sic enim appellant illi saniem draconis elisi elephantorum morientium pondere permixto utriusque animalis sanguine, ut diximus, neque est alius colos, qui in pictura proprie sanguinem reddat.
passages.english: I am not surprised that the colour was held in esteem. For already in Trojan times red ochre was in honour, as Homer witnesses, who commends ships for it, though otherwise sparing [in mentioning] pigments and paintings. The Greeks call it milton, and minium [they call] cinnabaris. Hence an error was born from ignorance of the names. For they give this name to the gore of a dragon crushed by the weight of dying elephants, the blood of both animals being mixed, as we have said, and there is no other colour that properly renders blood in painting.

passages.original: Isidorus testamento suo edixit, quamvis multa bello civili perdidisset, tamen relinquere servorum IIII CXVI, iuga boum III DC, reliqui pecoris CCLVII, in numerato HS |DC|, funerari se iussit HS |X|. congerant excedentes numerum opes, quota tamen portio erunt Ptotemaei, quem Varro tradit Pompeio res gerente circa Iudaeam octona milia equitum sua pecunia toleravisse, mille convivas totidem aureis potoriis, mutantem ea vasa cum ferculis, saginasse ! quota vero ille ipse—neque enim de regibus loquor—portio fuerit Pythis Bithyni, qui platanum auream vitemque nobiles illas Dario regi donavit, Xerxis copias, hoc est |VII|LXXXVIII hominum, excepit epulo, stipendium quinque mensum frumentumque pollicitus, ut e quinque liberis in dilectu senectuti suae unus saltem concederetur!
passages.english: [...Gaius Caecilius Isidorus, freedman of Gaius,] declared in his will that, although he had lost much in the civil war, he nevertheless was leaving 4,116 slaves, 3,600 yoke of oxen, 257,000 other cattle, and 60,000,000 sesterces in cash, and he ordered that 1,000,000 sesterces be spent on his funeral. Let them heap up riches beyond counting, yet what fraction will they be of Ptolemy, who, as Varro records, when Pompey was campaigning around Judaea, maintained eight thousand cavalry at his own expense, and feasted a thousand guests with as many gold drinking cups, changing those vessels with each course! And what fraction, in turn, would he himself have been (for I am not speaking of kings) of Pythis the Bithynian, who gave King Darius that famous golden plane tree and vine, and entertained the forces of Xerxes, that is 788,000 men, at a banquet, promising five months' pay and grain, on condition that of his five sons at least one should be granted, at the levy, to his old age!
passages.notes: The numerals with bars (|DC|, |X|, |VII|) are read as multiplied by 100,000; 'reliqui pecoris CCLVII' is taken as 257,000 per the usual understanding of the figure. 'Ptotemaei' is a scanning error for Ptolemaei; this Ptolemy is not further identified. 'Pythis' is the Pythius of Herodotus.

passages.original: item Mercurium, qui fuit Lysimacheae, Herculem, qui Romae, hagetera arma sumentem, Artemona, qui periphoretos appellatus est. hic consummasse hanc scientiam iudicatur et toreuticen sic erudisse, ut Phidias aperuisse. proprium eius est, uno crure ut insisterent signa, excogitasse , quadrata tamen esse ea ait Varro et paene ad exemplum.
passages.english: Likewise a Mercury, which was at Lysimachea; a Hercules, which is at Rome; a *hageter* [leader] taking up arms; and an Artemon, who was called *periphoretos* ["the one carried around"]. He is judged to have brought this science to perfection and to have refined the art of metal-chasing (*toreutice*) just as Phidias opened it up. It is his own particular invention that statues should stand with their weight on one leg; yet Varro says they are square-built and almost all to one pattern.
passages.notes: The sculptor is Polyclitus (from preceding context). 'hagetera arma sumentem' is uncertain; possibly a corrupt reading.

passages.original: Eutychides Eurotam, in quo artem ipso amne liquidiorem plurimi dixere.—Hegiae Minerva Pyrrhusque rex laudatur et celetizontes pueri et Castor ac Pollux ante aedem Iovis Tonantis, Hagesiae in Pario colonia Hercules, Isidoti buthytes.—Lycius Myronis discipulus fuit, qui fecit dignum praeceptore puerum sufflantem languidos ignes et Argonautas; Leochares aquilam sentientem, quid rapiat in Ganymede et cui ferat, parcentemque unguibus etiam per vestem puero, Autolycum pancratii victorem, propter quem Xenophon symposium scripsit, Iovemque ilium Tonantem in Capitolio ante cuncta laudabilem, item Apollinem dia-o dematum, Lyciscum mangonem, puerum subdolae ac fucatae vernilitatis, Lycius et ipsepuerum suffitorem.—Menaechmi vitulus genu premitur replicata cervice.
passages.english: Eutychides [made] the Eurotas, in which very many have said the art was more liquid than the river itself. Of Hegias are praised a Minerva and King Pyrrhus, and the boys riding racehorses (celetizontes), and Castor and Pollux before the temple of Jupiter the Thunderer; of Hagesias, a Hercules in the colony of Parium; of Isidotus, a buthytes [sacrificer of an ox]. Lycius was a pupil of Myron, who made, worthy of his teacher, a boy blowing on a dying fire, and the Argonauts; Leochares [made] the eagle that is aware what it is snatching in Ganymede and to whom it is carrying him, and sparing the boy with its talons even through his clothing; Autolycus, victor in the pancratium, on account of whom Xenophon wrote the Symposium; and that Jupiter the Thunderer on the Capitol, praiseworthy above all; likewise an Apollo wearing a diadem; Lyciscus the slave-dealer, a boy with the sly and deceitful air of a home-born slave. Lycius too himself [made] a boy burning incense. Of Menaechmus, a calf pressed down by a knee, with its neck bent back.
passages.notes: 'dia-o dematum' read as diadematum. Some names (Hegias/Hagesias, Isidotus) are uncertain in the text.

passages.original: Non est praetereundum et novicium inventum, siquidem non ex auro argentove, at certe ex aere in bibliothecis dicantur illis, quorum inmortales animae in locis iisdem locuntur, quin immo etiam quae non sunt finguntur, pariuntque desideria non traditos vultus, sicut in Homero evenit. quo mains, ut equidem arbitror, nullum est felicitatis specimen quam semper omnes scire cupere, qualis fuerit aliquis. Asini Pollionis hoc Romae inventum, qui primus bibliothecam dicando ingenia hominum rem publica m fecit.
passages.english: A new invention too must not be passed over: that [portraits], if not of gold or silver, at least of bronze, are dedicated in libraries to those whose immortal spirits speak in those same places; indeed even those that do not exist are fashioned, and longing gives birth to faces not handed down, as has happened with Homer. No greater proof of good fortune, as I at least think, exists than that everyone should always desire to know what someone was like. At Rome this was the invention of Asinius Pollio, who, by dedicating the first library, made men's talents public property.
passages.notes: 'mains' is a scan error for maius; 'rem publica m' for rem publicam.

passages.original: ante hanc aedem Tuscanica omnia in aedibus fuisse auctor est Varro, et ex hac, cum reficeretur, crustas parietum excisas tabulis marginatis inclusas esse, item signa ex fastigiis dispersa. fecit et Chalcosthenes cruda opera Athenis, qui locus ab officina eius Ceramicos appellatur. M. Varro tradit sibi cognitum Romae Possim nomine, a quo facta poma et uvas nemo posset aspectu discernere a veris. idem magnificat Arcesilaum, L. Luculli familiarem, cuius proplasmata pluris venire solita artificibus ipsis quam aliorum opera;
passages.english: Varro states that before this temple everything in temples was Tuscan [work], and that from this one, when it was being restored, the plaster facings of the walls were cut out and enclosed in framed panels, and likewise the statues from the pediments were dispersed. Chalcosthenes too made works of unfired clay at Athens, and the place is called the Ceramicus after his workshop. Marcus Varro records that he knew at Rome a man named Possis, by whom fruit and grapes were made which no one could tell by sight from real ones. He also extols Arcesilaus, an intimate of Lucius Lucullus, whose clay models used to sell for more, to artists themselves, than the finished works of others;

passages.original: inhonorus est nec in templo ullo Hercules, ad quem Poeni omnibus annis humana sacrificaverant victima, humi stans ante aditum porticus ad nationes. sitae fuere et Thespiades ad aedem Felicitatis, quarum unam amavit eques 1 Romanus lunius Pisciculus, ut tradit Varro, admirator et Pasitelis, qui et quinque volumina scripsit nobilium operum in toto orbe. natus hic in Graeca Italiae ora et civitate Romana donatus cum iis oppidis, Iovem fecit eboreum in Metelli aede, qua campus petitur.
passages.english: Without honour, and in no temple, is the Hercules to whom the Carthaginians used to offer human victims every year; he stands on the ground before the entrance of the Portico of the Nations. The Thespiades too were placed at the temple of Felicitas; one of them was loved by a Roman knight, Junius Pisciculus, as Varro records—Varro being also an admirer of Pasiteles, who also wrote five volumes on famous works throughout the world. This man, born on the Greek coast of Italy and granted Roman citizenship along with those towns, made the ivory Jupiter in the temple of Metellus, on the way to the Campus.
passages.notes: The stray '1' before Romanus is a footnote mark; 'lunius' read as Iunius. Whose admirer 'admirator' refers to (Varro or Pisciculus) is ambiguous.

passages.original: columnis demum utebantur in templis, nec lautitiae causa—nondum enim ista intellegebantur—, sed quia firmiores aliter statui non poterant. sic est inchoatum Athenis templum Iovis Olympii, ex quo Sulla Capitolinis aedibus advexerat columnas. fuit tamen inter lapidem atque marmor differentia iam et apud Homerum; dicit enim marmoreo saxo percussum, sed hactenus, regias quoque domus, cum lautissime, praeter aes, aurum, electrum, argentum ebore tantum adornans. primum, ut arbitror, versicolores istas maculas Chiorum lapicidinae ostenderunt, cum exstruerent muros, faceto in id M.
passages.english: They used columns at length in temples, not for the sake of luxury, for such things were not yet understood, but because stronger ones could not be set up otherwise. Thus was begun at Athens the temple of Olympian Jupiter, from which Sulla had brought columns for the Capitoline temple. Yet there was already a distinction between stone and marble even in Homer; for he speaks of [a man] struck with a marble rock, but only so far, and even when adorning royal palaces most lavishly, [he adorns them] besides bronze, gold, electrum and silver only with ivory. The first, as I think, to display these multicoloured spots were the quarries of the Chians, when they were building their walls, at which M.
passages.notes: Sentence continues into context: Cicero's witticism.

passages.original: Primum Romae parietes crusta marmoris operuisse totos domus suae in Caelio monte Cornelius Nepos tradit Mamurram, Formiis natum equitem Romanum, praefectum fabrum C. Caesaris in Gallia, ne quid indignitati desit, tali auctore inventa re. hic namque est Mamurra Catulli Veroniensis carminibus proscissus, quem, ut res est, domus ipsius clarius quam Catullus dixit habere quidquid habuisset Comata Gallia. namque adicit idem Nepos primum totis aedibus nullam nisi e marmore columnam habuisse et omnes solidas e Carystio aut Luniensi. M. Lepidus Q. Catuli in consulatu conlega primus omnium limina ex Numidico marmore in domo posuit magna reprensione.
passages.english: Cornelius Nepos records that the first at Rome to cover the whole walls of his house on the Caelian hill with a veneer of marble was Mamurra, born at Formiae, a Roman knight, prefect of engineers to Gaius Caesar in Gaul, so that nothing might be lacking to the indignity, the thing having been invented by such an author. For this is the Mamurra torn to pieces in the poems of Catullus of Verona, whom, as is the fact, his own house declared more clearly than Catullus did to possess whatever long-haired Gaul had possessed. For the same Nepos adds that he was the first to have in his whole house no column except of marble, and all of them solid, of Carystian or Luna marble. Marcus Lepidus, colleague of Quintus Catulus in the consulship, was the first of all to place thresholds of Numidian marble in his house, to great censure.

passages.original: Dicamus et labyrinthos, vel portentosissimum humani inpendii opus, sed non, ut existimari potest, falsum . durat etiam nunc in Aegypto in Heracleopolite nomo qui primus factus est ante annos, ut tradunt, III DC a Petesuchi rege sive Tithoe, quamquam Herodotus totum opus XII regum esse dicit novissimique Psammetichi. causas faciendi varie interpretantur, Demoteles regiam Moteridis fuisse, Lyceas sepulchrum Moeridis, plures Soli sacrum id exstructum, quod maxime creditur. hinc utique sumpsisse Daedalum exemplar eius labyrinthi, quem fecit in Creta, non est dubium, sed centensimam tantum portionem eius imitatum, quae itinerum ambages occursusque ac recursus inexplicabiles continet, non—ut in pavimentis puerorumve ludicris campestribus videmus—brevi lacinia milia passuum plura ambulationis continentem, sed crebris foribus inditis ad fallendos occursus redeundumque in errores eosdem.
passages.english: Let us speak also of labyrinths, the most monstrous work of human expenditure, but not, as might be supposed, a fiction. There still survives even now in Egypt, in the Heracleopolite nome, the one which was made first, 3,600 years ago, as they report, by King Petesuchis or Tithoes, although Herodotus says that the whole work belongs to the twelve kings and to the last of them, Psammetichus. The reasons for building it are variously explained: Demoteles [says] that it was the palace of Moteris, Lyceas the tomb of Moeris, most [say] that it was built as a shrine sacred to the Sun, which is the most widely believed. At any rate there is no doubt that Daedalus took from here the model for the labyrinth which he made in Crete, but that he imitated only a hundredth part of it, the part which contains windings of paths and encounters and returns that cannot be unravelled; not, as we see on pavements or in boys' games in the fields, [a pattern] containing several miles of walking within a small strip, but with many doors set in to mislead the encounters and to lead back into the same wanderings.
passages.notes: 'Ut tradunt, III DC': the numeral is taken as 3,600 years. 'Moteridis' and 'Moeridis' are probably variant forms of the same king's name (Moeris). The phrase 'ad fallendos occursus' is obscure; rendered literally.

passages.original: Palmati circa Mundam in Hispania, ubi Caesar dictator Pompeium vicit, reperiuntur idque quotiens fregeris. sunt et nigri, quorum auctoritas venit in marmora, sicut Taenarius . Varro nigros ex Africa firmiores esse tradit quam in Italia, e diverso albos Coranos duriores quam Parios, idem Luniensem silicem serra secari, Tusculanum dissilire igni, Sabinum fuscum addito oleo etiam lucere. idem molas versatiles Volsinis inventas;
passages.english: Palm-marked stones are found near Munda in Spain, where Caesar the dictator defeated Pompey, and [the pattern appears] however often you break one. There are also black ones, whose prestige has reached the level of marbles, such as the Taenarian. Varro records that black stones from Africa are stronger than those in Italy, and conversely that the white stones of Cora are harder than the Parian; he also says that Luna flint is cut with a saw, that Tusculan splits apart in fire, and that dark Sabine stone even shines when oil is added. He also [says] that rotary mills were invented at Volsinii;
passages.notes: The subject is a stone ('silex'), likely lava or flint; 'Palmati' are stones bearing a palm-like pattern.

passages.original: appellantur quidem ita erosa saxa in aedificiis, quae musaea vocant, dependentia ad imaginem specus arte reddendam , sed ii pumices, qui sunt in usu corporum levandorum feminis, iam quidem et viris, atque, ut ait Catullus, libris, laudatissimi sunt in Melo, Nisyro et Aeoliis insulis. probatio in candore minimoque pondere et ut quam maxime spongiosi aridique sint, teri faciles nec harenosi in fricando. vis eorum in medicina extenuare , siccare, trina ustione ita, uti torreantur carbone puro, totiens vino restinguantur albo.
passages.english: The name is indeed given to the eaten-away rocks in buildings which they call *musaea* [grottoes], hanging down so as to reproduce by art the likeness of a cave; but those pumice-stones which are used by women for smoothing the body, and by now indeed by men too, and, as Catullus says, for books, are most highly praised from Melos, Nisyros and the Aeolian islands. The test lies in whiteness and very little weight, and in their being as spongy and dry as possible, easy to grind and not gritty in rubbing. Their power in medicine is to reduce and to dry, by a threefold burning, done so that they are roasted on pure charcoal and quenched as many times in white wine.

passages.original: Gemmas plures primus omnium Romae habuit— quod peregrino appellant nomine dactyliothecam—privignus Sullae Scaurus, diuque nulla alia fuit, done Pompeius Magnus eam, quae Mithridatis regis fuerat, inter dona in Capitolio dicaret, ut Varro aliique aetatis eius auctores confirmant, multum praelata Scauri. hoc exemplo Caesar dictator sex dactyliothecas in aede Veneris Genetricis consecravit, Marcellus Octavia genitus unam in aede Palatini Apollinis.
passages.english: The first person at Rome to own a number of gems—which they call by a foreign name, a *dactyliotheca* [gem cabinet]—was Scaurus, Sulla's stepson, and for a long time there was no other, until Pompey the Great dedicated on the Capitol, among his gifts, the one which had belonged to King Mithridates, as Varro and other authors of that age confirm; it far surpassed that of Scaurus. Following this example Caesar the dictator consecrated six gem cabinets in the temple of Venus Genetrix, and Marcellus, son of Octavia, one in the temple of Palatine Apollo.
passages.notes: 'done' read as donec.

passages.original: Phaethontis fulmine icti sorores luctu mutatas in arbores populos lacrimis electrum omnibus annis fundere iuxta Eridanum amnem, quem Padum vocavimus, electrum appellatum, quoniam sol vocitatus sit Elector, plurimi poëtae dixere primique, ut arbitror, Aeschylus, Philoxenus, Euripides , Nicander, Satyrus. quod esse falsum Italiae testimonio patet. diligentiores eorum Electridas insulas in mari. Hadriatico esse dixerunt, ad quas delaberetur Pado. qua appellatione nullas umquam ibi fuisse certum est, nec vero ullas ita positas esse, in quas quidquam cursu Padi devehi posset. nam quod Aeschylus in Hiberia [hoc est in Hispania] Eridanum esse dixit eundemque appellari Rhodanum, Euripides rursus et Apollonius in Hadriatico litore confluere Rhodanum et Padum, faciliorem veniam facit ignorati sucini tanta ignorantia orbis. modestiores, sed aeque falsum, prodidere in extremis Hadriatici sinus inviis rupibus arbores stare, quae canis ortu hanc effunderent cummim. Theophrastus effodi in Liguria dixit, Chares vero Phaëthontem in Aethiopia ῞ἅμμωνος νήσῳ obisse, ibi et delubrum eius esse atque oraculum electrumque gigni. Philemon fossile esse et in Scythia erui duobus locis, candidum atque cerei coloris quod vocaretur electrum, in alio fulvum quod appellaretur sualiternicum.
passages.english: That the sisters of Phaethon, who was struck by a thunderbolt, were changed by grief into poplar trees and every year pour out amber with their tears beside the river Eridanus, which we have called the Po, and that it was called *electrum* because the sun was called Elector, very many poets have said, and first, as I think, Aeschylus, Philoxenus, Euripides, Nicander, Satyrus. That this is false is evident from the testimony of Italy. The more careful of them said that the Electrid islands were in the Adriatic Sea, to which it was carried down by the Po. It is certain that no islands of that name have ever been there, nor indeed are there any so situated that anything could be carried to them by the current of the Po. For when Aeschylus said that the Eridanus was in Iberia [that is, in Spain] and that the same river was called the Rhone, and Euripides again and Apollonius [said] that the Rhone and the Po flow together on the Adriatic shore, such great ignorance of the world makes it easier to pardon ignorance of amber. More moderate [writers], but equally falsely, have reported that at the far end of the Adriatic gulf, on pathless cliffs, there stand trees which at the rising of the Dog Star pour out this gum. Theophrastus said it is dug up in Liguria; Chares, however, that Phaethon died in Ethiopia on the island of Ammon, and that his shrine and oracle are there, and that amber is produced there. Philemon [said] that it is a mineral and is dug up in Scythia in two places: in one white and wax-coloured, which was called *electrum*; in the other tawny, which was called *sualiternicum*.
passages.notes: The Greek phrase is garbled in the scan ('῞ἅμμωνος νήσῳ'); read as Ἄμμωνος νήσῳ, 'on the island of Ammon'. 'Hoc est in Hispania' is bracketed in the edition, probably as a gloss.

passages.original: Ab his Aethiopici laudantur ab Copto dierum itinere, ut auctor est luba, xxv, acriter virides, sed non facile puri aut concolores. Democritus in hoc genere ponit Thermiaeos et Persicos, illos intumescentes pinguiter, Persicos vero non tralucidos, sed iucundi tenoris visum inplere, quem non admittant, felium pantherarumque oculis similes, namque et illos radiare nec perspici, eosdem in sole hebetari, in umbra refulgere et longius quam ceteros nitere.
passages.english: After these, the Ethiopian [emeralds] are praised, from a place twenty-five days' journey from Coptos, as Juba reports; they are sharply green, but not easily [found] clear or of uniform colour. Democritus places in this class the Thermiaean and the Persian: the former swelling out with a rich, oily look; the Persian, however, not transparent, but filling the sight with a pleasing evenness which they do not let pass through, like the eyes of cats and panthers; for these too gleam and cannot be seen through, and they are dulled in the sun, shine out in the shade, and glitter at a greater distance than the rest.
passages.notes: 'luba' is a scanning error for 'Iuba' (Juba). 'Thermiaeos' is unidentified; perhaps a corruption of a place name.

passages.original: Inseritur smaragdis et quae vocatur tanos e Persis veniens gemma, ingrate viridis atque intus sordida, itidem chalcosmaragdos e Cypro, turbida aereis venis. Theophrastus tradit in Aegyptiorum commentariis reperiri regi eorum a rege Babylonio muneri missum smaragdum quattuor cubitorum longitudine ac trium latitudine , et fuisse apud eos in lovis delubro obeliscum e quattuor smaragdis quadraginta cubitorum longitudine, latitudine vero in parte quattuor, in parte duorum, se autem scribente esse in Tyro Herculis templo stelen amplam e smaragdo, nisi potius pseudosmaragdus sit, nam et hoc genus reperiri, et in Cypro inventum ex dimidia parte smaragdum, ex dimidia iaspidem, nondum umore in totum transfigurato.
passages.english: Among emeralds is also included the gem called *tanos*, coming from Persia, of an unpleasant green and dirty inside; likewise the *chalcosmaragdos* from Cyprus, clouded with copper-coloured veins. Theophrastus reports that it is found in the records of the Egyptians that an emerald four cubits long and three wide was sent as a gift to their king by the king of Babylon, and that there was among them, in the shrine of Jupiter, an obelisk of four emeralds, forty cubits long, and in width four [cubits] in one part and two in another; and that at the time he was writing there was in Tyre, in the temple of Hercules, a large pillar of emerald, unless it is rather a false emerald, for this kind too is found; and that in Cyprus [a stone] was found half emerald, half jasper, the moisture not yet having been wholly transformed.
passages.notes: 'lovis' is a scanning error for 'Iovis' (Jupiter, i.e. Ammon/Amun in Egypt).

passages.original: inveniuntur et circa Leucada Epiri et in Aegypto quae brattea aurea sublinuntur. et in his autem mares excitatius fulgent, feminae pigriores et crassius nitent. nec fuit alia gemma apud antiquos usu frequentior —hac certe apud Menandrum et Philemonem fabulae superbiunt—, nec ullae tralucentium tardius subfusae umore hebetantur, oleoque magis quam alio liquore. damnantur ex iis melleae ac validius testaceae.
passages.english: They are found also around Leucas in Epirus and in Egypt, [stones] which are backed with gold foil. Among these too the males shine more vividly, the females are more sluggish and gleam more dully. Nor was any other gem more often used among the ancients — certainly the plays of Menander and Philemon pride themselves on this one — nor are any of the transparent stones more slowly dulled when steeped in moisture, and by oil more than by any other liquid. Of these, the honey-coloured ones and those strongly of an earthenware colour are rejected.
passages.notes: The stone discussed is named in the preceding text (apparently the sard/carnelian).

passages.original: hanc putant contra dolores nervorum prodesse habentibus.— Aromatitis et ipsa in Arabia invenitur, sed et in Aegypto circa Philas, ubique lapidosa et murrae coloris et odoris, ob hoc reginis frequentata. —Asbestos in Arcadiae montibus nascitur coloris ferrei.—Aspisatim Democritus in Arabia nasci tradit, ignei coloris, et oportere cum cameli fimo splenicis adalligari, inveniri utique in nido Arabicarum alitum; et aliam eodem nomine ibi in Leucopetra nasci, argentei coloris, radiantem; cum.....
passages.english: They think that this is helpful to those who wear it against pains of the sinews. — Aromatitis too is found in Arabia, but also in Egypt around Philae, everywhere stony, with the colour and smell of myrrh, and for this reason much used by queens. — Asbestos occurs in the mountains of Arcadia, iron-coloured. — Democritus reports that aspisatis occurs in Arabia, of a fiery colour, and that it should be tied on to those with spleen disease together with camel dung, and that it is found in particular in the nest of Arabian birds; and that another of the same name occurs there at Leucopetra, of a silver colour, radiant; with.....
passages.notes: The text breaks off with a lacuna marked in the edition ('cum.....'); the following context resumes 'against frenzy for those who wear it'.

passages.original: Balanitae duo genera sunt, subviridis et Corinthii aeris similitudine, illa a Copto, haec ab Trogodytica veniens, medias secante flammea vena.—Batrachitas quoque Coptos mittit, unam ranae similem colore, alteram et venis, tertiam rubetis e nigro.—Baptes, mollis alioqui, odore excellit.—Beli oculus albicans pupillam cingit nigram e medio aureo colore fulgentem et propter speciem sacratissimo Assyriorum deo dicatam. Belum autem aliam, quam sic vocant, in Arbelis nasci Democritus tradit nucis iuglandis magnitudine, vitrea specie. —Baroptenus sive baripe, nigra sanguineis et albis nodis, adalligata proicitur veluti portentosa.—Botryitis alia nigra est, alia pampinea, incipienti uvae similis.—Bostrychitin Zoroastres crinibus mulierum similiorem vocat.—Bucardia, bubulo cordi similis, Babylone tantum nascitur.—Brontea , capiti testudinum, e tonitribus cadit, ut putant, restinguitque fulmine icta, si credimus.—Boloe in Hibero inveniuntur, glaebae similitudine.
passages.english: Of balanitis there are two kinds, one greenish and the other resembling Corinthian bronze, the former coming from Coptos, the latter from the Trogodytic region, with a flame-coloured vein cutting through the middle.—Coptos also sends batrachitae: one like a frog in colour, another also in its veins, a third reddish on black.—Baptes, though soft, excels in scent.—The 'Eye of Belus' is whitish and encircles a black pupil shining with a golden colour from its centre, and because of its appearance it is dedicated to the most sacred god of the Assyrians. Democritus records that another [stone], which they call Belus, grows at Arbela, the size of a walnut, glassy in appearance.—Baroptenus or baripe, black with blood-red and white knots, is thrown away when tied on [as an amulet], as if portentous.—Of botryitis, one kind is black, another vine-leaf coloured, resembling a grape beginning to form.—Zoroaster calls bostrychitis rather like women's hair.—Bucardia, like an ox heart, grows only at Babylon.—Brontea, [like] the head of a tortoise, falls with thunder, so they believe, and extinguishes [the effects in things] struck by lightning, if we are to believe it.—Boloe are found in the Hiberus, resembling a clod of earth.
passages.notes: 'adalligata proicitur' is obscure; possibly 'is rejected for use as an amulet'. 'restinguitque fulmine icta' is elliptical. 'capiti testudinum' implies 'similis'.

passages.original: Daphnean Zoroastres morbis comitialibus demonstrat .—Diadochos berullo similis est.—Diphyes duplex, candida ac nigra, mas ac femina, genitale utriusque , sexus distinguente linea.—Dionysias, nigra ac dura, mixtis rubentibus maculis, ex aqua trita saporem vini facit et ebrietati resistere putatur.
passages.english: Zoroaster points to daphnea [as a remedy] for epilepsy.—Diadochos resembles beryl.—Diphyes is double, white and black, male and female, with a line marking off the genitals of each sex.—Dionysias, black and hard, with red spots mixed in, produces the taste of wine when ground in water and is thought to counteract drunkenness.

passages.original: Encardia cognominatur enariste, in nigro colore effigie cordis eminente; altera eodem nomine viridi colore cordis speciem, tertia nigrum cor ostendit, reliqua sui parte candida.—Enorchis candida est divisisque fragmentis testium effigiem repraesentat.—Exhebenum Zoroastres speciosam et candidam tradit, qua aurifices aurum poliant. —Erythallis, cum sit candida, ad inclinationes rubescere videtur.—Erotylos sive amphicomos sive hieromnemon Democrito laudatur in argumentis divinationum.—Eumeces in Bactris nascitur, silici similis , et capiti supposita visa nocturna oraculi modo reddit.
passages.english: Encardia is surnamed enariste, with the image of a heart standing out on a black ground; another of the same name shows the appearance of a heart in a green colour; a third shows a black heart, the rest of it being white.—Enorchis is white, and when divided into fragments represents the image of testicles.—Zoroaster describes exhebenus as handsome and white; goldsmiths polish gold with it.—Erythallis, though white, appears to redden when tilted.—Erotylos, also called amphicomos or hieromnemon, is praised by Democritus in his works on divination.—Eumeces grows in Bactria, resembling flint, and placed under the head it gives night visions after the manner of an oracle.
passages.notes: 'enariste' is an uncertain reading.

passages.original: Zathenen in Media nasci Democritus tradit electri colore et, si quis terat in vino palmeo et croco cerae modo lentescere odore magnae suavitatis.—Zamilampis in Euphrate nascitur, Proconnesio marmori similis, medio colore glauco.—Zoraniscaeos in Indo flumine Magorum gemma narratur, neque aliud amplius de ea.
passages.english: Democritus reports that zathene occurs in Media, of the colour of amber, and that if one grinds it in palm wine and saffron it becomes soft like wax, with a smell of great sweetness. — Zamilampis occurs in the Euphrates, similar to Proconnesian marble, with a grey-green colour in the middle. — Zoraniscaeos is said to be a gem of the Magi found in the river Indus, and nothing more [is told] about it.
